arxiv_record.abstract:
The robustness of neural network classifiers is important in the
safety-critical domain and can be quantified by robustness verification. At
present, efficient and scalable verification techniques are always sound but
incomplete, and thus, the improvement of verified robustness results is the key
criterion to evaluate the performance of incomplete verification approaches.
The multi-variate function MaxPool is widely adopted yet challenging to verify.
In this paper, we present Ti-Lin, a robustness verifier for MaxPool-based CNNs
with Tight Linear Approximation. Following the sequel of minimizing the
over-approximation zone of the non-linear function of CNNs, we are the first to
propose the provably neuron-wise tightest linear bounds for the MaxPool
function. By our proposed linear bounds, we can certify larger robustness
results for CNNs. We evaluate the effectiveness of Ti-Lin on different
verification frameworks with open-sourced benchmarks, including LeNet,
PointNet, and networks trained on the MNIST, CIFAR-10, Tiny ImageNet and
ModelNet40 datasets. Experimental results show that Ti-Lin significantly
outperforms the state-of-the-art methods across all networks with up to 78.6%
improvement in terms of the certified accuracy with almost the same time
consumption as the fastest tool. Our code is available at
https://github.com/xiaoyuanpigo/Ti-Lin-Hybrid-Lin.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion shift from tightening general CNN verification through both S-shaped and MaxPool bounds to a MaxPool-focused contribution. The first neuron-wise-tightest MaxPool claim persists, while integration across backsubstitution, multi-neuron, and branch-and-bound frameworks becomes central. The separate S-shaped superiority contribution is withdrawn.

C2.justification: v1's discussion of Newise's advantage on non-negative networks is removed. v2 explains the conditional advantages and complementarity of MaxLin and Ti-Lin, attributes transformation overhead to deeper MaxPool2ReLU networks, and discusses framework-dependent runtime differences. Table 3 additionally warns that model-format conversion affects robustness and prevents direct accuracy comparisons across tables.

D1.justification: v2 adds per-network sources, node counts, property counts, and perturbation radii in Table 4, plus integration and model-conversion information. It provides a different Ti-Lin-Hybrid-Lin repository link and changes reported hardware from 8 cores/15 GB RAM to 48 cores/125 GB. Conversely, v1's explicit software versions and model-training recipe are no longer supplied.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates image classification on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Tiny ImageNet. v2 retains these datasets and adds ModelNet40 point-cloud classification using PointNets (Tables 1 and 4), substantially extending the represented data and application domain.

E2.justification: DeepCert, VeriNet, and Newise evaluations disappear. v2 adds evaluated comparisons with 3DCertify, MN-BaB, ERAN, α, β-CROWN, MaxLin, and MaxPool2ReLU. DeepPoly is removed from the CNN-Cert radius comparison but retained in separate accuracy comparisons. Appendix 7.5.2 clarifies that MaxPool2ReLU substitutes for unavailable OSIP code; OSIP itself was not evaluated.

E3.justification: v2's main evaluation uses fixed-radius certified accuracy on correctly classified properties selected from the first 100 inputs, versus v1's average bounds on 10 random images. It adds PGD reference bounds, timeout rates, and verifier-specific protocols. The retained 10-input CNN-Cert experiment changes its stated initial search radius from 0.05 to 0.005. The general 180-second timeout statement conflicts with the 3,600-second BaB setting.

E4.justification: v2 adds output-bound comparisons across 100 inputs, a MaxLin-versus-Ti-Lin trajectory over BaB rounds, and Hybrid-Lin comparisons under CROWN and α-CROWN (Appendix 7.5.3–7.5.4, Figures 3–6). These new analyses investigate when neuron-wise bounds help and how the two bounding approaches complement each other; they are absent from v1.

E5.justification: v1 Section 4.6 and Table 10 report Wilcoxon/Mann–Whitney testing at significance level 0.05 with dataset-specific comparator p-values. v2 removes this statistical validation without replacement significance tests or confidence intervals. Neither version documents repeated-run or seed-based uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: S-shaped comparison tables disappear, while certified-accuracy, PointNet, timeout, and Hybrid-Lin results are added. For the four-layer CIFAR-10 CNN under l1 perturbation, v1 Table 8 reports Ti-Lin's bound as 0.07137, whereas v2 Table 5 reports 0.03029 under revised settings. New Table 3 reports 85.7% versus 7.1% accuracy against α, β-CROWN on CIFAR-10's six-layer CNN: a 78.6 percentage-point gap, not a cross-version gain.

M1.justification: v2 removes v1's dedicated S-shaped activation bounding construction and introduces Hybrid-Lin, which selects Ti-Lin or MaxLin according to the ReLU bound form (Appendix 7.5.4). The underlying MaxPool coefficients are largely retained through reorganized cases, while selecting the three largest upper bounds replaces sorting all interval endpoints.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, methodological narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work moves before preliminaries, research-question-based experiments become verifier-family-based sections, and the standalone threats-to-validity section disappears. The appendix is reorganized into numbered proofs, experimental settings, and additional analyses.

P2.justification: The original S-shaped illustration and network-propagation diagram are replaced by MaxPool geometry and four-case illustrations. v2 adds four analytical figures and restructures tables around certified accuracy, runtime, timeouts, and verifier families. CNN-Cert results are consolidated into appendix Table 5; the notation and p-value tables disappear. Headers, typography, and table styling also change substantially.

R1.justification: The activation-by-activation positioning is replaced by a broader discussion of MaxPool verification, attacks, and certified defenses. New substantive comparisons address OSIP, MN-BaB, modern CROWN frameworks, and especially MaxLin's block-wise tightness. Previously described as unsuitable for image perturbations, 3DCertify becomes a central comparator for both image and point-cloud evaluations.

T1.justification: v1's S-shaped bounds theorem and proof, standalone ReLU theorem, and layer-wise/network-wise formal treatment are removed. v2 retains the central MaxPool midpoint and diagonal-endpoint arguments, but expands case-coverage reasoning in Appendix 7.1 and adds explicit computational-complexity analysis. The theoretical scope changes substantially despite preservation of the core MaxPool guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the retained MaxPool contribution beyond v1's single-framework evaluation. Public image and point-cloud benchmarks across several verifier families, detailed experimental settings, and analyses explaining Ti-Lin/MaxLin complementarity address important gaps in generality and mechanism evidence. The narrower contribution and removal of significance testing are tradeoffs; conflicting timeout descriptions and OSIP claims based on a substitute remain weaknesses. Nevertheless, the broader controlled validation and substantive explanatory analyses provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Ti-Lin and share the central MaxPool bounding construction, despite substantial changes in title and scope. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original verification experiments across multiple frameworks and four datasets, including new PointNet evaluations and appendix analyses of Hybrid-Lin.

before.justification: v1 reports original certified robustness bounds, runtimes, and statistical comparisons on CNNs evaluated using MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Tiny ImageNet.

arxiv_record.abstract:
We develop a method that recovers the surface, materials, and illumination of
a scene from its posed multi-view images. In contrast to prior work, it does
not require any additional data and can handle glossy objects or bright
lighting. It is a progressive inverse rendering approach, which consists of
three stages. In the first stage, we reconstruct the scene radiance and signed
distance function (SDF) with a novel regularization strategy for specular
reflections. We propose to explain a pixel color using both surface and volume
rendering jointly, which allows for handling complex view-dependent lighting
effects for surface reconstruction. In the second stage, we distill light
visibility and indirect illumination from the learned SDF and radiance field
using learnable mapping functions. Finally, we design a method for estimating
the ratio of incoming direct light reflected in a specular manner and use it to
reconstruct the materials and direct illumination. Experimental results
demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the current state-of-the-art
in recovering surfaces, materials, and lighting without relying on any
additional data.

Yue Fan, Ningjing Fan, Ivan Skorokhodov, Oleg Voynov, Savva Ignatyev,

C1.justification: v2 explicitly limits its stated research scope to implicit representations, distinguishing the contribution from Gaussian-splatting approaches. The central claims of image-only, three-stage glossy-object reconstruction and superior geometry/material reconstruction remain. Its stronger emphasis on joint surface and volume rendering describes a component already present in v1.

C2.justification: v2 proposes model complexity and training instability as explanations for specular-albedo-related lighting degradation, clarifies that Stage 1 colors are not a physical BRDF, and discusses Fresnel-versus-texture tradeoffs. Appendix G explains limited DTU97 gains through the small proportion of glossy regions, replacing v1's broader smooth-surface restriction while retaining fine-detail limitations.

D1.justification: Appendices B and E newly disclose grayscale Stage 1 specular radiance, NeRF++ background modeling, the default Fresnel value, the Glossy loss weight, and 32 visibility-sampling directions. Architecture, schedules, hardware, and training-time information largely remain. Conversely, v1's explicit image resolutions and several view/train/test counts are omitted.

E1.justification: v2 adds the 13-scene Glossy benchmark, covering real and synthetic reflective objects, and extends DTU evaluation from four glossy scenes to 15 scenes including regular objects. Figure 22 additionally evaluates relighting under changed illumination. The original four datasets remain represented.

E2.justification: NeRO is added to existing geometry comparisons and IndiSG material comparisons. Ref-NeuS, previously only discussed, is evaluated in Figure 7. Figures 9 and 25 introduce UniSDF and Ref-NeRF/S3-NeRF-based architectural comparisons. Original principal baselines remain; Figure 18's inconsistent replacement labels do not establish additional material-baseline evaluations.

E3.justification: Added controlled experiments introduce auxiliary SfM point-cloud/image-pair supervision and a Fresnel comparison of 0.02 versus 0.75, alongside an indirect-illumination removal condition. The retained evaluations preserve Chamfer distance, foreground PSNR, and the reported 300K/40K training budgets. Newly disclosed default settings are distinguished from these experimental interventions.

E4.justification: v2 adds indirect-light removal tests, auxiliary-supervision comparisons, rendering-architecture alternatives, and Fresnel sensitivity analysis (Table 3, Table 7, Figures 9 and 24–26). Figure 13 extends surface-reconstruction ablations to additional objects. The original specular-albedo, visibility, and surface-component ablations remain, including relocated or renamed presentations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Reported means aggregate scene results rather than repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: Many quantitative and qualitative results are added, while matched entries from v1 Tables 2–4 remain unchanged in v2 Tables 1, 3, and 4. New results include a 15-scene DTU mean Chamfer distance of 0.76 versus NeuS's 0.83, and a Glossy mean of 0.0044 versus NeRO's 0.0033. Additional results document indirect-light, supervision, architecture, and Fresnel effects.

M1.justification: The core three-stage pipeline and principal losses remain. Appendix F.2 adds an evaluated adaptation incorporating Geo-NeuS point-cloud and image-pair supervision. Stage 3 also describes the BRDF as Ward rather than Disney; the PDFs do not establish whether this reflects an implementation change or a corrected description.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work are substantially condensed and revised. Preliminaries, implementation details, detailed training equations, Stage 2 explanations, and limitations move into organized appendices, while the main method and experimental narrative are restructured. Ablation terminology and author/header information also change.

P2.justification: The opening figures are merged, the pipeline diagram gains Stage 2, existing comparison grids are split or relocated, and numerous new figures and tables are introduced. Table ordering, highlighting, and page layout change extensively. Some edits introduce errors: Figure 3's caption reverses dataset sides, and Figure 18 assigns inconsistent method labels to retained material panels.

R1.justification: v2 substantially updates the research context through discussion of Gaussian-splatting reconstruction and inverse rendering, explicitly motivating continued work on implicit representations. It adds NeRO, UniSDF, S3-NeRF, Ward, and other references with substantive connections to the method and comparisons. The earlier capabilities survey table is removed.

T1.justification: Appendix E, Equation 27, newly specifies the visibility–Spherical Gaussian approximation through illumination-weighted visibility scaling of the lobe amplitude, previously left implicit in the product notation. Most earlier rendering and loss equations are retained or relocated. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central glossy-reconstruction claims through relevant reflective-object baselines, the Glossy benchmark, regular DTU scenes, and targeted component and sensitivity tests. The new evidence also exposes a boundary: NeRO performs better on Glossy overall. These gains address important comparison and generalization gaps in v1 and outweigh the loss of some dataset details and newly introduced figure-label/reference errors, although those errors reduce clarity and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Factored-NeuS and contain readable text, equations, tables, and figures. The shared methods and experiments can be matched despite extensive reorganization. v1 has no separate appendix; v2 includes Appendices A–G, which were included in the comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix F retain original experiments and add Glossy evaluations, broader DTU results, additional baseline comparisons, and controlled ablations.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original reconstruction and inverse-rendering experiments on DTU, SK3D, Shiny, and IndiSG, including quantitative results and component ablations.

arxiv_record.abstract: Readout multiplexing is a promising solution to overcome hardware limitations and data bottlenecks in imaging with single-photon detectors. Conventional multiplexed readout processing creates an upper bound on photon counts at a very fine time scale, where frames with multiple detected photons must either be discarded or allowed to introduce significant bias. We formulate multiphoton coincidence resolution as an inverse imaging problem and introduce a solution framework to probabilistically resolve the spatial locations of photon incidences. Specifically, we develop a theoretical abstraction of row--column multiplexing and a model of photon events that make readouts ambiguous. Using this, we propose a novel estimator that spatially resolves up to four coincident photons. Monte Carlo simulations show that our proposed method increases the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of reconstruction by 3 to 4 dB compared to conventional methods under optimal incident flux conditions. Additionally, this method reduces the required number of readout frames to achieve the same mean-squared error as other methods by a factor of ~4. Finally, our method matches the Cramer--Rao bound for detection probability estimation for a wider range of incident flux values compared to conventional methods. While demonstrated for a specific detector type and readout architecture, this method can be extended to more general multiplexing with different detector models.

Finally, our solution matches the Cramer-Rao bound for detection probability estimation for a wider range of incident flux values compared to conventional methods. While demonstrated for a specific detector type and readout architecture, this method can be extended to more general multiplexing with different detector models.

arxiv_record.abstract: Neural fields have become widely used in various fields, from shape representation to neural rendering, and for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). With the advent of hybrid neural field representations like Instant NGP that leverage small MLPs and explicit representations, these models train quickly and can fit large scenes. Yet in many applications like rendering and simulation, hybrid neural fields can cause noticeable and unreasonable artifacts. This is because they do not yield accurate spatial derivatives needed for these downstream applications. In this work, we propose two ways to circumvent these challenges. Our first approach is a post hoc operator that uses local polynomial fitting to obtain more accurate derivatives from pre-trained hybrid neural fields. Additionally, we also propose a self-supervised fine-tuning approach that refines the hybrid neural field to yield accurate derivatives directly while preserving the initial signal. We show applications of our method to rendering, collision simulation, and solving PDEs. We observe that using our approach yields more accurate derivatives, reducing artifacts and leading to more accurate simulations in downstream applications.

arxiv_record.abstract:
To enable machines to understand the way humans interact with the physical
world in daily life, 3D interaction signals should be captured in natural
settings, allowing people to engage with multiple objects in a range of
sequential and casual manipulations. To achieve this goal, we introduce our
ParaHome system designed to capture dynamic 3D movements of humans and objects
within a common home environment. Our system features a multi-view setup with
70 synchronized RGB cameras, along with wearable motion capture devices
including an IMU-based body suit and hand motion capture gloves. By leveraging
the ParaHome system, we collect a new human-object interaction dataset,
including 486 minutes of sequences across 207 captures with 38 participants,
offering advancements with three key aspects: (1) capturing body motion and
dexterous hand manipulation motion alongside multiple objects within a
contextual home environment; (2) encompassing sequential and concurrent
manipulations paired with text descriptions; and (3) including articulated
objects with multiple parts represented by 3D parameterized models. We present
detailed design justifications for our system, and perform key generative
modeling experiments to demonstrate the potential of our dataset.
arxiv_record.authors: Jeonghwan Kim, Jisoo Kim, Jeonghyeon Na, Hanbyul Joo

ParaHome: Parameterizing Everyday Home Activities Towards 3D Generative
  Modeling of Human-Object Interactions

arxiv_record.abstract:
Large kernels make standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs) great again
over transformer architectures in various vision tasks. Nonetheless, recent
studies meticulously designed around increasing kernel size have shown
diminishing returns or stagnation in performance. Thus, the hidden factors of
large kernel convolution that affect model performance remain unexplored. In
this paper, we reveal that the key hidden factors of large kernels can be
summarized as two separate components: extracting features at a certain
granularity and fusing features by multiple pathways. To this end, we leverage
the multi-path long-distance sparse dependency relationship to enhance feature
utilization via the proposed Shiftwise (SW) convolution operator with a pure
CNN architecture. In a wide range of vision tasks such as classification,
segmentation, and detection, SW surpasses state-of-the-art transformers and CNN

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes hardware-friendly sparse large-kernel replacement, computational savings, and ImageNet superiority. v2 reframes the contribution around separating feature-extraction granularity from multi-path dependency modeling, explicitly claims successful replacement with 3×3 convolutions, and broadens its superiority claims to classification, segmentation, and detection.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting shuffled paths to feature utilization, reparameterization effects to sparsity initialization, and pruning patterns to stage transitions. Appendices A–E explicitly acknowledge slower throughput than optimized competitors, an unoptimized operator, unresolved hyperparameter interactions, and resource-limited scaling. These substantially qualify v1's emphasis on efficiency and future optimization.

D1.justification: v2 adds extensive training disclosures covering optimizer, learning rate, augmentation, batch size, pruning settings, architecture dimensions, and eight 4090D GPUs (Table 8). Appendices A–B document inference precision, software versions, and the atomicAdd-based implementation. The repository link is retained. Unlike v1's throughput caption, v2 does not specify the inference batch size.

E1.justification: ImageNet-1K classification is retained. v2 additionally evaluates COCO object detection and instance segmentation, ADE20K semantic segmentation, and nuScenes monocular 3D detection (Section 4, Tables 4–6). These substantially extend the tasks and represented domains.

E2.justification: The ImageNet comparison adds FastViT, PVTv2, CoAtNet, DeiT III, SwinV2, HorNet, and ConvNeXt-S, while removing Swin-T, CSwin-T, and InternImage-T from that comparison (Table 3 in both versions). v2 also separately compares standard, reparameterized, and optimized SLaK implementations in its throughput evaluation.

E3.justification: Both versions use 120- and 300-epoch ImageNet experiments, but v2 changes the default padding from N−1 to N//2 and adds explicitly retuned final training configurations and small-model evaluations. New downstream protocols use Cascade Mask R-CNN for 36 epochs, UPerNet for 160,000 iterations, and FCOS3D with a 1x schedule.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's padding/reparameterization experiments and first-layer pruning analysis, v2 tests kernel granularity, shuffled paths, branch counts, mask synchronization, depth versus width, SE, ghost channels, and sparsity (Tables 1, 2, 9). It also adds feature-utilization analysis, pruning profiles across layers, COCO case studies, and effective-receptive-field comparisons.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for performance. v2's pruning distributions characterize trained model structure rather than estimate experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: The 81.36% and 81.26% padding results are retained, but v2 adds 300-epoch SW-tiny/small accuracies of 83.4%/83.9%, downstream results, and numerous ablation findings. SW-small ties UniRepLKNet-S on ImageNet and trails it on COCO and ADE20K. v1's single-operator timings disappear, while v2 reports full-model throughput. These are largely new results under revised conditions, not same-setting gains.

M1.justification: v1 already includes shifting, coarse pruning, ghost channels, and reparameterization. v2 introduces multiple shuffled feature-fusion paths and altered sparsity initialization/mask-sharing procedures. Its final architecture uses 3×3 instead of 5×5 kernels, incorporates SE, deepens the tiny backbone, and replaces the stride-4 stem with two stride-2 convolutions (Sections 3.5–3.9).

P1.justification: The title changes from Shift-ConvNets to ShiftwiseConv, and the abstract, introduction, related work, method exposition, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The original method/theory organization becomes a nine-part architecture-development narrative, followed by separate results and analysis sections and Appendices A–F.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column presentation. Background schematics are removed, retained module concepts are redrawn, and tables are substantially reorganized. New displays include the retinal analogy, feature-utilization plots, pruning profiles, downstream comparisons, training configurations, COCO predictions, and receptive-field visualizations.

R1.justification: The literature discussion is substantially refocused: many earlier multiscale, segmentation, and deformable-kernel references disappear, while PeLK, ShiftViT, receptive-field research, retinal organization, and new evaluation methods are added. v2 develops a substantive contrast between its data-driven connections and PeLK's manually designed peripheral structure, emphasizing granularity and connectivity over hardware compatibility.

T1.justification: v1's generalized focus-length/focus-width operator definition and Equation 3 are removed, alongside the explicit cost-ratio derivations and approximation assumptions in Section 3.4. v2 retains basic decomposition reasoning and tabulated cost expressions, and adds relations such as R(1−G)=1 and the 2E+1 movement bound, but substantially reduces the original formal treatment.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's validation and reproducibility: it directly tests major design choices, demonstrates transfer beyond ImageNet, supplies detailed training settings, and candidly documents throughput and scaling limitations. arxiv_record.abstract:
Recent advances in text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models have significantly
improved the quality of generated images. However, providing efficient control
over individual subjects, particularly the attributes characterizing them,
remains a key challenge. While existing methods have introduced mechanisms to
modulate attribute expression, they typically provide either detailed,
object-specific localization of such a modification or full-scale fine-grained,
nuanced control of attributes. No current approach offers both simultaneously,
resulting in a gap when trying to achieve precise continuous and
subject-specific attribute modulation in image generation. In this work, we
demonstrate that token-level directions exist within commonly used CLIP text
embeddings that enable fine-grained, subject-specific control of high-level
attributes in T2I models. We introduce two methods to identify these
directions: a simple, optimization-free technique and a learning-based approach
that utilizes the T2I model to characterize semantic concepts more
specifically. Our methods allow the augmentation of the prompt text input,
enabling fine-grained control over multiple attributes of individual subjects
simultaneously, without requiring any modifications to the diffusion model
itself. This approach offers a unified solution that fills the gap between
global and localized control, providing competitive flexibility and precision
in text-guided image generation. Project page:
https://compvis.github.io/attribute-control. Code is available at
https://github.com/CompVis/attribute-control.

C2.justification: V2 adds specific qualifications about persistent color and animal-attribute leakage, rare success with spatial relations, and possible benefits of nonlinear modulations. Appendix A.2 explains leakage through inherited model behavior and attention interactions. V1 already discussed inherited limitations and global correlations, so these refine an existing interpretation.

V1's single-image delta-training recipe and explicit own-code availability statement are removed. Shared settings such as 1,000 training steps, batch size 10, and optimizer hyperparameters remain unchanged.

V1 instead used real photographs for its now-removed single-image semantic-delta learning experiments. Human, vehicle, furniture, and most noun-transfer and compositional coverage remain.

V1 primarily compared its own variants quantitatively and demonstrated competitors qualitatively. Appendix A.1 also adds direct-guidance and noise-direction approximation alternatives; v1's capability table does not constitute equivalent evaluated comparisons.

New protocols include clipped bounding-box specificity ratios, normalized change slopes, 20-by-20 attribute-coverage grids, and measured runtime. PixArt-α/T5 and SDXL Turbo introduce additional model settings; SD1.5 and aMUSEd transfer already appeared in v1.

E4.justification: V2 adds ablations of scale variation, direct CLIP embeddings, direct guidance, and noise-direction averaging, plus challenging-attribute and embedding-perturbation analyses. It removes the single-image learning/transfer case study and two age–makeup composition grids. Most noun-transfer, multi-subject, and continuous-modulation appendix analyses are retained and reorganized.

E5.justification: V2 adds an explicitly documented statistical density analysis: Figure 6 and Appendix B.3 use 20 samples per scale, matched generation seeds, and Gaussian kernel density estimation with Scott's rule. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty across repeated training runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and A add substantial numerical results, including standalone specificity of 3.35 and runtime of 12.0 seconds, and normalized LPIPS of 0.31 for the no-scale ablation versus 0.10 for the full method. V1's DINOv2 curves and several qualitative results disappear. These are added or replaced evaluations, not established same-setting improvements over v1.

V2 also permits positive-versus-neutral contrasts and adds AdapEdit and ReNoise integration procedures. The two underlying direction-identification approaches remain.

Experiments are reorganized around specificity, disentanglement, continuity, and generalization; appendices are restructured into additional results, implementation details, and visualization documentation.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main layout, replaces the capability table with quantitative comparisons, adds diagrams and evaluation plots, and merges earlier figures. Most appendix grids are retained but repacked, captions are revised, and unmodified-image highlighting changes from orange to green.

It adds discussion and citations for methods such as AdapEdit, MasaCtrl, ReNoise, and newer token-embedding studies, while removing the personalization discussion and references to Textual Inversion, DreamBooth, and Custom Diffusion.

Its identity-change and normalized-disentanglement definitions also change the evaluation formulation. Neither version develops theorems or proofs; much of the remaining mathematical rewriting is notation or explanation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central control claims: quantitative competitor and runtime comparisons replace reliance on largely qualitative competitive demonstrations, while new ablations, explicit failure cases, and detailed evaluation recipes improve validation and reproducibility. arxiv_record.abstract:
In this paper, we present GyroDeblurNet, a novel single-image deblurring
method that utilizes a gyro sensor to resolve the ill-posedness of image
deblurring. The gyro sensor provides valuable information about camera motion
that can improve deblurring quality. However, exploiting real-world gyro data
is challenging due to errors from various sources. To handle these errors,
GyroDeblurNet is equipped with two novel neural network blocks: a gyro
refinement block and a gyro deblurring block. The gyro refinement block refines
the erroneous gyro data using the blur information from the input image. The
gyro deblurring block removes blur from the input image using the refined gyro
data and further compensates for gyro error by leveraging the blur information
from the input image. For training a neural network with erroneous gyro data,
we propose a training strategy based on the curriculum learning. We also
introduce a novel gyro data embedding scheme to represent real-world intricate
camera shakes. Finally, we present both synthetic and real-world datasets for
training and evaluating gyro-based single image deblurring. Our experiments
demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art deblurring quality by
effectively utilizing erroneous gyro data.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Customized text-to-image generation, which synthesizes images based on
user-specified concepts, has made significant progress in handling individual
concepts. However, when extended to multiple concepts, existing methods often
struggle with properly integrating different models and avoiding the unintended
blending of characteristics from distinct concepts. In this paper, we propose
MC$^2$, a novel approach for multi-concept customization that enhances
flexibility and fidelity through inference-time optimization. MC$^2$ enables
the integration of multiple single-concept models with heterogeneous
architectures. By adaptively refining attention weights between visual and
textual tokens, our method ensures that image regions accurately correspond to
their associated concepts while minimizing interference between concepts.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that MC$^2$ outperforms training-based
methods in terms of prompt-reference alignment. Furthermore, MC$^2$ can be
seamlessly applied to text-to-image generation, providing robust compositional
capabilities. To facilitate the evaluation of multi-concept customization, we
also introduce a new benchmark, MC++. The code will be publicly available at
https://github.com/JIANGJiaXiu/MC-2.

  Pei, Fan Li, Wangmeng Zuo

arxiv_record.abstract:
We propose PyTorchGeoNodes, a differentiable module for reconstructing 3D
objects and their parameters from images using interpretable shape programs.
Unlike traditional CAD model retrieval, shape programs allow reasoning about
semantic parameters, editing, and a low memory footprint. Despite their
potential, shape programs for 3D scene understanding have been largely
overlooked. Our key contribution is enabling gradient-based optimization by
parsing shape programs, or more precisely procedural models designed in
Blender, into efficient PyTorch code. While there are many possible
applications of our PyTochGeoNodes, we show that a combination of
PyTorchGeoNodes with genetic algorithm is a method of choice to optimize both
discrete and continuous shape program parameters for 3D reconstruction and
understanding of 3D object parameters. Our modular framework can be further
integrated with other reconstruction algorithms, and we demonstrate one such
integration to enable procedural Gaussian splatting. Our experiments on the
ScanNet dataset show that our method achieves accurate reconstructions while
enabling, until now, unseen level of 3D scene understanding.

  Friedrich Fraundorfer

arxiv_record.abstract:
Image editing has advanced significantly with the introduction of
text-conditioned diffusion models. Despite this progress, seamlessly adding
objects to images based on textual instructions without requiring user-provided
input masks remains a challenge. We address this by leveraging the insight that
removing objects (Inpaint) is significantly simpler than its inverse process of
adding them (Paint), attributed to inpainting models that benefit from
segmentation mask guidance. Capitalizing on this realization, by implementing
an automated and extensive pipeline, we curate a filtered large-scale image
dataset containing pairs of images and their corresponding object-removed
versions. Using these pairs, we train a diffusion model to inverse the
inpainting process, effectively adding objects into images. Unlike other
editing datasets, ours features natural target images instead of synthetic ones
while ensuring source-target consistency by construction. Additionally, we
utilize a large Vision-Language Model to provide detailed descriptions of the
removed objects and a Large Language Model to convert these descriptions into
diverse, natural-language instructions. Our quantitative and qualitative
results show that the trained model surpasses existing models in both object
addition and general editing tasks. Visit our project page for the released
dataset and trained models at https://rotsteinnoam.github.io/Paint-by-Inpaint.
arxiv_record.authors: Navve Wasserman, Noam Rotstein, Roy Ganz, Ron Kimmel
arxiv_record.title: Paint by Inpaint: Learning to Add Image Objects by Removing Them First

native_poster_event.abstract: Image editing has advanced significantly with the introduction of text-conditioned diffusion models. Despite this progress, seamlessly adding objects to images based on textual instructions without requiring user-provided input masks remains a challenge. We address this by leveraging the insight that removing objects (Inpaint) is significantly simpler than its inverse process of adding them (Paint), attributed to the utilization of segmentation mask datasets alongside inpainting models that inpaint within these masks. Capitalizing on this realization, by implementing an automated and extensive pipeline, we curate a filtered large-scale image dataset containing pairs of images and their corresponding object-removed versions. Using these pairs, we train a diffusion model to inverse the inpainting process, effectively adding objects into images. Unlike other editing datasets, ours features natural target images instead of synthetic ones; moreover, it maintains consistency between source and target by construction. Additionally, we utilize a large Vision-Language Model to provide detailed descriptions of the removed objects and a Large Language Model to convert these descriptions into diverse, natural-language instructions. Our quantitative and qualitative results show that the trained model surpasses existing models in both object addition and general editing tasks. To propel future research, we will release the dataset alongside the trained models.

arxiv_record.abstract: Language is often used to describe physical interaction, yet most 3D human pose estimation methods overlook this rich source of information. We bridge this gap by leveraging large multimodal models (LMMs) as priors for reconstructing contact poses, offering a scalable alternative to traditional methods that rely on human annotations or motion capture data. Our approach extracts contact-relevant descriptors from an LMM and translates them into tractable losses to constrain 3D human pose optimization. Despite its simplicity, our method produces compelling reconstructions for both two-person interactions and self-contact scenarios, accurately capturing the semantics of physical and social interactions. Our results demonstrate that LMMs can serve as powerful tools for contact prediction and pose estimation, offering an alternative to costly manual human annotations or motion capture data. Our code is publicly available at https://prosepose.github.io.

native_poster_event.abstract: We present a zero-shot pose optimization method that enforces accurate physical contact constraints when estimating the 3D pose of humans. Our central insight is that since language is often used to describe physical interaction, large pretrained text-based models can act as priors on pose estimation.We can thus leverage this insight to improve pose estimation by converting natural language descriptors, generated by a large multimodal model (LMM), into tractable losses to constrain the 3D pose optimization. Despite its simplicity, our method produces surprisingly compelling pose reconstructions of people in close contact, correctly capturing the semantics of the social and physical interactions. We demonstrate that our method rivals more complex state-of-the-art approaches that require expensive human annotation of contact points and training specialized models. Moreover, unlike previous approaches, our method provides a unified framework for resolving self-contact and person-to-person contact.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Self-supervised learning (SSL) models are vulnerable to backdoor attacks.
Existing backdoor attacks that are effective in SSL often involve noticeable
triggers, like colored patches or visible noise, which are vulnerable to human
inspection. This paper proposes an imperceptible and effective backdoor attack
against self-supervised models. We first find that existing imperceptible
triggers designed for supervised learning are less effective in compromising
self-supervised models. We then identify this ineffectiveness is attributed to
the overlap in distributions between the backdoor and augmented samples used in
SSL. Building on this insight, we design an attack using optimized triggers
disentangled with the augmented transformation in the SSL, while remaining
imperceptible to human vision. Experiments on five datasets and six SSL
algorithms demonstrate our attack is highly effective and stealthy. It also has
strong resistance to existing backdoor defenses. Our code can be found at
https://github.com/Zhang-Henry/INACTIVE.

Hanrong Zhang, Zhenting Wang, Boheng Li, Fulin Lin, Tingxu Han, Mingyu

C2.justification: V2 extends the retained entanglement explanation through learned augmentation-space relaxation and interprets resistance to adaptive HSV defenses. It acknowledges CTRL's better LPIPS despite other disadvantages. The human-inspection discussion newly qualifies imperceptibility by admitting detectable color artifacts in Section A5.4.2 and Figure A9.

D1.justification: V2 supplies actual reference-input images in Figures A7–A8 and human-study preparation, randomization, and response-checking details. Most architecture, loss-weight, dataset-size, and training-budget information is retained. However, v1's explicit description of feature extractor M, with ResNet34 as an example, disappears from the stealth-loss explanation.

E1.justification: The five image datasets and existing classification tasks remain. V2 adds human discrimination between clean and backdoored ImageNet images and evaluation under HSV noise during downstream training and inference. These are bounded extensions of the evaluated population and input conditions; DINO's removal concerns model configuration.

E2.justification: V2 adds DRUPE to Table 1's retained BadEncoder-trigger comparisons. New Table 2 compares against POIENC, SSLBKD, SSLBKD-fixed, BLTO, and CTRL using their default attacks on matched CIFAR10 datasets. E4.justification: The original component ablations, sensitivity plots, conventional noise tests, and feature visualizations are retained. arxiv_record.abstract:
Image steganography can hide information in a host image and obtain a stego
image that is perceptually indistinguishable from the original one. This
technique has tremendous potential in scenarios like copyright protection,
information retrospection, etc. Some previous studies have proposed to enhance
the robustness of the methods against image disturbances to increase their
applicability. However, they generally cannot achieve a satisfying balance
between the steganography quality and robustness. Instead of image-in-image
steganography, we focus on the issue of message-in-image embedding that is
robust to various real-world image distortions. This task aims to embed
information into a natural image and the decoding result is required to be
completely accurate, which increases the difficulty of data concealing and
revealing. Inspired by the recent developments in transformer-based vision
models, we discover that the tokenized representation of image is naturally
suitable for steganography task. In this paper, we propose a novel message
embedding framework, called Robust Message Steganography (RMSteg), which is
competent to hide message via QR Code in a host image based on an normalizing
flow-based model. The stego image derived by our method has imperceptible
changes and the encoded message can be accurately restored even if the image is
printed out and photoed. To our best knowledge, this is the first work that
integrates the advantages of transformer models into normalizing flow. Our
experiment result shows that RMSteg has great potential in robust and
high-quality message embedding.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Human image generation is a key focus in image synthesis due to its broad
applications, but even slight inaccuracies in anatomy, pose, or details can
compromise realism. To address these challenges, we explore Direct Preference
Optimization (DPO), which trains models to generate preferred (winning) images
while diverging from non-preferred (losing) ones. However, conventional DPO
methods use generated images as winning images, limiting realism. To overcome
this limitation, we propose an enhanced DPO approach that incorporates
high-quality real images as winning images, encouraging outputs to resemble
real images rather than generated ones. However, implementing this concept is
not a trivial task. Therefore, our approach, HG-DPO (Human image Generation
through DPO), employs a novel curriculum learning framework that gradually
improves the output of the model toward greater realism, making training more
feasible. Furthermore, HG-DPO effectively adapts to personalized text-to-image
tasks, generating high-quality and identity-specific images, which highlights
the practical value of our approach.

native_poster_event.abstract: Human image generation is a key focus in image synthesis due to its broad applications. However, generating high-quality human images remains challenging because even slight inaccuracies in anatomy, pose, or fine details can compromise visual realism. To address these challenges, we explore Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), a method that trains models to generate images similar to preferred (winning) images while diverging from non-preferred (losing) ones. Conventional DPO approaches typically employ generated images as winning images, which may limit the model's ability to achieve high levels of realism. To overcome this limitation, we propose an enhanced DPO approach that incorporates high-quality real images as winning images, encouraging the model to produce outputs that resemble those real images rather than generated ones. Specifically, our approach, \textbf{HG-DPO} (\textbf{H}uman image \textbf{G}eneration through \textbf{DPO}), employs a novel curriculum learning framework that allows the model to gradually improve toward generating realistic human images, making the training more feasible than attempting the improvement all at once. Furthermore, we demonstrate that HG-DPO effectively adapts to personalized text-to-image tasks, generating high-quality, identity-specific images, which highlights the practical value of our approach.

C1.justification: V1 centers its contributions on inexpensive in-distribution preference construction and artifact suppression. V2 redefines the central contribution around real-image realism through a three-stage curriculum, adds GAN-inspired positioning, and emphasizes improvements in fine visual details. AI feedback and transfer to personalized generation remain central claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds domain-gap explanations for naive training failure, tentatively attributes hard-stage FID deterioration to reduced diversity, and explains alignment losses and recovery through preference selection and text-encoder training. It also discusses SFT forgetting earlier stages. Finger failures and the quality–diversity tradeoff already existed in v1; their discussion is revised rather than newly introduced.

D1.justification: V2 Appendix F newly specifies stage update counts of 300k/20k/20k, reconstruction and winner-selection timesteps, text-encoder LoRA rank 64, and timestep/block restrictions on inference adapters. It also supplies model-estimated dataset demographics. These substantially expand implementation information; the reported step counts do not establish an increase over v1's undisclosed training duration.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates on the people subset of PartiPrompts; v2 replaces this with held-out captions and reference photographs from its internal human-image collection. Preference training also introduces intermediate and near-real image domains beyond v1's generated preference pairs. Human image generation and InstantBooth personalization remain the underlying tasks.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated NCP-DPO, MAPO and Curriculum-DPO comparisons in Table 1, plus DPOK and D3PO in Appendix Table 5. AlignProp and unfiltered HPD/Pick-a-Pic comparisons remain, while v1's human-only HPD/Pick-a-Pic comparator rows disappear. V2 also evaluates Diffusion-DPO in a new naive real-versus-generated training setting.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a 5,000-image held-out evaluation split with Qwen2-VL test captions. It adds FID, CLIP-IQA quality/sharpness and ATHEC metrics, and reports absolute scores alongside win rates. Color evaluation changes from percentage differences in mean HSV channels to circular-mean hue distance. These substantially revise the evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: V2 adds curriculum-stage, omitted-stage, joint-training and stage-wise SFT ablations (Table 2), real-versus-reconstructed hard-target comparisons (Table 9), and a normal-versus-hard user study (Figure 22). V1's quantitative dataset-size and losing-rank ablations and qualitative LoRA-weight sweep disappear. The ranked image-pool gallery and LAN/statistics-matching analyses are retained in revised form.

E5.justification: V2 Appendix A.1 and Tables 5–6 newly report quantitative evaluation using ten sampling seeds. V1 illustrates multiple seeds qualitatively but does not document an equivalent repeated-seed benchmark. Neither version provides confidence intervals or significance tests; independent training-run counts remain unspecified.

E6.justification: Benchmark, ablation and personalization results are substantially replaced and expanded for the revised model and protocol. For example, v2 Table 2 reports FID values of 37.34 for the base model, 26.05 after the normal stage and 28.66 after the hard stage, alongside new quality/sharpness results. These are within-v2 findings, not same-setting improvements over v1's win-rate results.

M1.justification: V1 uses generated winning/losing pairs and a statistics-matching loss in a single DPO stage. V2 retains this as the easy stage, adds normal and hard stages using reconstructed real-image targets and filtered preference datasets, and introduces separate text-encoder training and selective LoRA application at inference. The default hard-stage winners are lightly reconstructed images, not unmodified photographs.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution framing and method narrative are extensively rewritten. Related work moves before the method, the RLHF/DPO preliminaries disappear, and the appendices are reorganized around curriculum stages. The title and affiliation also change.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the single-column format with a two-column layout, rebuilds the opening visual presentation, adds a curriculum diagram and stage-specific detail comparisons, and expands table structures and highlighting. User-study displays also change. Some illustrations are retained and reformatted, including v1 Figure 6 becoming v2 Figure 14.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands curriculum-learning, GAN and newer DPO literature. Positioning shifts from applying Diffusion-DPO with AI-labeled synthetic preferences, presented as orthogonal to real-image dataset work in v1 Section 6, to a real-image curriculum approach explicitly contrasted with Curriculum-DPO in v2 Section 2.

T1.justification: V2 adds mathematical definitions for intermediate-domain pools, timestep-constrained selection, filtering and hard-stage preference triplets (Eqs. 5–9). The formal additions concern these constructions; neither version contains theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for its realism claims: v1 mainly reported preference win rates, whereas v2 adds real-reference FID, quality/sharpness metrics, controlled stage and SFT comparisons, target-choice tests, and ten-seed baseline evaluation. after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark comparisons, curriculum-stage experiments, user studies and personalization results, including additional appendix evaluations.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Test-time adaptation (TTA) aims to improve the performance of source-domain
pre-trained models on previously unseen, shifted target domains. Traditional
TTA methods primarily adapt model weights based on target data streams, making
model performance sensitive to the amount and order of target data. The
recently proposed diffusion-driven TTA methods mitigate this by adapting model
inputs instead of weights, where an unconditional diffusion model, trained on
the source domain, transforms target-domain data into a synthetic domain that
is expected to approximate the source domain. However, in this paper, we reveal
that although the synthetic data in diffusion-driven TTA seems
indistinguishable from the source data, it is unaligned with, or even markedly
different from the latter for deep networks. To address this issue, we propose
a \textbf{S}ynthetic-\textbf{D}omain \textbf{A}lignment (SDA) framework. Our
key insight is to fine-tune the source model with synthetic data to ensure
better alignment. Specifically, we first employ a conditional diffusion model
to generate labeled samples, creating a synthetic dataset. Subsequently, we use
the aforementioned unconditional diffusion model to add noise to and denoise
each sample before fine-tuning. This Mix of Diffusion (MoD) process mitigates
the potential domain misalignment between the conditional and unconditional
models. Extensive experiments across classifiers, segmenters, and multimodal
large language models (MLLMs, \eg, LLaVA) demonstrate that SDA achieves
superior domain alignment and consistently outperforms existing
diffusion-driven TTA methods. Our code is available at
https://github.com/SHI-Labs/Diffusion-Driven-Test-Time-Adaptation-via-Synthetic-Domain-Alignment.

native_poster_event.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) aims to improve the performance of source-domain pre-trained models on previously unseen, shifted target domains. Traditional TTA methods primarily adapt model weights based on target data streams, making model performance sensitive to the amount and order of target data. The recently proposed diffusion-driven TTA methods mitigate this by adapting model inputs instead of weights, where an unconditional diffusion model, trained on the source domain, transforms target-domain data into a synthetic domain that is expected to approximate the source domain. However, in this paper, we reveal that although the synthetic data in diffusion-driven TTA seems indistinguishable from the source data, it is unaligned with, or even markedly different from the latter for deep networks. To address this issue, we propose a Synthetic-Domain Alignment (SDA) framework. Our key insight is to fine-tune the source model with synthetic data to ensure better alignment. Specifically, we first employ a conditional diffusion model to generate labeled samples, creating a synthetic dataset. Subsequently, we use the aforementioned unconditional diffusion model to add noise to and denoise each sample before fine-tuning. This Mix of Diffusion (MoD) process mitigates the potential domain misalignment between the conditional and unconditional models. Extensive experiments across classifiers, segmenters, and multimodal large language models (MLLMs, \eg, LLaVA) demonstrate that SDA achieves superior domain alignment and consistently outperforms existing diffusion-driven TTA methods. Our code will be open-sourced.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Text-to-image generation has recently emerged as a viable alternative to
text-to-image retrieval, driven by the visually impressive results of
generative diffusion models. Although query performance prediction is an active
research topic in information retrieval, to the best of our knowledge, there is
no prior study that analyzes the difficulty of queries (referred to as prompts)
in text-to-image generation, based on human judgments. To this end, we
introduce the first dataset of prompts which are manually annotated in terms of
image generation performance. Additionally, we extend these evaluations to
text-to-image retrieval by collecting manual annotations that represent
retrieval performance. We thus establish the first joint benchmark for prompt
and query performance prediction (PQPP) across both tasks, comprising over 10K
queries. Our benchmark enables (i) the comparative assessment of prompt/query
difficulty in both image generation and image retrieval, and (ii) the
evaluation of prompt/query performance predictors addressing both generation
and retrieval. We evaluate several pre- and post-generation/retrieval
performance predictors, thus providing competitive baselines for future
research. Our benchmark and code are publicly available at
https://github.com/Eduard6421/PQPP.

Eduard Poesina, Adriana Valentina Costache, Adrian-Gabriel Chifu,

C1.justification: The central contribution remains the first human-annotated joint benchmark for prompt/query performance prediction. V2 updates its stated extent to 10,200 queries and over 1.6 million annotations, and explicitly claims utility for cross-model, cross-dataset, and cross-task evaluation in the introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of transfer failures involving dataset mismatch, limited DrawBench training data, and weak alignment between generation and retrieval. It also discusses practical uses and automatic-label predictability. V1's boxplot-based failure interpretations and natural-image-only limitation disappear, while the principal annotation limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds extensive dataset documentation covering formats, fields, directory structure, an example record, maintenance, support, licensing, and intended uses. It also supplies detailed annotation examples, graph-predictor construction, and the reformulation prompt. Most existing training hyperparameters and hardware specifications are retained or relocated; estimated fine-tuning time changes from 48 to 50 hours.

E1.justification: V2 adds 200 DrawBench prompts to v1's 10,000 MS COCO captions. This introduces generator-oriented prompts with substantially different retrieval difficulty: Appendix 12 reports that approximately half have no relevant MS COCO images. Separate-source and cross-dataset evaluations extend coverage beyond the original caption population.

E2.justification: V2 adds HPSv2 and removes Score Variance @100. Its Table 5 also expands individual-system comparisons beyond the six predictors in v1 Tables 4–6 to the wider linguistic and graph-based suite previously reported only against averaged performance. These are substantive changes in comparator coverage, beyond renamed predictors.

E3.justification: The training/validation/test split changes from 6,000/2,000/2,000 to 6,080/2,040/2,080. V2 additionally introduces cross-model, bidirectional cross-dataset, cross-task, and separate-source training/testing protocols, plus evaluation against HPSv2 and CLIP-derived relevance targets. These substantially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: V2 adds systematic generalization analyses, automatic-versus-human assessment experiments, and generator-selection and prompt-reformulation case studies. Conversely, v1's prediction-error boxplots and associated analyses in Appendix A.8 are removed. The generation-versus-retrieval analysis is retained and moved into the main text.

E5.justification: V1 Figures 7–8 report prediction dispersion through boxplots conditioned on ground-truth performance; v2 removes these distribution summaries. This concerns variation across predictions, not repeated-run uncertainty. Student's t-testing at the 0.01 and 0.001 thresholds remains, and neither version reports repeated-run confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Numerical results and rankings change, and numerous transfer and automatic-assessment results are added. For example, fine-tuned CLIP's GLIDE/HBPP Pearson correlation is 0.615 in v1 Table 4 and 0.649 in v2 Table 3; changed data and settings prevent interpreting this as an isolated same-setting gain. V1's averaged predictor-result tables are no longer reported.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction and principal predictor designs are retained. V2 specifies Long-CLIP/ViT-B/32 and per-system BERT fine-tuning, whereas v1 describes CLIP generically and task-specific tuning while already reporting per-system results. The PDFs do not clearly distinguish implementation changes from expanded documentation.

P1.justification: The introduction and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten. Generation-versus-retrieval analysis moves from Appendix A.6 to main Section 4, predictor implementation details move into Appendix 11, and the supplementary material is extensively reorganized. These structural changes go beyond simply inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the benchmark pipeline to include DrawBench, and consolidates per-system comparisons into wide tables. It adds transfer tables and application figures, updates the embedding visualizations, and removes the two prediction-error boxplots. Several retained displays are resized or relocated.

R1.justification: V2 adds a focused human-feedback discussion covering Pick-a-Pic, ImageReward, and rich human feedback, alongside references supporting its new resources and predictors. It removes the QPP-evaluation discussion concerning correlation and alternative measures. Most QPP positioning, including the comparison with Bizzozzero and colleagues, remains.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs. The substantive HBPP, precision, and reciprocal-rank definitions remain unchanged. V2's expanded explanation of existing graph-based predictors supplies implementation context rather than new mathematical results.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's restricted data coverage and lack of transfer validation through DrawBench and systematic cross-model, cross-dataset, and cross-task experiments. These reveal important generalization failures rather than merely adding favorable scores. The dataset documentation also materially improves reuse. Although error-distribution plots are lost and some implementation details remain ambiguous, the gains in empirical scrutiny and documentation support a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the PQPP benchmark. Their complete main texts and appendices, including tables and figures, are readable and support comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: V2 reports original annotations and predictor evaluations, supplemented by cross-model, cross-dataset, cross-task, and application experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original human relevance annotations, predictor evaluations, generation-versus-retrieval correlations, and qualitative analyses, including appendix results.

arxiv_record.abstract:
This work presents a progressive image vectorization technique that
reconstructs the raster image as layer-wise vectors from semantic-aligned macro
structures to finer details. Our approach introduces a new image simplification
method leveraging the feature-average effect in the Score Distillation Sampling
mechanism, achieving effective visual abstraction from the detailed to coarse.
Guided by the sequence of progressive simplified images, we propose a two-stage
vectorization process of structural buildup and visual refinement, constructing
the vectors in an organized and manageable manner. The resulting vectors are
layered and well-aligned with the target image's explicit and implicit semantic
structures. Our method demonstrates high performance across a wide range of
images. Comparative analysis with existing vectorization methods highlights our
technique's superiority in creating vectors with high visual fidelity, and more
importantly, achieving higher semantic alignment and more compact layered
representation. The project homepage is
https://szuviz.github.io/layered_vectorization/.
arxiv_record.authors:
Zhenyu Wang, Jianxi Huang, Zhida Sun, Yuanhao Gong, Daniel Cohen-Or,
  Min Lu

C1.justification: The central contribution remains progressive simplification for compact, editable layered vectors. v2 presents two-stage reconstruction and superior semantic alignment as explicit contributions, while removing v1's claim that the optimization avoids local minima.

C2.justification: v2 Section 4.2 explicitly acknowledges shape distortion during ordinary SDS simplification and explains preserving macrostructure through unconditional noise. v1 instead emphasizes increased variation from reduced guidance. v2 also removes the concluding qualification that the method excludes stylization and leaves it to future work.

D1.justification: PyTorch, Adam, learning rates, and hardware disclosures remain. v2's supplement supplies Douglas–Peucker tolerance, filter parameters, and comparator initialization schedules. However, v1's explicit 100/500-iteration vector-optimization schedule and project-homepage link are no longer provided.

E1.justification: v2 explicitly includes emoji-style inputs alongside photos and clipart, modestly extending the reported image variety. v1 already covers flat illustrations and realistic images in Figures 10–11. The vectorization and recoloring tasks remain; the increase from ten to 100 evaluation images primarily changes sample size.

E2.justification: The main comparison expands from LIVE and O&R in v1 to LIVE, O&R, DiffVG, and SGLIVE in v2. Bilateral filtering also joins Gaussian filtering and superpixel simplification in the simplification comparisons.

E3.justification: The principal evaluation changes from ten images at 256 primitives to 100 images with 64, 128, and 256 primitives. v2 adds VGG-based LPIPS and caption-based CLIP evaluation, changes VeC containment from over 90% to over 85%, and caps structural primitives at half the comparison budget.

E4.justification: v1 already compares SDS simplification with Gaussian filtering and superpixels. v2 extends this comparison to reconstructed vector layers and adds controlled tests without the simplification sequence, structural optimization, and overlap loss (Figures 9–10 and supplementary Figures 17–19). These directly examine previously untested component contributions.

E5.justification: v1 Table 2 reports cross-image standard deviations for both MSE and VeC. v2 retains VeC standard deviations in Table 1 but presents MSE curves without dispersion in Figure 12. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 replaces the ten-image numerical comparisons with broader aggregate results and adds LPIPS, CLIP, and ablation findings. Reported mean VeC changes from 43.9% to 73.8%, but the dataset and containment threshold differ, preventing a same-setting performance comparison. v1's per-image runtime results are removed.

M1.justification: v1 jointly optimizes structural and pixel-wise primitives at successive simplification levels using visual, structural, and length losses. v2 instead optimizes structural vectors with an overlap penalty, fits and freezes their colors, then performs separate visual refinement. SDS simplification also changes from reduced guidance with a text prompt to an empty prompt.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method narrative are extensively rewritten. The method is reorganized around two reconstruction stages, the earlier Results and Experiments organization becomes an integrated Evaluation section, and dedicated supplementary sections organize ablations and implementation details.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the pipeline and introductory illustrations, adds ablation displays and metric curves, restructures tables, and substantially reorganizes the galleries and page layout. Some examples are retained. Supplementary Figures 20–21 have mismatched captions describing simplification filters although their panels compare vectorization methods.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially recast around image vectorization and layer decomposition. v2 adds positioning against SAMVG, SuperSVG, SGLIVE, and texture-aware vectorization, alongside extensive layer-decomposition literature. v1's separate vector-generation and sketch-abstraction discussions, including several associated citations, are removed.

T1.justification: Mathematical changes are concentrated in the objective definitions: v1's length-regularized joint objective is replaced by an overlap-regularized structural objective and separate visual fidelity loss in v2. improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central claims: comparisons include a relevant segmentation-guided baseline, multiple primitive budgets, perceptual and semantic measures, and controlled component ablations missing from v1. These address important weaknesses of the earlier ten-image evaluation. Runtime evidence and some reproducibility details are lost, and caption errors remain, but the stronger experimental validation provides a clear net improvement. The changed VeC settings do not establish a direct cross-version performance gain.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Endowing Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) with visual grounding capability can
significantly enhance AIs' understanding of the visual world and their
interaction with humans. However, existing methods typically fine-tune the
parameters of LMMs to learn additional segmentation tokens and overfit
grounding and segmentation datasets. Such a design would inevitably cause a
catastrophic diminution in the indispensable conversational capability of
general AI assistants. In this paper, we comprehensively evaluate
state-of-the-art grounding LMMs across a suite of multimodal question-answering
benchmarks, observing drastic performance drops that indicate vanishing general
knowledge comprehension and weakened instruction following ability. To address
this issue, we present F-LMM -- grounding frozen off-the-shelf LMMs in human-AI
conversations -- a straightforward yet effective design based on the fact that
word-pixel correspondences conducive to visual grounding inherently exist in
the attention mechanism of well-trained LMMs. Using only a few trainable CNN
layers, we can translate word-pixel attention weights to mask logits, which a
SAM-based mask refiner can further optimise. Our F-LMM neither learns special
segmentation tokens nor utilises high-quality grounded instruction-tuning data,
but achieves competitive performance on referring expression segmentation and
panoptic narrative grounding benchmarks while completely preserving LMMs'
original conversational ability. Additionally, with instruction-following
ability preserved and grounding ability obtained, F-LMM can be directly applied
to complex tasks like reasoning segmentation, grounded conversation generation
and visual chain-of-thought reasoning. Our code can be found at
https://github.com/wusize/F-LMM.

It drops v1's VisualGenome-exclusion-based argument about the origin of grounding priors. The stated limitations concerning inherited biases, modality coverage, and F-LMM model size are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix A1.3 newly documents dialogue formatting and concatenation of RES expressions; Table A4 summarizes training datasets by method. v2 specifies selector settings and describes code as available rather than promising a future release, while dropping the XTuner implementation disclosure. Main training budgets, optimizer settings, and hardware remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds reasoning-segmentation evaluation requiring knowledge or logical inference and GCG evaluation requiring generated text with interleaved masks (Tables 2–3). v1 includes grounded-conversation illustrations but lacks these benchmark evaluations. F-LMM's RefCOCO(+/g) and PNG training coverage remains unchanged.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Localizing events in videos based on semantic queries is a pivotal task in
video understanding, with the growing significance of user-oriented
applications like video search. Yet, current research predominantly relies on
natural language queries (NLQs), overlooking the potential of using multimodal
queries (MQs) that integrate images to more flexibly represent semantic queries
-- especially when it is difficult to express non-verbal or unfamiliar concepts
in words. To bridge this gap, we introduce ICQ, a new benchmark designed for
localizing events in videos with MQs, alongside an evaluation dataset
ICQ-Highlight. To accommodate and evaluate existing video localization models
for this new task, we propose 3 Multimodal Query Adaptation methods and a novel
Surrogate Fine-tuning on pseudo-MQs strategy. ICQ systematically benchmarks 12
state-of-the-art backbone models, spanning from specialized video localization
models to Video LLMs, across diverse application domains. Our experiments
highlight the high potential of MQs in real-world applications. We believe this
benchmark is a first step toward advancing MQs in video event localization.
