C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion expand the contribution from a benchmark with three training-free adaptations to include SUIT as a central training strategy. v3 additionally claims its effectiveness and transferability, while retaining the original benchmark novelty and multimodal-query feasibility claims.

C2.justification: v3 explains adaptation failures through generated-query distribution shift and interprets SUIT as reducing that mismatch. It also interprets the artifact experiment as supporting benchmark generalizability and discusses residual cross-modal semantic distortion. v1's explicit model-availability limitation and malicious-image safety/privacy caveat are dropped.

D1.justification: v3 Section 5.1, Appendix B.1, and Table 10 document pseudo-query construction, BLIP-2 caption generation, GPT-3.5 templates, and SUIT implementation. Added details include LoRA placement, rank 32, alpha 64, learning rate 0.0002, one epoch, and up to 16 hours on an NVIDIA A40. Existing code/data access statements remain.

E1.justification: v3 introduces Flickr30K and COCO image-caption data for surrogate training and evaluates retrieved reference images paired with generated images across four styles. The original ICQ-Highlight video coverage and four-style evaluation dataset are retained.

E2.justification: TimeChat and VTimeLLM join the MQ-Cap and MQ-Sum recall/mAP comparisons in v3 Table 1 and Appendix Table 7. TimeChat was previously cited but not evaluated. Existing comparators remain, making this a targeted expansion of the Video-LLM group.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce SUIT training with 89,420 training and 4,785 validation pseudo-queries for one epoch, plus an 84-pair generated/retrieved comparison selected for semantic and stylistic similarity. The original ICQ test coverage and recall/mAP evaluation metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds an artifact-control experiment, qualitative image/caption case studies, and a t-SNE analysis of query distributions (Figures 5, 6, and 11). v1's detailed per-prompt analyses and Figures 7–8 disappear. Refinement-text ablations and rank-correlation analyses are retained, partly relocated.

E5.justification: v3 adds averages with plus/minus values across training seeds for SUIT, without specifying the seed count. The original practice of reporting standard deviations across three prompts for captioning and summarization remains. These two sources of variability are different.

E6.justification: Matched original recall/mAP entries are unchanged. v3 adds SUIT results, TimeChat/VTimeLLM results, and artifact-control findings; for example, Table 1 newly reports TR-DETR with SUIT at 58.85 R1@0.5 on scribble. This is a new trained condition, not a correction to an earlier score. Detailed per-prompt results are removed.

M1.justification: v3 Section 4.2 adds SUIT: GPT-3.5 constructs pseudo-queries and forged target captions, then LoRA fine-tunes the multimodal summarizer using next-token prediction. This introduces a learned adaptation procedure. The original CAP, SUM, and VISENC methods remain as MQ-Cap, MQ-Sum, and VQ-Enc.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, adaptation becomes a standalone section, and results are reorganized around explicit research questions. Terminology changes throughout, and the appendix is restructured into dataset, implementation, and extended-results sections.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the overview and adaptation diagrams, and adds SUIT, artifact-control, embedding, and case-study figures. The mAP table and refinement-type plots move to the appendix. Tables are reorganized, and the old per-prompt plots are removed.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands composed image/video retrieval coverage, including Pic2Word, EgoCVR, and CoVR-2, and adds audio-visual localization and SUIT-related references. References supporting v1's episodic-memory motivation are removed. The claimed distinction between holistic retrieval and multimodal event localization remains.

T1.justification: The image-plus-refinement query definition and temporal-localization target retain their mathematical meaning. Neither version develops theoretical results or proofs; SUIT adds an algorithmic training procedure without a new formal derivation.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses v1's explicitly unresolved training-data problem with a documented surrogate-training pipeline and substantial empirical evaluation of SUIT. Additional Video-LLM comparisons and the artifact-control study strengthen the benchmark's evidence. The artifact study remains small, seed variability does not directly establish prompt robustness, and detailed prompt plots and some caveats are lost. Nevertheless, the methodological and empirical gains substantially improve the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ICQ/ICQ-Highlight research. Their main text, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching renamed methods and relocated analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark experiments and adds SUIT evaluations, additional backbone results, and generated-versus-retrieved image experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original ICQ-Highlight recall/mAP evaluations, refinement-text ablations, and prompt-sensitivity experiments in the main text and appendix.

arxiv_record.abstract:
A fundamental aspect of compositional reasoning in a video is associating
people and their actions across time. Recent years have seen great progress in
general-purpose vision or video models and a move towards long-video
understanding. While exciting, we take a step back and ask: are current models
good at compositional reasoning on short videos? To this end, we introduce
VELOCITI, a benchmark to study Video-LLMs by disentangling and assessing the
comprehension of agents, actions, and their associations across multiple
events. We adopt the Video-Language Entailment setup and propose StrictVLE that
requires correct classification (rather than ranking) of the positive and
negative caption. We evaluate several models and observe that even the best,
LLaVA-OneVision (44.5%) and Gemini-1.5-Pro (49.3%), are far from human accuracy
at 93.0%. Results show that action understanding lags behind agents, and
negative captions created using entities appearing in the video perform worse
than those obtained from pure text manipulation. We also present challenges
with ClassicVLE and multiple-choice (MC) evaluation, strengthening our
preference for StrictVLE. Finally, we validate that our benchmark requires
visual inputs of multiple frames making it ideal to study video-language
compositional reasoning.

While exciting, we take a step back and ask: are today’s models good at compositional reasoning on short videos? To this end, we introduce VELOCITI, a benchmark to study Video-LLMs by disentangling and assessing the comprehension of agents, actions, and their associations across multiple events. We adopt the Video-Language Entailment setup and propose StrictVLE that requires correct classification (rather than ranking) of the positive and negative caption. We evaluate several models and observe that even the best, LLaVA-OneVision (42.5%) and GPT-4o (44.3%), are far from human accuracy at 89.6%. Results show that action understanding lags behind agents, and negative captions created using entities appearing in the video perform worse than those obtained from pure text manipulation. We also present challenges with ClassicVLE and multiple-choice (MC) evaluation, strengthening our preference for StrictVLE. Finally, we validate that our benchmark requires visual inputs of multiple frames making it ideal to study video-language compositional reasoning.

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds a benchmark exposing perception and binding failures across contrastive and generative models. v2 makes StrictVLE a central contribution and focuses its primary evaluation on Video-LLMs. Its abstract and contributions also foreground action-versus-agent difficulty, shortcomings of ClassicVLE and multiple-choice evaluation, and the requirement for visual inputs spanning multiple frames.

C2.justification: v2 develops substantive explanations involving yes-response bias, nearly indistinguishable entailment scores, model-size effects and why simultaneous caption presentation makes multiple-choice evaluation easier. Appendix D explicitly limits StrictVLE's applicability to models supporting yes/no decisions. Human-centric scope and scaling limitations persist, while v1's discussion of societal stereotypes and the unexplored audio modality is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds model-specific evaluation prompts, input details and an OV-7B runtime of approximately 2.6 hours on one RTX 4090 (Appendices B.6–C). However, it removes v1's datasheet documenting JSON distribution, a loading notebook, licensing and maintenance, and omits the earlier explicit decoding settings. This changes reproducibility documentation without establishing that the underlying resources became unavailable.

E1.justification: The VidSitu movie domain and seven caption tests remain, including Agent Identification renamed Agent Random and Action Modifier renamed Action Manner. However, v2 removes the separate Intra-Video Association Test using two cropped video segments and the text-to-video control task. The new input ablations use the retained benchmark.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated Qwen2-VL, LLaVA-OneVision, Gemini-1.5-Pro and GPT-4o models. Compared with v1 Tables 2–3, the ClassicVLE comparison in v2 Table 4 drops CLIP, EVA-CLIP, CLIP-ViP and mPLUG-Owl-Video rows while retaining several other comparators. Table 6 additionally evaluates a base language model and a single-image checkpoint.

E3.justification: v2 makes paired yes/no classification under StrictVLE primary, while retaining relative ranking as ClassicVLE and systematically testing both multiple-choice orders. Filtering changes the reported base from 900 videos and 4,500 event captions to 864 videos and 3,101 pairs. Human evaluation changes from five volunteers making retrieval judgments to three classifying individual video-caption pairs. Appendix B.3 also specifies subset selection through trials matching OV-72B performance, and new experiments vary prompts and frame sampling.

E4.justification: v2 adds extensive positive/negative decision analyses, quantified choice-order bias, blind-model and single-frame controls, chain-of-thought and frame-rate ablations, and scored success/failure cases (Sections 5.2–5.5 and Appendix A). These investigate response bias, dependence on visual and temporal inputs, and prompting sensitivity beyond v1's plausibility check and brief qualitative discussion of choice bias.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for model performance. v2's scatter plots display individual examples' entailment scores, not estimates of experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive StrictVLE and diagnostic results, including subset averages of 44.5% for OV-72B, 49.3% for Gemini-1.5-Pro and 93.0% for humans (Table 2). Retained relative-ranking results also change: PLLaVA averages 55.3% in v1 Table 3 and 59.5% in v2 Table 4. These concern revised data/settings, not demonstrated same-setting model improvements. IVAT results are removed.

M1.justification: The retained tests use the same basic construction procedures: LLaMA-3 converts SRL dictionaries into captions, entities or actions are substituted, and templates construct coreference and chronology examples. No predictive architecture or training objective is introduced. StrictVLE changes the evaluation criterion, assessed under E3 and T1.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and much of the explanatory narrative are rewritten. Tests are regrouped around agents, actions, multiple events and negation strategies; StrictVLE receives a dedicated section. The appendices are extensively reorganized around results, benchmark construction, prompts and limitations, replacing the earlier prompts/annotation/statistics/datasheet structure.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a predominantly single-column layout to two columns. v2 adds a Venn diagram, redraws the benchmark schematic, introduces extensive diagnostic tables and scatter plots, and presents scored qualitative examples. Appendix prompts are reformatted, dataset plots are revised, and a categorized action word cloud replaces the earlier frequency-chart presentation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through a comparative benchmark table and a dedicated entailment discussion. Newly discussed works include VITATECS, Vinoground, TVBench, TempCompass and NaturalBench. The distinction from prior work now emphasizes strict entailment and evaluation bias alongside in-video negation, rather than mainly contrasting perception with concept binding.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4 introduces the formal StrictVLE condition requiring positive-caption entailment above 0.5 and negative-caption entailment below 0.5, with 25% random accuracy. It adds a numerical counterexample demonstrating why relative ranking can accept incorrect yes/no responses. v1's IVAT matching and group-score definitions disappear; neither version contains substantial theorem or proof development.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evaluation validity and diagnostic value: StrictVLE and the score/choice-bias analyses expose errors hidden by v1's relative ranking, while blind and single-frame controls directly test the benchmark's dependence on video information. These gains outweigh reduced datasheet and access documentation. Important qualifications remain: Appendix B.3 conditions subset selection on OV-72B performance, and Table 9 labels its main-result OV-72B scores as 8fps despite the stated 1fps default, weakening the frame-rate interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VELOCITI, built from VidSitu movie clips and semantic role annotations. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, equations and appendices are readable. The substantial reframing and changed evaluation settings can be identified reliably.

after.justification: v2 reports original StrictVLE, ClassicVLE and multiple-choice evaluations, human results, and additional diagnostic experiments in the main text and Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 Tables 2–3 report original evaluations of contrastive models, Video-LLMs, Gemini and humans on VELOCITI, supported by appendix annotation and dataset analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Most of the existing methods for video understanding primarily focus on
videos only lasting tens of seconds, with limited exploration of techniques for
handling long videos. The increased number of frames in long videos poses two
main challenges: difficulty in locating key information and performing
long-range reasoning. Thus, we propose DrVideo, a document-retrieval-based
system designed for long video understanding. Our key idea is to convert the
long-video understanding problem into a long-document understanding task so as
to effectively leverage the power of large language models. Specifically,
DrVideo first transforms a long video into a coarse text-based long document to
initially retrieve key frames and then updates the documents with the augmented
key frame information. It then employs an agent-based iterative loop to
continuously search for missing information and augment the document until
sufficient question-related information is gathered for making the final
predictions in a chain-of-thought manner. Extensive experiments on long video
benchmarks confirm the effectiveness of our method. DrVideo significantly
outperforms existing LLM-based state-of-the-art methods on EgoSchema benchmark
(3 minutes), MovieChat-1K benchmark (10 minutes), and the long split of
Video-MME benchmark (average of 44 minutes).

C1.justification: The central contributions remain video-to-document conversion and iterative retrieval/augmentation. v2 narrows headline superiority to existing LLM-based methods, replaces the LLaMA-Vid-QA performance claim with Video-MME and subtitle-assisted claims, and explicitly claims to be the first such document-retrieval system with a training-free, accessible implementation.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of subtitle dominance, restricted subtitle coverage in VideoAgent, and information redundancy or loss across iteration and sampling settings. It replaces v1's proprietary-model transparency/end-to-end-training limitation with a limitation about balancing sufficient and irrelevant information. Component dependence and context-length limits remain, with new failure analysis illustrating the former.

D1.justification: Supplementary Section 7 adds full EgoSchema agent prompts, RTX 4090/24 GB hardware information, temperature settings, captioner specifications and checkpoint links, and detailed baseline reproduction procedures. These materially expand reproducibility information. The LaViLa training-overlap exclusion was already stated in v1; v2 documents it more fully rather than establishing newly changed training.

E1.justification: v1's constructed LLaMA-Vid-QA evaluation, comprising 400 questions over 23 movies lasting approximately 1–2 hours, is removed. v2 replaces it with multiple-choice evaluation on Video-MME's 30–60-minute long split, including conditions with and without subtitles. EgoSchema and MovieChat-1K remain.

E2.justification: Comparator membership changes substantially within retained benchmarks. EgoSchema Table 1 adds Vamos, ProViQ and MVU while removing SeViLA, InternVideo, LongViViT and MC-ViT-L, among others. MovieChat-1K Table 2 adds MM-VID, LLoVi, VideoAgent, MovieChat+ and Jeoung et al.; Video-MME also introduces comparisons with newer proprietary and open-source multimodal models.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 changes the reported sampling rate from 2 FPS for all videos to 0.5 FPS for EgoSchema/MovieChat-1K and 0.2 FPS for Video-MME. v2 also introduces DeepSeek V2.5 evaluation and controlled comparisons across interaction counts, agent models and sampling rates. These establish reported protocol changes, but the unchanged retained DrVideo scores do not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component, augmentation-type, top-K and captioner ablations, v2 adds interaction-count comparisons with VideoAgent (Figure 3), agent-model comparisons (Table 7), sampling-rate sensitivity (Table 8), and a subtitle-only control (Table 3). New success and failure cases examine frame selection, long-video reasoning and captioning errors.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or empirical error bars. Agent-generated confidence outputs occur in both versions and are not statistical uncertainty estimates for the reported performance.

E6.justification: v2 removes the LLaMA-Vid-QA results and adds Video-MME accuracies of 51.7% without subtitles, 71.7% with subtitles and 68.5% using subtitles alone, plus numerous diagnostic results. MovieChat-1K baseline values also change, including MovieChat's global accuracy from 55.1% in v1's Gemini-Pro row to 68.3% in v2. DrVideo's reported EgoSchema and MovieChat-1K headline scores remain unchanged; these revisions do not demonstrate same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The five-component retrieval, augmentation and agent-loop procedure remains intact. However, v2 introduces subtitle-conditioned inference on Video-MME, feeding frame-aligned subtitles into the LLM, whereas v1 explicitly uses visual information without prior language information. This extends the inputs without redesigning the core algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction, method exposition and results discussion undergo extensive rewriting, especially the explanation of prior-method limitations and the organization of comparisons. v2 adds a structured supplement covering implementation, ablations, the algorithm and case studies, and moves Algorithm 1 out of the main text.

P2.justification: v1's performance-summary plot and conversion/retrieval detail figure disappear; its overview is retained as v2 Figure 1, and the agent-loop illustration is redrawn. v2 adds an iteration plot and three case-study figures, restructures comparison tables, and introduces additional tables and boxed prompts in the supplement.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against the already-cited LLoVi and VideoAgent, contrasting holistic video documents and language-space augmentation with summarization and image-text retrieval. It adds references covering Video-MME, newer multimodal models and document reasoning, alongside an explicit claim to be the first document-retrieval-based system for this task.

T1.justification: Equations 1–4 retain the document construction, cosine-similarity retrieval, augmentation and frame-selection conditions. Algorithm 1 is relocated and reformatted with the same substantive operations. Neither version adds theoretical guarantees, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves reproducibility and the evidence supporting the retrieval framework. Previously missing prompts, checkpoints and reproduction settings are supplied, while Video-MME comparisons, the subtitle-only control, sensitivity studies and failure analysis make the results easier to assess and qualify. Removing the 1–2-hour benchmark narrows duration coverage, and the changed sampling description remains unreconciled with unchanged scores, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in documentation and empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DrVideo and provide readable text, equations, tables and figures. The retained method and experiments can be matched reliably, including the additional supplementary material in v2, Sections 7–10.

after.justification: v2 retains original EgoSchema and MovieChat-1K results and reports Video-MME evaluations, additional ablations and qualitative case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on EgoSchema, MovieChat-1K and its constructed LLaMA-Vid-QA benchmark, together with component and parameter ablations.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Recently, Depth Anything Models (DAMs) - a type of depth foundation models -
have demonstrated impressive zero-shot capabilities across diverse perspective
images. Despite its success, it remains an open question regarding DAMs'
performance on panorama images that enjoy a large field-of-view (180x360) but
suffer from spherical distortions. To address this gap, we conduct an empirical
analysis to evaluate the performance of DAMs on panoramic images and identify
their limitations. For this, we undertake comprehensive experiments to assess
the performance of DAMs from three key factors: panoramic representations, 360
camera positions for capturing scenarios, and spherical spatial
transformations. This way, we reveal some key findings, e.g., DAMs are
sensitive to spatial transformations. We then propose a semi-supervised
learning (SSL) framework to learn a panoramic DAM, dubbed PanDA. Under the
umbrella of SSL, PanDA first learns a teacher model by fine-tuning DAM through
joint training on synthetic indoor and outdoor panoramic datasets. Then, a
student model is trained using large-scale unlabeled data, leveraging
pseudo-labels generated by the teacher model. To enhance PanDA's generalization
capability, M"obius transformation-based spatial augmentation (MTSA) is
proposed to impose consistency regularization between the predicted depth maps
from the original and spatially transformed ones. This subtly improves the
student model's robustness to various spatial transformations, even under
severe distortions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PanDA exhibits
remarkable zero-shot capability across diverse scenes, and outperforms the
data-specific panoramic depth estimation methods on two popular real-world
benchmarks.

Zidong Cao, Jinjing Zhu, Weiming Zhang, Hao Ai, Haotian Bai,
  Hengshuang Zhao, Lin Wang

C1.justification: The claimed first comprehensive benchmark becomes a three-factor empirical analysis covering both DAM generations. v2 adds EPNL-based equatorial accuracy and synthetic indoor/outdoor joint training to its central contribution narrative, replacing v1's emphasis on metric-depth supervision and newly collected data. The broader SSL/MTSA generalization claim remains.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes disparity supervision and metric-head tradeoffs when explaining equatorial failures. v2 develops explanations involving global normalization, polar-region dominance and equator-focused supervision. Appendix E.6 newly acknowledges that visualization normalization can conceal DAM details; Appendix A identifies extremely dark scenes as problematic. Limited labeled-scene coverage remains a stated limitation.

D1.justification: v2 documents dataset-specific scaling/clipping, frame extraction and dark-scene filtering, sky masking, doubled-resolution pseudo-label generation, representation patch/FoV settings, EPNL sampling, LoRA rank, and inference hardware/timing. These substantially expand reproducibility information. v1's Diverse360 collection procedure and metric-head implementation details disappear with those components.

E1.justification: Teacher training moves from real indoor Matterport3D to synthetic indoor Structured3D and outdoor Deep360. The stated unlabeled training set replaces self-collected Diverse360 with 360+x while retaining ZInD. v2 adds Stanford2D3D evaluation and controlled camera-height/location scenarios (Sections 3.2 and 5; Appendix A).

E2.justification: The Matterport3D comparison drops OmniFusion and adds BiFuse, BiFuse++, HoHoNet, HRDFuse, S2Net, Elite360D and Depth Anywhere (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 5). v2 also introduces quantitative zero-shot comparisons against DAM v1, DAM v2 and Marigold, and evaluates RPNL against EPNL.

E3.justification: v2 separates aligned zero-shot PanDA evaluation from unaligned, 30-epoch dataset fine-tuning, adds threshold-accuracy metrics and evaluation resizing, and changes student training from 20/40 epochs to four. Default training zoom expands from 1–1.2 to 1–1.5. DAM robustness testing expands from three rotation/zoom settings each to ranges of −90°–90° and 0.4–4.0.

E4.justification: v2 adds local-output representation analysis, controlled camera placement, EPNL/RPNL and equator/pole comparisons, pseudo-label-only training, limited-label fine-tuning, LoRA-rank sensitivity, and pseudo-label-resolution analysis. Existing loss, data-volume and augmentation-range ablations use revised designs. The metric-head comparison in v1 Table 5 is removed.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix E.8 newly states that inference timings are averaged over 100 measurements; v1 has no corresponding procedure. Neither version reports repeated training runs, training seeds, or uncertainty intervals for depth-accuracy results.

E6.justification: DAM v1 representation RMSE values remain unchanged, but method results are substantially replaced and extended. v1 Table 3 reports student Matterport3D RMSE 0.3931; v2 Table 5 reports PanDA-S/L values 0.3950/0.3305, and Table 6 adds Stanford2D3D results, including PanDA-L RMSE 0.2540. Changed training and evaluation prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The teacher–student framework remains, but v1's DAM v1 adaptation with metric-depth heads and SILog-based objectives becomes DAM v2 adaptation producing normalized affine-invariant depths. v2 introduces equator-aware patch normalization loss, equator-biased sampling with boundary continuity, and gradient loss in supervised and pseudo-label training (Section 4).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, analysis and methodology are extensively rewritten. The five-aspect benchmark becomes a three-factor analysis, experiments are organized around zero-shot and dataset-specific evaluation, and appendices become separate supplementary sections A–F. Any360D is renamed PanDA, with accompanying terminology and author-header changes.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the opening demonstration and pipeline, introduces transformation curves, camera-position illustrations, error maps and point clouds, and restructures comparison tables by dataset and evaluation setting. Large appendix image galleries are removed. Retained Möbius geometry material moves into the supplement rather than constituting a new analysis.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes its approach from Depth Anywhere's unlabeled-panorama distillation and positions EPNL relative to Metric3D's random patch normalization. DAM v2 and synthetic-data training become central reference points, while Marigold and diffusion-based depth estimation enter the discussion. This substantially revises the closest-work positioning beyond citation updates.

T1.justification: v2 adds formal definitions of percentile depth normalization and the patch-normalized EPNL objective (Equations 1–3). The spherical projections, Möbius transformation and inverse-projection mathematics are retained from v1 Appendix C.1 in v2 Appendix D.3. No new theorem, proof or theoretical guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's generalization evidence beyond Matterport3D is mainly qualitative. v2 substantially strengthens it through separate quantitative zero-shot and fine-tuned evaluations on two real datasets, plus EPNL/RPNL and equator/pole controls. Appendix E.6 also addresses a visualization confound. Outdoor accuracy and training variability remain unquantified, and zero-shot scores require scale/shift alignment, but the more diagnostic evidence and clearer protocols provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Despite renaming Any360D to PanDA and extensive revisions, both describe the same panoramic-depth research built around teacher–student learning, LoRA and Möbius augmentation. The text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original PanDA results on Matterport3D and Stanford2D3D, camera-position experiments, and extensive component and sensitivity analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original representation and transformation experiments, trained teacher/student results, and loss, architecture and augmentation ablations, including appendix experiments.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Existing research on avatar creation is typically limited to laboratory
datasets, which require high costs against scalability and exhibit insufficient
representation of the real world. On the other hand, the web abounds with
off-the-shelf real-world human videos, but these videos vary in quality and
require accurate annotations for avatar creation. To this end, we propose an
automatic annotating pipeline with filtering protocols to curate these humans
from the web. Our pipeline surpasses state-of-the-art methods on the EMDB
benchmark, and the filtering protocols boost verification metrics on web
videos. We then curate WildAvatar, a web-scale in-the-wild human avatar
creation dataset extracted from YouTube, with $10000+$ different human subjects
and scenes. WildAvatar is at least $10\times$ richer than previous datasets for
3D human avatar creation and closer to the real world. To explore its
potential, we demonstrate the quality and generalizability of avatar creation
methods on WildAvatar. We will publicly release our code, data source links and
annotations to push forward 3D human avatar creation and other related fields
for real-world applications.

C1.justification: V1 primarily claims a large in-the-wild dataset, challenging avatar benchmarks and improved generalization. V4 elevates the annotation/filtering pipeline to a central contribution and adds claims of superiority on EMDB and improved downstream reconstruction through better annotations. The dataset-scale and generalization claims remain.

C2.justification: V4 adds interpretations of filtering benefits, improved extremity alignment and high SSIOU arising from loose clothing rather than erroneous fitting. It removes v1's detailed annotation-noise, clothing and lighting challenge discussion, explicit limitations concerning backgrounds, static activities and human interactions, and specific portrait-rights and bias caveats.

D1.justification: The appendices newly document model variants, filtering thresholds, frame selection, loss weights, L-BFGS settings, pipeline runtime and evaluation details. V4 also supplies a project address and S-Lab License 1.0 statement. V1's per-baseline training-time and rendering-FPS entries are removed.

E1.justification: V4 adds quantitative SMPL annotation evaluation on EMDB and consistency and qualitative comparisons using 3DPW, extending evaluation beyond avatar rendering and dataset characterization. WildAvatar and the four laboratory datasets remain in generalization experiments; ZJU-Mocap's separate per-subject comparison disappears.

E2.justification: V4 Table 2 adds eight annotation comparators: SPIN, VIBE, PARE, TRACE, CLIFF, TCMR, HybrIK and HMR2.0. Table 4 additionally compares HMR2.0 annotations against the proposed annotations for downstream reconstruction. The seven avatar reconstruction methods and four generalization methods are retained.

E3.justification: Per-subject evaluation changes from 10 subjects with 10 training and 10 test frames each to 133 subjects with 100 training and 100 test frames each. V4 adds an annotation-source control and new protocols using EMDB-1, joint/vertex errors, PCK at threshold 0.1 and SOIOU. Cross-version reconstruction scores therefore are not directly comparable.

E4.justification: V4 adds sequential filtering/refinement analysis measuring consistency and retained clip counts in Table 3. Appendix figures examine unusual viewpoints, high-SSIOU clothing examples, coarse versus refined SMPL, and accepted/rejected masks. V1's detailed per-subject failure-case comparison is replaced by annotation-source comparisons.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for experimental results. V4's standard deviation across annotating experts is a filtering component, not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V4 adds EMDB and filtering results and replaces the per-subject results under its revised protocol. Corresponding generalization entries also change: the first MPS-NeRF row's laboratory novel-view PSNR changes from 18.46 to 16.99, while WildAvatar generalization scores remain unchanged. The resolution chart corrects the 720×1280 label from 70.3% to 23.1%, and Appendix D adds population and scene statistics.

M1.justification: The four-stage annotation backbone remains, but v4 adds multi-expert prediction fusion and agreement-based filtering across detection, pose and SMPL models. Protocol III also introduces PCK-based consistency filtering between projected SMPL joints and estimated 2D keypoints. These materially extend the procedure described with YOLO and PARE in v1.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list and conclusion are substantially rewritten around the pipeline. Existing collection, processing and dataset-analysis material is reorganized into Methodology, WildAvatar and appendices, while the experimental narrative shifts from diagnosing reconstruction challenges to demonstrating annotation benefits.

P2.justification: V4 adopts a two-column layout, redesigns the opening overview and dataset graphics, expands the pipeline diagram, and adds filtering illustrations and annotation tables. It replaces the per-subject comparison display and adds six appendix figures. Retained generalization illustrations are reformatted and faces are blurred.

R1.justification: V4 substantially strengthens positioning around automatic SMPL annotation and filtering, including direct comparison with HMR2.0. It adds relevant references such as EMDB, HMR2.0, TCMR, Detectron2, HRNet and DWPose, and extends application positioning to human interactions and relightable avatars. The earlier dataset and avatar-method survey largely remains.

T1.justification: Appendix B newly specifies constant body shape across frames, temporal and alignment losses, GMM pose-prior regularization, and their weighted objective in Equations 1–4. V1 describes refinement verbally. This adds limited mathematical specification; neither version develops theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens a central weakness of v1: annotation quality was asserted without direct quantitative validation. EMDB evaluation, staged filtering analysis and downstream annotation-source comparisons provide important supporting evidence, while the appendices make the pipeline substantially more reproducible. These gains outweigh the removal of useful failure and limitations discussion. A remaining documentation problem is the unexplained relationship between selecting 20 frames per clip and evaluating 200 frames per subject.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WildAvatar, retaining the 10,647-clip dataset and identifiable pipeline and avatar experiments. Text, tables, figures and equations support reliable comparison. V4 includes Appendices A–D; the supplied v1 ends with references.

after.justification: V4 reports original annotation evaluations, filtering analyses, avatar experiments and qualitative comparisons, including evidence in its appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original dataset analyses, per-subject reconstruction experiments in Table 2, and generalization experiments with and without WildAvatar training in Table 3.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Advancements in large Vision-Language Models have brought precise, accurate
image captioning, vital for advancing multi-modal image understanding and
processing. Yet these captions often carry lengthy, intertwined contexts that
are difficult to parse and frequently overlook essential cues, posing a great
barrier for models like GroundingDINO and SDXL, which lack the strong text
encoding and syntax analysis needed to fully leverage dense captions. To
address this, we propose BACON, a prompting method that breaks down
VLM-generated captions into disentangled, structured elements such as objects,
relationships, styles, and themes. This approach not only minimizes confusion
from handling complex contexts but also allows for efficient transfer into a
JSON dictionary, enabling models without linguistic processing capabilities to
easily access key information. We annotated 100,000 image-caption pairs using
BACON with GPT-4V and trained an LLaVA captioner on this dataset, enabling it
to produce BACON-style captions without relying on costly GPT-4V. Evaluations
of overall quality, precision, and recall-as well as user studies-demonstrate
that the resulting caption model consistently outperforms other SOTA VLM models
in generating high-quality captions. Besides, we show that BACON-style captions
exhibit better clarity when applied to various models, enabling them to
accomplish previously unattainable tasks or surpass existing SOTA solutions
without training. For example, BACON-style captions help GroundingDINO achieve
1.51x higher recall scores on open-vocabulary object detection tasks compared
to leading methods.

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds hallucination mitigation across downstream tasks. V2 makes caption clarity and caption quality the central contribution, emphasizes training-free downstream integration, and explicitly claims CQA as a newly proposed benchmark. The underlying caption-to-QA evaluation already exists in v1, so its elevation to a named contribution changes the claims rather than establishing an entirely new procedure.

C2.justification: V2 adds an interpretation that stronger regional attention and more consistent answers indicate firmer visual understanding and greater confidence under element-focused prompts. V1 mainly explains improved completeness through explicit object separation. Dependence on human annotation and insufficient captioner grounding remain stated limitations.

D1.justification: V2 documents SAM-2 frame sampling and mask-ID merging, ECO-to-QA examples, and CLIP label matching for detection. It omits v1's maximum sequence length of 2048 and the planning evaluation's 1,000-image sample and matching thresholds. Most captioner hyperparameters, A100 hardware and approximately 100 GPU hours remain documented; these omissions do not establish changed training settings.

E1.justification: ECO retains the earlier BACON dataset, and CQA largely renames existing caption-based VQA coverage. However, v2 uses five additional caption-training datasets, adds MMVP evaluation, and introduces GQA, SQAI, POPE, MMB, MMBCN, SEED and MM-Vet evaluations in Table A2. The BACON/ECO scene-graph evaluation reported in v1 Table 2 is omitted.

E2.justification: V2 Table 2 adds comparisons with LLaVA captioners trained on DOCCI, IIW, DenseFusion, Recap and DCI. Table A2 adds a multimodal comparison including Qwen-VL, Qwen-VL-Chat and VILA-13B. Figure 7 also adds LLaVA to a qualitative detection comparison. The established quantitative detection and scene-graph comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: The scene-graph protocol changes substantially: v1 uses all Visual Genome annotations, separate subject/predicate/object CLIP matching at 0.85, and correct-triplet counts. V2 Appendix D.1 restricts evaluation to triplets outside common categories, matches concatenated triplets at 0.9, and reports recall in Figure 6. V2 also adds Qwen-14B as a fixed caption-QA evaluator and introduces new prompt-analysis protocols.

E4.justification: V2 Figure 2 and Appendix A.1.4 introduce a 1,000-image analysis comparing ordinary and element-focused prompts through spatial attention and answer consistency. Table 1 checks caption evaluation with another QA model, and Figure 7 adds qualitative grounding comparisons. The earlier CLIP/LLaVA grounding ablation is retained.

E5.justification: Appendix A.1.4 newly specifies ten repetitions with different random seeds for each question in the prompt study. Existing plus/minus uncertainty reporting for detection and human evaluations remains. This does not establish increased run counts for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: V2 adds results for caption-dataset comparisons, prompt analyses, another QA evaluator and seven multimodal benchmarks. All OK-VQA/OK-CQA scores are revised, including BACON from 32.1 to 56.8 in v1 Table 3 versus v2 Table 1; the reason is not explained. Scene-graph results are replaced under different conditions. Detection, region QA, user-preference win rates, image-generation and planning results remain unchanged apart from rounding.

M1.justification: The core prompting, graph construction, grounding pipeline and 13B LoRA captioner remain. The video extension switches from the Cheng et al. tracking method to SAM-2, with associated prompting and tracking procedures. Appendix D.6 also introduces LLaVA fine-tuning on automatically generated ECO question-answer pairs. These are bounded extensions to the retained framework.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and much explanatory prose are extensively rewritten. Experiments are reorganized around caption quality followed by downstream assistance; related work moves into the main text, dataset construction joins the method section, and appendices are reorganized into A–D. BACON dataset and captioner terminology changes throughout.

P2.justification: Figures are extensively redrawn and rearranged, with new attention plots, a CQA schematic and comparison tables. The scene-graph table becomes a recall plot; planning results and the editing example move to the appendix. Several illustrations are consolidated or removed, and the document template, captions and table layouts change substantially.

R1.justification: V2 adds substantial positioning against DOCCI, IIW, DenseFusion, Recap and DCI, discussing bounding-box support and annotation costs in Section 2. It also adds SAM-2 and caption-evaluation references. V1's text-decomposition emphasis and Guo et al. ZS-VQA attribution are dropped as caption-based QA is presented as CQA.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix A.1.4 introduces a formal symmetric semantic-consistency score using thresholded T5 sentence matching, including Equation A1. This mathematical definition is absent from v1. Neither version develops substantial theorem or proof content.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Digital imaging systems have traditionally relied on brute-force measurement
and processing of pixels arranged on regular grids. In contrast, the human
visual system performs significant data reduction from the large number of
photoreceptors to the optic nerve, effectively encoding visual information into
a low-bandwidth latent space representation optimized for brain processing.
Inspired by this, we propose a similar approach to advance artificial vision
systems. Latent Space Imaging introduces a new paradigm that combines optics
and software to encode image information directly into the semantically rich
latent space of a generative model. This approach substantially reduces
bandwidth and memory demands during image capture and enables a range of
downstream tasks focused on the latent space. We validate this principle
through an initial hardware prototype based on a single-pixel camera. By
implementing an amplitude modulation scheme that encodes into the generative
model's latent space, we achieve compression ratios ranging from 1:100 to
1:1000 during imaging, and up to 1:16384 for downstream applications. This
approach leverages the model's intrinsic linear boundaries, demonstrating the
potential of latent space imaging for highly efficient imaging hardware,
adaptable future applications in high-speed imaging, and task-specific cameras
with significantly reduced hardware complexity.

D1.justification: v2 adds projector dimensions and feature-selection details, and replaces the promised code release with a statement of implementation availability and a repository URL. Most optimizer, hardware, batch-size, and fine-tuning details are retained. The explicit 98,000-image training total and separate dataset-access instructions in v1 are omitted.

E1.justification: FFHQ, CelebA-HQ, and AFHQ cat/dog reconstruction coverage are retained. v2 adds evaluated tasks involving 40 facial attributes, 18 segmentation classes, and 68 landmarks, substantially extending v1's reconstruction and identity focus. Appendix C.3 also evaluates faces with uncontrolled backgrounds.

E2.justification: v2 retains FSI-DL and binary SAUNet but adds evaluated OCTUF, TCS-Net, CSGM, Non-Latent LSI, and an 8-bit SAUNet variant (Tables 2 and C.1). OCTUF was cited but not evaluated in v1. The earlier LSI-VAE comparison is removed.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Estimating canopy height and its changes at meter resolution from satellite
imagery is a significant challenge in computer vision with critical
environmental applications. However, the lack of open-access datasets at this
resolution hinders the reproducibility and evaluation of models. We introduce
Open-Canopy, the first open-access, country-scale benchmark for very
high-resolution (1.5 m) canopy height estimation, covering over 87,000 km$^2$
across France with 1.5 m resolution satellite imagery and aerial LiDAR data.
Additionally, we present Open-Canopy-$\Delta$, a benchmark for canopy height
change detection between images from different years at tree level-a
challenging task for current computer vision models. We evaluate
state-of-the-art architectures on these benchmarks, highlighting significant
challenges and opportunities for improvement. Our datasets and code are
publicly available at https://github.com/fajwel/Open-Canopy.

C1.justification: Both retain the same central contributions: an open-access, country-scale VHR canopy-height benchmark, a canopy-change benchmark, and evaluations of vision models. The conclusions about hierarchical-transformer performance and the difficulty of change detection remain. Added experiments support these contributions without redefining them.

C2.justification: v3 interprets field checks as supporting ALS reference reliability and distinguishes geographic transfer from strong SPOT-sensor dependence. It adds explanations concerning training from scratch, LoRA, and NIR initialization, plus limitations involving acquisition costs, cloud cover, and seasonal mismatch. The earlier limitation about canopy height being an imperfect biomass proxy is removed.

D1.justification: The detailed preparation and split instructions largely remain. v3 adds annotation-file instructions, LoRA implementation details, preprocessing compute estimates, updated GPU costs, and maintenance information. It reports training code and weights as available instead of promising later release. Prominent links become placeholders, but explicit project and dataset addresses remain in Appendix F.

E1.justification: The French benchmarks remain, but v3 adds a 30 km² Utah evaluation using NEON ground truth with SPOT and NAIP imagery (Table 5). It also evaluates heights against measurements from 135 field plots and 44 individual trees (Appendix A), substantially broadening geographic, sensor, and validation coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds SATLAS-pretrained SWIN to Table 2 and Pauls et al.’s canopy map to Table 3 and the 10 m comparison in Table B. LoRA is additionally compared with full fine-tuning in Tables 4 and D. These extend the retained comparison methods.

E3.justification: Change detection switches from 10 m/100 m² thresholds to 15 m/200 m², with expert review of 73 candidate areas and correction of false-positive reference labels. New protocols include maximum-height comparisons within field plots and tree neighborhoods, and resampling plus histogram matching for NAIP transfer. Existing French splits and standard training settings remain.

E4.justification: v3 adds ground-truth validation, geographic and sensor-transfer tests, NIR-removal ablations, initialization comparisons, LoRA-rank sensitivity, and model error-map comparisons. These investigate reliability, transferability, and design choices beyond v1’s analyses. The earlier height-bin and 10 m evaluations are retained, while change-threshold sensitivity results are revised.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Fixed-seed split sampling and prediction-error distributions remain documented; the new field-validation fit metrics do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Existing height-estimation scores remain, including PVTv2 MAE of 2.52 m. v3 adds substantial validation, transfer, baseline, and ablation results, including Utah PVTv2 MAEs of 2.08 m with SPOT and 4.38 m with NAIP. Change-detection IoU changes from 22.5% to 37.0%, but under revised thresholds and curated masks, not unchanged conditions.

M1.justification: Change-mask inference adopts 15 m/200 m² thresholds instead of 10 m/100 m². Section 3.2 also revises the stated output head from a simple linear layer to a transposed-convolution decoder, without establishing whether retained experiments were rerun. The RGB+NIR initialization scheme and L1 objective remain.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and introduction are rewritten, with greater emphasis on computer-vision challenges. Analysis and limitations passages are expanded or recast, comparison caveats are relocated, and the appendices are substantially reorganized into validation, results, ablations, dataset documentation, preparation, and a datasheet.

P2.justification: v3 switches to a two-column layout and extensively rearranges displays. Figure 1 is repacked and gains Pauls; Figure 4 replaces predicted-height illustrations with error maps. New validation, curation, transfer, and ablation displays are added, and Table 1 is restructured. Earlier appendix illustrations are retained as Figures B and E.

R1.justification: v3 adds literature on SATLAS, Pauls et al., LoRA, additional forest-change methods, alternative open data sources, and dataset documentation, while dropping some carbon-accounting references. The organizing framework and positioning around accessible VHR forestry benchmarks remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The regularized nMAE definition in v1 Equation A-1 is retained in v3 Equation A. Neither version develops formal theorems or proofs, and no substantive mathematical derivation or assumption is added.

improvement.justification: Field validation and expert label curation address previously unquantified reference-data reliability, while transfer and ablation studies expose important applicability limits and test design choices. These substantially strengthen the benchmark’s evidential foundation. Stricter change thresholds narrow the target, so higher IoU is not a demonstrated model improvement. Placeholder links and Figure 4 caption errors weaken presentation, but access addresses remain in Appendix F and the scientific gains outweigh these defects.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Open-Canopy and Open-Canopy-∆ research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and matchable despite substantial reorganization and added studies.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark results and adds field validation, Utah transfer experiments, and initialization and infrared-channel ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, canopy-map comparisons, change-detection results, and supplementary sensitivity analyses in Tables 2–4 and A-1–A-3.

arxiv_record.abstract:
State-space models (SSMs) have recently shown promise in capturing long-range
dependencies with subquadratic computational complexity, making them attractive
for various applications. However, purely SSM-based models face critical
challenges related to stability and achieving state-of-the-art performance in
computer vision tasks. Our paper addresses the challenges of scaling SSM-based
models for computer vision, particularly the instability and inefficiency of
large model sizes. We introduce a parameter-efficient modulated group mamba
layer that divides the input channels into four groups and applies our proposed
SSM-based efficient Visual Single Selective Scanning (VSSS) block independently
to each group, with each VSSS block scanning in one of the four spatial
directions. The Modulated Group Mamba layer also wraps the four VSSS blocks
into a channel modulation operator to improve cross-channel communication.
Furthermore, we introduce a distillation-based training objective to stabilize
the training of large models, leading to consistent performance gains. Our
comprehensive experiments demonstrate the merits of the proposed contributions,
leading to superior performance over existing methods for image classification
on ImageNet-1K, object detection, instance segmentation on MS-COCO, and
semantic segmentation on ADE20K. Our tiny variant with 23M parameters achieves
state-of-the-art performance with a classification top-1 accuracy of 83.3% on
ImageNet-1K, while being 26% efficient in terms of parameters, compared to the
best existing Mamba design of same model size. Code and models are available
at: https://github.com/Amshaker/GroupMamba.

Abdelrahman Shaker, Syed Talal Wasim, Salman Khan, Juergen Gall, Fahad
  Shahbaz Khan

C1.justification: The central grouped-scanning, CAM and distillation contributions and headline accuracy claims are retained. The conclusion extends the claimed efficiency advantage to measured throughput, beyond v1's concluding emphasis on fewer parameters.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of scale-dependent distillation gains and the four-group efficiency tradeoff. Its new limitations section acknowledges modest downstream gains over VMamba, discusses localization and task-specific requirements, and identifies reliance on external teachers. These materially qualify applicability and efficiency claims that v1 leaves largely unqualified.

D1.justification: v2 Table 6 supplies previously missing per-variant channel widths, block depths, convolution kernels and strides, substantially improving architectural documentation. Figure 4 specifies the throughput hardware and batch size. The code/model access link is unchanged, while the relationship between the newly specified depths and v1's schematic remains unexplained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same tasks on ImageNet-1K, COCO 2017 and ADE20K. Added ablations and qualitative examples remain within this coverage. Video recognition and time-series applications appear only as future work.

E2.justification: v2 removes EffNet-B6 from Table 1, PVTv2-B2 from the COCO comparison, and DeiT-S + MLN, ViM-S and EfficientVMamba-B from the ADE20K comparison. Figure 4 adds a separate VMamba-T V1 comparator alongside V2 and broadens the component comparison to other existing SSM baselines.

E3.justification: v2 introduces throughput evaluation using one NVIDIA A100 and batch size 128, with additional scanning/group-count controls and Small/Base distillation comparisons. The stated benchmark splits, training schedules and optimization settings remain unchanged. ADE20K parameter and FLOP metrics are no longer reported.

E4.justification: v1's Tiny-model CAM, distillation and parameter-matched tests are retained and reorganized. v2 substantially expands analysis through 4-D versus 1-D scanning, one/two/four-direction comparisons, two/four/eight-group sensitivity, Small/Base distillation ablations, training-loss curves and additional qualitative examples. The parameter-matched comparison in v2 Table 5 already existed in v1 Table 4.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 5 newly reports shaded standard-deviation bands for training loss, described in Section 8 as variability across training epochs. Neither version specifies independent-run counts or seeds, and v2 does not explain the band-estimation procedure sufficiently to infer repeated-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial throughput, scanning/grouping and loss-curve results, including undistilled Small/Base accuracies of 83.0%/83.2%. Main classification, AP and mIoU scores remain unchanged. Tiny-model FLOPs change from 4.6G to 4.5G in Table 1; the matched 31M variant changes from 5.4G to 5.2G between v1 Table 4 and v2 Table 5. Several baseline entries and ADE20K resource results disappear.

M1.justification: The VSSS, CAM and distillation equations remain unchanged. However, v1 Figure 2 specifies stage depths of 3/4/6/3, whereas v2 replaces these with symbols and Table 6 specifies 2/2/9/2 for Tiny and 2/2/20/2 for Small/Base. The PDFs do not establish whether this corrects the earlier diagram or reflects an actual architecture change.

P1.justification: Most introduction, related-work and method prose retains its wording and sequence. v2 revises the title and affiliations, expands selected explanations, rewrites the ablation narrative, extends the conclusion with future work, and organizes supplementary material into dedicated sections.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws Figure 2, merges the COCO/ADE20K tables, and introduces throughput and training-loss graphics plus an architecture table. The earlier qualitative grids move to supplementary Figures 6–7, while the main qualitative display includes additional examples. These are substantial display and layout revisions.

R1.justification: v2 adds Squeeze-and-Excitation Networks and explicitly discusses CAM's relationship to SE in Section 3.3.3, positioning CAM around inter-group communication in Mamba. The PVT v2 reference disappears with its comparison row. The broader related-work discussion remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 changes the stated dimensions of both SSM projection matrices B and C from N×1 to 1×N, a limited revision to the formal specification. The continuous/discrete SSM equations and model/loss equations otherwise remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for central efficiency and stabilization claims through measured throughput, scanning/grouping controls, and larger-model distillation analyses, beyond v1's Tiny-model component tests. Detailed architecture configurations and explicit limitations also improve reproducibility and interpretation. These gains outweigh removed comparator/resource entries, although unexplained stage-depth differences, inconsistent FLOP reporting and underspecified loss-variability bands remain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GroupMamba, and their text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 includes readable supplementary Sections 7–11. Changes in title, layout and placement do not prevent matching content.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds throughput measurements, scanning and grouping ablations, larger-model distillation comparisons, and training-loss analysis.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.4 report original ImageNet-1K classification, COCO detection and instance segmentation, ADE20K semantic segmentation, and component-ablation results.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Text-to-video (T2V) generative models have advanced significantly, yet their
ability to compose different objects, attributes, actions, and motions into a
video remains unexplored. Previous text-to-video benchmarks also neglect this
important ability for evaluation. In this work, we conduct the first systematic
study on compositional text-to-video generation. We propose T2V-CompBench, the
first benchmark tailored for compositional text-to-video generation.
T2V-CompBench encompasses diverse aspects of compositionality, including
consistent attribute binding, dynamic attribute binding, spatial relationships,
motion binding, action binding, object interactions, and generative numeracy.
We further carefully design evaluation metrics of multimodal large language
model (MLLM)-based, detection-based, and tracking-based metrics, which can
better reflect the compositional text-to-video generation quality of seven
proposed categories with 1400 text prompts. The effectiveness of the proposed
metrics is verified by correlation with human evaluations. We also benchmark
various text-to-video generative models and conduct in-depth analysis across
different models and various compositional categories. We find that
compositional text-to-video generation is highly challenging for current
models, and we hope our attempt could shed light on future research in this
direction.

C1.justification: The headline benchmark contribution increases from 700 to 1,400 prompts in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. The central claims remain: the first systematic compositional T2V benchmark, seven categories, tailored metrics validated against humans, and substantial difficulties for existing generators.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations distinguishing successful object generation from relationship understanding and motion magnitude from directional control, alongside explanations of subgroup difficulty. Appendix G newly explains why fixed-frame evaluation may fail for longer videos and why longer duration can favor motion scores. The earlier limitation concerning the absence of a unified metric is retained.

D1.justification: v2 documents vocabulary-selection thresholds and word-list access, generated frame counts, MLLM repetition settings, and detailed AMT worker screening and quality-control rules. Conversely, it omits v1's explicit list of six human-study generators and six category-specific annotation interfaces. Reproducibility information is substantially expanded and revised, with some detail lost.

E1.justification: The seven compositional tasks remain, but v2 revises the represented prompt vocabulary using frequent nouns and verbs from VidProM's real-user prompts and TempCompass examples for attribute changes. These sources inform benchmark construction; they are not separately evaluated video-generation benchmarks. The increase in prompt count is assessed under E3.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds Vico, T2V-Turbo-V2, CogVideoX-5B, and Mochi, replaces Open-Sora-Plan v1.1.0 with v1.3.0, and removes Dream Machine. Table 1 adds B-BLEU, ViCLIP, VPEval-S, and M-GDino. It also removes the LLaVA comparisons for dynamic attributes and motion, while retaining LLaVA in other categories.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from 100 to 200 prompts per category, revises subgroup allocations, and introduces matched quantity-group prompts and diagnostic measures. Reported generation settings also change: VideoCrafter2 moves from 2.7 seconds at 24 FPS to 2 seconds at 8 FPS. Human evaluation decreases from 656 to 651 videos, with interaction ground-truth videos reduced from 16 to 11. These are reported protocol changes, without independently establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds sample-count stability studies across all seven categories in Appendix A.4 and extensive diagnostic analyses in Appendix D. These separate object coexistence from spatial correctness, motion magnitude from direction accuracy, common from uncommon actions, and physical from social interactions. Table 4 and Figure 22 add subgroup and object-count analyses beyond v1's aggregate results and qualitative examples.

E5.justification: v1 reports three human raters but no MLLM seed-variability study. v2's Appendix C.2 reports eight seed-varied Grid-LLaVA evaluations, repeated sampling of two- and three-run averages, and correlation distributions in Figure 19. It adopts averaging three scores per video, adding an explicit statistical reliability study and aggregation practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 contain extensive numerical and ranking changes, and Table 4 adds subgroup results. For example, Grid-LLaVA's consistent-attribute Spearman correlation changes from 0.8679 to 0.7893, while v2's Table 2 places PixVerse-V3 first in six categories. Changed prompts, scoring procedures, and model versions prevent treating these revisions as matched-setting performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: The MLLM evaluation procedures change substantively. v1's joint action and interaction scoring prompts become presence-conditioned, multi-stage queries in v2's Appendix C.1 and Figure 18. Dynamic-attribute grading adds an intermediate-frame option for both states. v2 also introduces frequency-based vocabulary selection into benchmark construction, beyond the category-based GPT-4 prompting documented in v1.

P1.justification: The benchmark-construction and experimental narratives are extensively rewritten and reorganized. Model descriptions move from the appendix into Section 5.1, related work gains numbered subsections, and the appendices are reorganized from A–D into A–H with a contents list. Prompt templates move to Appendix H, while limitations and societal impacts receive separate sections.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws overview and prompt-generation figures, replaces the word-cloud display with new statistics, and restructures comparison tables by metric family and model architecture. It adds stability plots, an MLLM query diagram, subgroup tables, and diagnostic visualizations. Seven human-evaluation interface figures are reduced to one.

R1.justification: Related work adds a substantive comparison with ChronoMagic-Bench concerning natural versus artificial attribute changes, alongside references supporting new data sources, evaluators, and generators. The model discussion shifts toward UNet versus DiT architectures. The central positioning relative to compositional image benchmarks and general video benchmarks remains.

T1.justification: Appendix D.3–D.4 adds quantitative definitions for coexistence, conditional spatial accuracy, correct-layout scores, and motion accuracy requiring at least five units of displacement after 100-by-100 normalization. These are limited additions to mathematical measurement definitions. The existing spatial and relative-motion formulations remain, and neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens benchmark validation through sample-size stability and seed-variability evidence absent from v1. Its subgroup analyses make aggregate scores more interpretable, while documented vocabulary selection, annotation controls, and long-video limitations improve assessability. These gains outweigh lost annotation details and localized reporting errors, including Appendix D.2 assigning the dynamic-attribute score 0.0687 to PixVerse-V3 although Table 2 assigns it to Gen-3.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe T2V-CompBench, with the same authors, research objective, and seven compositional categories. Their complete main texts, appendices, tables, figures, and mathematical content support reliable comparison despite extensive revision and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 reports original model evaluations, human correlations, prompt-distribution analyses, seed and sample-size studies, and category-specific results in Tables 1–4 and the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original generated-video evaluations and human-correlation experiments in Section 5 and Tables 1–2, with study details in the appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: Object-centric learning aims to decompose an input image into a set of meaningful object files (slots). These latent object representations enable a variety of downstream tasks. Yet, object-centric learning struggles on real-world datasets, which contain multiple objects of complex textures and shapes in natural everyday scenes. To address this, we introduce Guided Latent Slot Diffusion (GLASS), a novel slot-attention model that learns in the space of generated images and uses semantic and instance guidance modules to learn better slot embeddings for various downstream tasks. Our experiments show that GLASS surpasses state-of-the-art slot-attention methods by a wide margin on tasks such as (zero-shot) object discovery and conditional image generation for real-world scenes. Moreover, GLASS enables the first application of slot attention to the compositional generation of complex, realistic scenes.
arxiv_record.authors: Krishnakant Singh, Simone Schaub-Meyer, Stefan Roth
arxiv_record.title: GLASS: Guided Latent Slot Diffusion for Object-Centric Learning

C1.justification: V2 reframes the contribution around joint semantic and instance guidance and better instance-level representations. Its abstract, introduction, and conclusion add zero-shot discovery claims and a claimed first high-fidelity compositional generation capability for complex real-world scenes using slot attention. Property prediction changes from comparable or slightly worse performance in v1 to claimed superiority over StableLSD in v2.

C2.justification: V1 identifies grouping same-class instances as a limitation. V2 explains how semantic guidance causes this drift and how feature reconstruction counteracts it, supported by component analyses. It adds limitations concerning slot-count sensitivity, residual semantic grouping, and generation quality, discusses weaker FG-ARI results, and explicitly qualifies the comparability of image-based GLASS and text-based Composable Diffusion.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands reproducibility information: explicit dataset splits, MLP architecture, per-module learning rates for both training phases, pseudo-mask thresholds and ignored regions, and property-prediction optimization details. Hardware reporting changes to an A6000 Ada GPU. V2 states that code is available and supplies access information, whereas v1 promises release upon acceptance.

E1.justification: V2 retains COCO and VOC experiments but adds zero-shot object discovery on CLEVRTex and Objects365 (Table 4), object-position prediction alongside label prediction (Table 8), and demonstrated object addition, removal, and cross-image composition (Figures 6, 9, 12, and 13). These substantially expand the evaluated tasks and environments.

E2.justification: V2 adds SPOT to OCL comparisons and DeepSpectral, COMUS, DiffCut, and EmerDiff to semantic segmentation comparisons. It also evaluates SAMv2-derived guidance, an adapted DatasetDiffusion control, and Composable Diffusion. V1's StableLSD-Mask and StableLSD-Box guidance comparators disappear; bounding-box initialization remains a separate retained comparator.

E3.justification: Reported generated training-set sizes change from approximately 118K/12K to 100K/10K images for COCO/VOC, GRU iterations from three to five, and VOC slots from six to seven. V2 adds instance mIoU, SO-PO-GO, FG-ARI, and additional reconstruction metrics while dropping CorLoc/DetRate. FID uses 512 COCO images instead of 1,024 images per dataset, and property-prediction training changes from 6K steps to epoch-based training with early stopping.

E4.justification: V2 adds loss-component ablations, encoder comparisons, SAMv2 guidance failure analysis, slot-count sensitivity, and caption-generator/template ablations (Table 6; supplement Sections 4 and 7). Zero-shot transfer and SO-PO-GO examine generalization and segmentation errors, while an adapted DatasetDiffusion control tests the source of gains. V1's stronger-guidance and guided-DINOSAUR analyses are removed rather than relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run or seed counts or reports standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The expanded result tables retain single-score reporting.

E6.justification: Results are extensively revised and expanded. V1 Table 2 reports GLASS semantic mIoU of 43.7/64.0 on COCO/VOC; v2 Table 9 reports 46.7/68.9 for the new GLASS-Sem variant. MaskCLIP's reported COCO score changes from 23.6 to 20.6. COCO FID for StableLSD/GLASS changes from 78.47/73.06 to 140.62/71.30, but model and sampling changes prevent a same-setting performance comparison. Zero-shot, ablation, position-prediction, and compositional results are newly reported.

M1.justification: V1 combines image reconstruction with semantic-mask guidance and keeps the diffusion decoder frozen. V2 adds an MLP feature decoder and instance-guidance loss, introduces weighted semantic/instance objectives, and uses two-phase training that includes training the diffusion decoder. It also introduces the semantic-focused GLASS-Sem variant (Section 4; supplement Section 2).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, experiments, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Experiments are reorganized into instance-aware discovery, generation, property prediction, and semantic discovery. Dataset and training documentation moves into a restructured supplement, limitations move into the main text, and the broader-impact statement is removed.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Architecture diagrams are redrawn to show instance guidance and the MLP decoder. Segmentation and reconstruction displays are reorganized, earlier bar/scatter presentations give way to tables, and new ablation, SAMv2, and compositional-generation displays are added. The guided-DINOSAUR and dedicated drawback figures are removed.

R1.justification: V2 substantially revises positioning toward instance-aware representations and real-world compositional generation. It incorporates work including SPOT, SAM 2, DiffCut, EmerDiff, and Composable Diffusion, while trimming Gestalt and general self-supervised-learning background. Section 2 and Table 1 now distinguish instance-level discovery, semantic discovery, and compositional capabilities, and novelty is framed around combining semantic and instance guidance.

T1.justification: The formally defined objective changes from reconstruction plus binary cross-entropy in v1 Equation 4 to weighted semantic guidance plus an additional feature-reconstruction term in v2 Equation 3. This extends the mathematical specification, while the slot-attention and Hungarian-matching formulations remain essentially unchanged. Neither version develops theorem or proof results.

improvement.justification: V2 directly addresses v1's important limitation of grouping same-class instances and tests the proposed remedy through controlled loss ablations. In v2 Table 6a, adding instance guidance to reconstruction plus semantic guidance raises COCO instance mIoU from 30.9 to 38.9. Stronger comparators, transfer tests, and substantially fuller implementation documentation strengthen the paper's evidence and reproducibility. Some earlier analyses are lost and changed protocols limit cross-version score comparisons, but the improved validation of the central mechanism provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GLASS by the same authors. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary material support a reliable comparison despite substantial revision.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Image-based virtual try-on is an increasingly popular and important task to
generate realistic try-on images of the specific person. Recent methods model
virtual try-on as image mask-inpaint task, which requires masking the person
image and results in significant loss of spatial information. Especially, for
in-the-wild try-on scenarios with complex poses and occlusions, mask-based
methods often introduce noticeable artifacts. Our research found that a
mask-free approach can fully leverage spatial and lighting information from the
original person image, enabling high-quality virtual try-on. Consequently, we
propose a novel training paradigm for a mask-free try-on diffusion model. We
ensure the model's mask-free try-on capability by creating high-quality
pseudo-data and further enhance its handling of complex spatial information
through effective in-the-wild data augmentation. Besides, a try-on localization
loss is designed to concentrate on try-on area while suppressing garment
features in non-try-on areas, ensuring precise rendering of garments and
preservation of fore/back-ground. In the end, we introduce BooW-VTON, the
mask-free virtual try-on diffusion model, which delivers SOTA try-on quality
without parsing cost. Extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments have
demonstrated superior performance in wild scenarios with such a low-demand
input.
