C1.justification: The central claims about mask-free pseudo-data training, wild augmentation and localization loss remain. However, v2 strengthens the input-efficiency claim from requiring a source pose image to requiring no additional parser during inference, explicitly reflected in its abstract and contribution list.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of distillation overfitting, the differing benefits of refined pseudo-data and augmentation, and attention behavior across denoising stages. It qualifies the StreetVTON KID comparison and introduces a concrete controllability limitation: replacing a dress with only a top reference leaves the lower garment uncontrolled (Section 6).

D1.justification: v2 discloses SDXL/IP-Adapter/Reference Net details, loss attachment locations, training time, inference hardware and sampling steps, and standardized evaluation resolution. Supplementary Section 1 and Tables 4–5 add augmentation image counts, resolutions, probabilities, transformations and full prompts. Conversely, v1's promised code-release URL is omitted.

E1.justification: The four datasets and the in-shop, wild, anime and multi-garment scenarios are retained. v2 adds prompt-controlled garment rendering and missing-reference-garment demonstrations (Figures 9–10). WildVTON's increased sample count changes the protocol rather than establishing a new domain.

E2.justification: v2 removes GP-VTON from the VITON-HD comparison and adds CAT-DM. Its wild-scene comparisons additionally evaluate DCI-VTON, LaDI-VTON and TPD alongside StableVITON, OOTD and IDM-VTON. TPD corresponds to the baseline mislabeled 'TBD' in v1's Table 2, rather than being an entirely new comparator.

E3.justification: v1 reports only unpaired FID/KID testing. v2 adds paired testing using generated pseudo-pairs, with LPIPS, SSIM, PSNR and paired FID/KID, and expands WildVTON from 200 to 1,224 images. The stated learning rate, batch size and 12,000-step training budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 extends v1's augmentation/localization ablations with a high-quality pseudo-data component and in-shop evaluation. Figures 8 and 18–20 add component comparisons and attention analyses across denoising steps and network blocks. Figure 10 supplies a concrete failure case involving an unspecified garment.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Additional metric values and attention visualizations in v2 do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 add paired results and expanded ablations, while revising numerous unpaired scores. Reported VITON-HD FID/KID changes from 9.474/0.871 to 8.809/0.8176. In v2, newly evaluated DCI-VTON beats BooW-VTON on StreetVTON KID, 3.470 versus 4.494. WildVTON scores use the enlarged test set and are not same-setting improvements.

M1.justification: v1 conditions the try-on network on DensePose; v2 removes that input, enabling parser-free inference. v2 also introduces two-stage pseudo-image generation using a coarse mask followed by the union of original and intermediate garment regions (Section 4.2, Figure 3). The underlying augmentation and localization-loss approach remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related-work argument and results discussion undergo substantial rewriting. v2 reorganizes the method into numbered subsections, adds dedicated application and limitations sections, and supplies a structured supplement. These changes substantially revise the narrative beyond merely inserting new results.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the motivation and pipeline figures, reorganizes qualitative comparisons, and restructures quantitative tables to separate DressCode results and integrate ablations with paired metrics. New displays cover data generation, applications, failures, attention heatmaps, augmentation assets and dataset examples. v1's localization diagram is retained as Figure 5.

R1.justification: v1 motivates diffusion by characterizing earlier mask-free approaches as GAN-based. v2 acknowledges PFDM and repositions its contribution around overcoming errors transferred through teacher-student distillation. It also adds relevant architecture, try-on and attention-analysis literature, including SDXL, IP-Adapter, AnyFit and diffusion correspondence studies.

T1.justification: The conditioning definition accompanying Equation 4 changes from concatenated person and DensePose latents to the person latent alone. The remaining diffusion derivation and attention-regularization mathematics retain their substantive forms; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper's experimental support and reproducibility: paired fidelity measurements supplement v1's distribution metrics, broader wild-scene comparisons and component analyses improve validation, and the supplement supplies previously missing augmentation and inference details. Concrete limitations also clarify applicability. The paired tests use pseudo-pairs, expanded WildVTON scores are not directly comparable, and the code-release link disappears, but these qualifications do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BooW-VTON and provide readable text, equations, tables and figures. The comparison includes all supplementary material in v2; v1 ends with references and has no supplementary section.

after.justification: v2 reports original paired and unpaired evaluations, component ablations, application examples and supplementary attention analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract:
We present Text-driven object-centric style editing model named Style-Editor,
a novel method that guides style editing at an object-centric level using
textual inputs. The core of Style-Editor is our Patch-wise Co-Directional (PCD)
loss, meticulously designed for precise object-centric editing that are closely
aligned with the input text. This loss combines a patch directional loss for
text-guided style direction and a patch distribution consistency loss for even
CLIP embedding distribution across object regions. It ensures a seamless and
harmonious style editing across object regions. Key to our method are the
Text-Matched Patch Selection (TMPS) and Pre-fixed Region Selection (PRS)
modules for identifying object locations via text, eliminating the need for
segmentation masks. Lastly, we introduce an Adaptive Background Preservation
(ABP) loss to maintain the original style and structural essence of the image's
background. This loss is applied to dynamically identified background areas.
Extensive experiments underline the effectiveness of our approach in creating
visually coherent and textually aligned style editing.
arxiv_record.authors: Jihun Park, Jongmin Gim, Kyoungmin Lee, Seunghun Lee and Sunghoon Im
arxiv_record.title: Style-Editor: Text-driven object-centric style editing

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of the patch-size fidelity/stylization tradeoff, smooth boundaries versus binary segmentation, and the expanded evaluation's quality-speed balance and generalization implications. The existing limitation concerning CLIP's coverage of unfamiliar objects and styles is retained.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies PRS threshold tau = 2, documents the default 64–128 patch-size range, and explains foreground masking and cropping for evaluation in Appendix C. It also clarifies that optimization uses only the source image and texts. These disclosures do not demonstrate changes to previously run experiments.

E1.justification: The work retains text-guided object editing of natural images, COCO 2017 evaluation, and color, texture, artistic-style and complex-prompt scenarios. The expanded COCO sample and new application illustrations retain the existing task and input requirements.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the existing baselines and adds pix2pix-zero, LEDITS++, local-prompt-mixing and StylerDALLE. The user study adds FlexIT, LEDITS++ and Null-text inversion as competitors. Appendix B.5 also compares the proposed outputs with an ODISE-masked variant.

E3.justification: The original 16-image, 10-style evaluation remains. v3 adds a 50-image, 500-output evaluation with comparative timing, fixed and variable patch-size controls, and two user-study rounds involving different competitor sets. The reported participant count remains 50. These substantially extend evaluation design without establishing changes to the original training setup.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained loss ablations, training visualization, complex-prompt examples and failure cases, v3 adds fixed and adaptive patch-size sensitivity experiments in Tables 4–5. Appendix B.5 and Figure 11 add a boundary-artifact case comparing unmasked outputs with ODISE-masked outputs, extending analysis of the patch-based design.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Appendix B.3 retains the same 10-repeat timing procedure. The additional user-study round introduces different comparison conditions, rather than repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The original values in Tables 1–3 remain unchanged, while v3 adds baseline, sensitivity and expanded-evaluation results. Table 7 reports SimF 0.31, ConF 3.09 and PSNRB 26.71 for the proposed method. User-study style/background/content preferences change from 65.1/65.7/82.2% to averages of 66/64.4/78.6%. Changed samples and comparison panels prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains or losses.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2, losses in Equations 1–6, StyleNet architecture and target-text construction remain unchanged. The TEXTOC-to-Style-Editor renaming and newly documented threshold and patch-size range do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: v3 renames the paper and method, revises selected introductory and related-work passages, and retains most methodological prose. Complex-input experiments move to Appendix D, the mask-guided comparison moves into Section 4.5, and references move before the appendices. The overall narrative structure remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the main comparison table and image grid, adds Tables 4–5 and 7, and introduces application, segmentation-comparison and metric-visualization figures. Existing appendix galleries are enlarged, detail crops are added, and several figures are relocated. These are substantive display changes beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: Sections 2.1 and 2.3 update the discussion with attention-based style transfer and more detailed diffusion-editing context, including AdaAttN, Aespa-Net and newer editing methods. ArtFlow, VQGAN-CLIP and Generative Artisan are removed. The central positioning around content-preserving, mask-free object editing remains.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the retained method: patch-size tests and the boundary comparison examine previously untested design choices, additional baselines broaden comparison, and the larger COCO evaluation tests whether findings persist across more images. arxiv_record.abstract:
In this paper, we present DV-Matcher, a novel learning-based framework for
estimating dense correspondences between non-rigidly deformable point clouds.
Learning directly from unstructured point clouds without meshing or manual
labelling, our framework delivers high-quality dense correspondences, which is
of significant practical utility in point cloud processing. Our key
contributions are two-fold: First, we propose a scheme to inject prior
knowledge from pre-trained vision models into geometric feature learning, which
effectively complements the local nature of geometric features with global and
semantic information; Second, we propose a novel deformation-based module to
promote the extrinsic alignment induced by the learned correspondences, which
effectively enhances the feature learning. Experimental results show that our
method achieves state-of-the-art results in matching non-rigid point clouds in
both near-isometric and heterogeneous shape collection as well as more
realistic partial and noisy data.
arxiv_record.authors: Zhangquan Chen, Puhua Jiang, Ruqi Huang
arxiv_record.title:
DV-Matcher: Deformation-based Non-Rigid Point Cloud Matching Guided by
  Pre-trained Visual Features

arxiv_record.abstract:
Estimating video depth in open-world scenarios is challenging due to the
diversity of videos in appearance, content motion, camera movement, and length.
We present DepthCrafter, an innovative method for generating temporally
consistent long depth sequences with intricate details for open-world videos,
without requiring any supplementary information such as camera poses or optical
flow. The generalization ability to open-world videos is achieved by training
the video-to-depth model from a pre-trained image-to-video diffusion model,
through our meticulously designed three-stage training strategy. Our training
approach enables the model to generate depth sequences with variable lengths at
one time, up to 110 frames, and harvest both precise depth details and rich
content diversity from realistic and synthetic datasets. We also propose an
inference strategy that can process extremely long videos through segment-wise
estimation and seamless stitching. Comprehensive evaluations on multiple
datasets reveal that DepthCrafter achieves state-of-the-art performance in
open-world video depth estimation under zero-shot settings. Furthermore,
DepthCrafter facilitates various downstream applications, including depth-based
visual effects and conditional video generation.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Touch contact and pressure are essential for understanding how humans
interact with and manipulate objects, insights which can significantly benefit
applications in mixed reality and robotics. However, estimating these
interactions from an egocentric camera perspective is challenging, largely due
to the lack of comprehensive datasets that provide both accurate hand poses on
contacting surfaces and detailed annotations of pressure information. In this
paper, we introduce EgoPressure, a novel egocentric dataset that captures
detailed touch contact and pressure interactions. EgoPressure provides
high-resolution pressure intensity annotations for each contact point and
includes accurate hand pose meshes obtained through our proposed multi-view,
sequence-based optimization method processing data from an 8-camera capture
rig. Our dataset comprises 5 hours of recorded interactions from 21
participants captured simultaneously by one head-mounted and seven stationary
Kinect cameras, which acquire RGB images and depth maps at 30 Hz. To support
future research and benchmarking, we present several baseline models for
estimating applied pressure on external surfaces from RGB images, with and
without hand pose information. We further explore the joint estimation of the
hand mesh and applied pressure. Our experiments demonstrate that pressure and
hand pose are complementary for understanding hand-object interactions. ng of
hand-object interactions in AR/VR and robotics research. Project page:
\url{https://yiming-zhao.github.io/EgoPressure/}.

However, existing contact pressure datasets lack egocentric views and hand poses, which are essential for accurate estimation during in-situ operation, both for AR/VR interaction and robotic manipulation.In this paper, we introduce  a novel dataset of touch contact and pressure interaction from an egocentric perspective, complemented with hand pose meshes and fine-grained pressure intensities for each contact. The hand poses in our dataset are optimized using our proposed multi-view sequence-based method that processes footage from our capture rig of 8 accurately calibrated RGBD cameras.  comprises 5.0 hours of touch contact and pressure interaction from 21 participants captured by a moving egocentric camera and 7 stationary Kinect cameras, which provided RGB images and depth maps at 30 Hz. In addition, we provide baselines for estimating pressure with different modalities, which will enable future developments and benchmarking on the dataset. Overall, we demonstrate that pressure and hand poses are complementary, which supports our intention to better facilitate the physical understanding of hand-object interactions in AR/VR and robotics research

arxiv_record.abstract:
High-quality view synthesis relies on volume rendering, splatting, or surface
rendering. While surface rendering is typically the fastest, it struggles to
accurately model fuzzy geometry like hair. In turn, alpha-blending techniques
excel at representing fuzzy materials but require an unbounded number of
samples per ray (P1). Further overheads are induced by empty space skipping in
volume rendering (P2) and sorting input primitives in splatting (P3). We
present a novel representation for real-time view synthesis where the (P1)
number of sampling locations is small and bounded, (P2) sampling locations are
efficiently found via rasterization, and (P3) rendering is sorting-free. We
achieve this by representing objects as semi-transparent multi-layer meshes
rendered in a fixed order. First, we model surface layers as signed distance
function (SDF) shells with optimal spacing learned during training. Then, we
bake them as meshes and fit UV textures. Unlike single-surface methods, our

C1.justification: Both versions claim that a small, bounded number of adaptively spaced mesh shells enables sorting-free rasterization, better fuzzy-object representation than single-surface approaches, and faster rendering than volumetric alternatives on modest hardware. V2 emphasizes smartphones more explicitly but retains the contribution's meaning and scope.

C2.justification: V2 revises the explanation for inward initialization: v1 emphasizes transparent outer layers losing gradients, whereas v2 emphasizes outward geometry expansion and poor test-view generalization. It also explains the baked-versus-implicit quality gap and adds grazing-angle limitations and the possible use of textured fins. Existing sparse-view, thin-structure, and solid-scene limitations remain.

D1.justification: New Section S1 supplies previously missing network widths, activations, encodings, density-schedule endpoints, finite-difference settings, ray-sample counts, batch limits, and data-loading information. V2 also identifies the 3DGS web viewer and its sorting behavior and explicitly states that its final quality metrics come from WebGL renders. These additions substantially improve implementation and evaluation reproducibility.

E1.justification: Both evaluate Shelly, the custom plushy and hairy-monkey scenes, DTU scans 83 and 105, and NeRF-Synthetic in the supplement. The smartphone and laptop environments also remain the same. Added comparisons use this existing coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds MobileNeRF to the speed/memory comparison in Table 2 and to the existing Custom image-quality comparison in Table 3 and Table S1. These comparisons were absent in v1. QuadFields' memory result remains available in the Table 3 caption rather than being removed.

E3.justification: V2 adds optimization conditions capping 3DGS at 50,000 and 75,000 Gaussians, introducing resource-budget controls in Table 2. The principal training budgets, image-quality metrics, cleaned Shelly evaluation, and stated 720p timing devices remain unchanged. Newly specified network and sampling settings primarily document existing experiments.

E4.justification: Table 4 adds an outside-versus-inside shell-initialization ablation: outside initialization yields 30.85 PSNR versus 34.25 for the full 5-Mesh model. Figures S5 and S6 add qualitative comparisons with capped 3DGS and MobileNeRF. The previous four ablations, texture-resolution study, and solid-scene generalization analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both primarily provide point estimates and averages across scenes; the discussed logistic-distribution standard deviation is a model parameter, not experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: Reported quality, speed, and memory results change substantially across the main and supplementary tables. For example, 7-Mesh smartphone speed changes from 27.5 to 42 FPS under the stated 720p Samsung A52s setup, while Shelly PSNR changes from 34.331 to 34.50. V2 also adds comparison and ablation results and corrects 3DGS Shelly SSIM/LPIPS from 0.964/0.064 to 0.975/0.089, matching the retained per-scene values. The PDFs do not explain the causes of all numerical revisions.

M1.justification: Both versions use nested k-SDF shells, learned offsets, view-dependent appearance and transparency, fixed-order blending, and staged optimization followed by mixed-resolution texture baking. V2 supplies architectural details and clarifies sampling descriptions without establishing a change to the underlying procedure.

P1.justification: V2 extensively edits the abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations, evaluation, and limitations. It consolidates v1 Sections 4.3–4.5 into Section 4.3 and reorganizes the supplement into S1–S4. The title terminology also changes from 'Multiple' to 'Layered' meshes.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redrawn with an additional explanatory panel, and Figure 6 switches from laptop to smartphone results with expanded comparisons. The two ablation tables are merged, the resolution study is relocated, and supplementary displays are reorganized. Render-buffer figures gain blending-weight panels, and new Figures S5–S6 present qualitative comparisons.

R1.justification: V2 explicitly grounds the representation in classical textured-shell fur rendering, citing Kenwright and Lengyel, and distinguishes its learned shells from Gaussian Shell Maps and Gaussian Frosting. It also adds SuGaR and implementation references. This materially expands the discussion of closely related foundations and alternatives beyond v1's positioning.

T1.justification: The rendering equations, shell construction, blending formulation, and transparency attenuation remain mathematically equivalent. Distinguishing relative from cumulative offsets clarifies existing notation. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves substantial reproducibility omissions through Section S1 and strengthens evidence for its central mobile-rendering claim through MobileNeRF timings and Gaussian-count controls. The initialization ablation tests a previously unquantified design choice, and corrected 3DGS averages restore agreement with the appendix. Better treatment of prior shell methods and clearer limitations further improve the paper. Unexplained numerical revisions and the retained Shelly comparability caveat limit interpretation, but the documentation and evidential gains are substantial.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction-quality results, rendering-speed measurements, ablations, and supplementary experiments on fully solid scenes.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have emerged as a promising substitute for
Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) due to their advantages of fast inference and
low power consumption. However, the lack of efficient training algorithms has
hindered their widespread adoption. Even efficient ANN-SNN conversion methods
necessitate quantized training of ANNs to enhance the effectiveness of the
conversion, incurring additional training costs. To address these challenges,
we propose an efficient ANN-SNN conversion framework with only inference scale
complexity. The conversion framework includes a local threshold balancing
algorithm, which enables efficient calculation of the optimal thresholds and
fine-grained adjustment of the threshold value by channel-wise scaling. We also
introduce an effective delayed evaluation strategy to mitigate the influence of
the spike propagation delays. We demonstrate the scalability of our framework
in typical computer vision tasks: image classification, semantic segmentation,
object detection, and video classification. Our algorithm outperforms existing
methods, highlighting its practical applicability and efficiency. Moreover, we
have evaluated the energy consumption of the converted SNNs, demonstrating
their superior low-power advantage compared to conventional ANNs. This approach
simplifies the deployment of SNNs by leveraging open-source pre-trained ANN
models, enabling fast, low-power inference with negligible performance
reduction. Code is available at
https://github.com/putshua/Inference-scale-ANN-SNN.

C1.justification: The central claim of inexpensive, high-performance conversion of pretrained ANNs remains. v2 reframes it around inference-scale complexity, makes delay selection an explicit contribution, extends claimed applicability to video, and proposes online on-chip conversion. These refine and extend the existing thesis rather than replace it.

C2.justification: v2 explains how spike propagation delays motivate the evaluation window and why one-time threshold optimization differs from timestep-specific calibration. Appendix G acknowledges LCP's timing advantage at 32 steps. The integration claim is qualified from improvement at all timesteps to most timesteps; the broad performance/cost and architectural limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability URL, delay-estimation and inference pseudocode, explicit ResNet architecture distinctions, and timing hardware information. Video implementation details include 15 fps, five 16-frame clips per video, and 112×112 crops. These substantially expand the documented information needed to reproduce and interpret the experiments.

E1.justification: v2 retains ImageNet, Pascal VOC/SBD, and COCO coverage and adds video classification on a Kinetics-400 subset using MC3-18 and R3D-18 (Section 5.6, Table 3). This extends evaluation from still images to spatiotemporal inputs and action recognition.

E2.justification: v2 adds QCFS to the integration comparison and includes QCFS and ACP in the main ImageNet comparison; ACP previously appeared only in the integration experiment. The LCP/ACP integration comparisons remain. v1's Figure 1 comparison with direct and hybrid training methods is removed, substantially changing the comparison scope.

E3.justification: Appendix D changes VOC calibration from 5/6 to 4/5 dataset traversals for FCN/DeepLab and detection calibration from 1000 to 5000 iterations. Reported ImageNet and detection preprocessing also changes. New protocols include the 12000/7881-video calibration/test split, video-level clip aggregation, and conversion-time comparisons using the same 4090 GPU environment.

E4.justification: v2 adds an explicit delayed-evaluation ablation, a delay-length sensitivity study across four inference budgets, QCFS integration analysis, and conversion-time scaling analysis. v1's clipping-error convergence plot is removed. The iteration-count sensitivity study and appendix detection/segmentation example grids are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for the empirical results. v2 continues reporting point estimates.

E6.justification: Numerous scores change: ImageNet ResNet-34 accuracy at 32 steps changes from 59.03% to 64.88%, while ResNet-18 at 512 steps changes from 69.66% to 69.21%. These accompany method/protocol revisions, so they are not same-setting gains or losses. v2 adds QCFS, video, and timing results and removes the 512-step segmentation/detection columns. Existing LCP/ACP integration scores and energy estimates remain.

M1.justification: The core threshold-balancing, channel-wise threshold, and pre-neuron max-pooling procedures remain. v2 adds data-dependent delay selection using an estimated first-spike time and t0 = min(estimated delay, T - 4), extending v1's fixed-window evaluation. The written threshold update also drops the 1/N normalization. These are localized procedural revisions.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and methodological explanations receive extensive editing, with revised terminology and notation. Experiments are reorganized to lead with integration and separate ablation, iteration, and delay analyses. The appendices are presented as supplementary material and gain a training-cost discussion.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figures 1–2 are redesigned, Figure 3 is recomposed, and a delay-sensitivity figure and timing table are added. Comparison tables are restructured. The existing appendix example grids are relocated and relabeled as Figures S1–S2, with their image content unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 expands citations to recent calibration, conversion, and spiking-transformer work, including FTBC and unified optimization, and adds video-related references. It explicitly positions delay selection as building on Hwang et al.'s delayed evaluation. The underlying distinction between backpropagation-dependent learning and lightweight conversion remains.

T1.justification: The conversion-error bound, max-pooling theorem, and their proofs remain substantively intact. v2 adds the delayed-window relation and first-spike-time estimate in Equations 18–19, corrects the preceding-layer threshold index in Equation 2, and revises the update-rule normalization and summation in Appendix B.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central efficiency claim through measured same-hardware conversion times in Appendix G, replacing reliance on largely qualitative or estimated cost comparisons. Dedicated delay-selection tests, broader validation, and improved implementation documentation also strengthen the paper. These gains outweigh the removed convergence analysis, although changed protocols prevent interpreting revised headline scores as controlled performance improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ANN-SNN conversion work despite the changed title and presentation. The complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on those tasks, plus video classification, delayed-evaluation analyses, and measured conversion times.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, segmentation, and detection experiments, conversion ablations, and energy estimates.

arxiv_record.abstract:
The increasing demand for high-quality 3D assets across various industries
necessitates efficient and automated 3D content creation. Despite recent
advancements in 3D generative models, existing methods still face challenges
with optimization speed, geometric fidelity, and the lack of assets for
physically based rendering (PBR). In this paper, we introduce 3DTopia-XL, a
scalable native 3D generative model designed to overcome these limitations.
3DTopia-XL leverages a novel primitive-based 3D representation, PrimX, which
encodes detailed shape, albedo, and material field into a compact tensorial
format, facilitating the modeling of high-resolution geometry with PBR assets.
On top of the novel representation, we propose a generative framework based on
Diffusion Transformer (DiT), which comprises 1) Primitive Patch Compression, 2)
and Latent Primitive Diffusion. 3DTopia-XL learns to generate high-quality 3D
assets from textual or visual inputs. We conduct extensive qualitative and
quantitative experiments to demonstrate that 3DTopia-XL significantly
outperforms existing methods in generating high-quality 3D assets with
fine-grained textures and materials, efficiently bridging the quality gap
between generative models and real-world applications.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Long video understanding poses a significant challenge for current
Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Notably, the MLLMs are constrained
by their limited context lengths and the substantial costs while processing
long videos. Although several existing methods attempt to reduce visual tokens,
their strategies encounter severe bottleneck, restricting MLLMs' ability to
perceive fine-grained visual details. In this work, we propose Video-XL, a
novel approach that leverages MLLMs' inherent key-value (KV) sparsification
capacity to condense the visual input. Specifically, we introduce a new special
token, the Visual Summarization Token (VST), for each interval of the video,
which summarizes the visual information within the interval as its associated
KV. The VST module is trained by instruction fine-tuning, where two optimizing
strategies are offered. 1.Curriculum learning, where VST learns to make small
(easy) and large compression (hard) progressively. 2. Composite data curation,
which integrates single-image, multi-image, and synthetic data to overcome the
scarcity of long-video instruction data. The compression quality is further
improved by dynamic compression, which customizes compression granularity based
on the information density of different video intervals. Video-XL's
effectiveness is verified from three aspects. First, it achieves a superior
long-video understanding capability, outperforming state-of-the-art models of
comparable sizes across multiple popular benchmarks. Second, it effectively
preserves video information, with minimal compression loss even at 16x
compression ratio. Third, it realizes outstanding cost-effectiveness, enabling
high-quality processing of thousands of frames on a single A100 GPU.

The VST module is trained by instruction fine-tuning, where two optimizing strategies are offered. 1. Curriculum learning, where VST learns to make small (easy) and large compression (hard) progressively. 2. Composite data curation, which integrates single-image, multi-image, and synthetic data to overcome the scarcity of long-video instruction data. Second, it effectively preserves video information, with minimal compression loss even at 16x compression ratio. Third, it realizes outstanding cost-effectiveness, enabling high-quality processing of thousands of frames on a single A100 GPU.

C1.justification: The contribution expands from image-trained visual context summarization to dynamic compression, curriculum learning, and composite/VICO training. v4 adds claims of minimal loss at 16× compression and broader leadership among comparable-size models. Its headline long-context demonstration changes from 1024 frames at nearly 100% accuracy to 2048 frames at about 95%.

C2.justification: v4 introduces explanations of complementary image/video supervision, the need to train with dynamic compression, and attention savings versus additional VST computation. Supplement A newly acknowledges substantial training-memory costs and errors beyond 1000 frames. These substantially expand v1's limited discussion of mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v4 adds learning rates, batch sizes, training hardware, Adam/ZeRO-2-offload/bf16 settings, benchmark-specific frame budgets, and VICO construction details and prompts. These materially expand reproducibility information beyond v1. However, Section 4.1 specifies linear learning-rate decay while Supplement F specifies cosine decay.

E1.justification: Training expands from image-only data to single-image, multi-image, video, and synthetic action-order supervision. Evaluation adds VideoVista, VideoChatGPT Bench, MVBench, GQA, POPE, and SEEDBench. MME and MMBench were already evaluated in v1 and are retained.

E2.justification: v4's main comparisons add VideoLLaMA2, Video-CCAM, and PLLaVA, while dropping Claude3-Opus and InternVL-Chat-V1.5 from their corresponding benchmark comparisons. New controlled compression comparisons include pooling, Q-Former, LLaMA-Adapter, and C-Abstractor. Supplementary image comparisons additionally evaluate VoCo-LLaMA.

E3.justification: v4 adds MLVU-test evaluation, memory and FLOPs measurements, a retrieval grid extending to 2048 frames, matched 16× compression comparisons, and testing at an unseen 32× ratio. Supplement D introduces backbone and training-regime controls. The main LLaVA-Next-Video comparator also changes from 7B to 34B.

E4.justification: v1's compression-ratio ablation expands into studies of dynamic compression during training versus testing, interval size, curriculum learning, data mixtures, VICO scaling, backbone choice, and context length. Qualitative comparisons and appendix cases expand substantially. The advertisement example is retained with an added LLaMA-VID comparison; the earlier surveillance-anomaly example is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The added experiments do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Under revised methods and training, v4 replaces MLVU-dev M-avg 57.0 with 64.9 and VideoMME without/with-subtitle scores 51.0/54.4 with 55.5/61.0. Numerous benchmark, efficiency, ablation, and image results are added. v1's VideoMME duration and VNBench task breakdowns disappear. These replacements do not establish isolated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The interleaved VST/KV compression mechanism remains, but fixed-size chunks become content-dependent intervals using CLIP similarities and depth scores. v4 also introduces progressive compression-ratio training and composite/VICO data curation, replacing v1's image-only training with randomly sampled ratios of 2, 4, and 8.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method, experimental narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work becomes a dedicated section, training is integrated into the method discussion, and detailed material is reorganized into supplementary Sections A–G. 'Visual Context Latent Summarization' is reframed as 'VST Compression.'

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. v4 adds a radar overview, redraws the architecture, combines retrieval heatmaps with resource plots, and adds data-generation diagrams. The original benchmark tables are consolidated and restructured, with numerous new ablation tables, plots, and qualitative displays.

R1.justification: A dedicated related-work section and Supplement B substantially expand positioning against LongVA and VoCo-LLaMA. New sparsity references motivate compression, and VideoLLaMB is credited for the segmentation approach. Conversely, v1's explicit attribution to Activation Beacon and its corresponding reference are removed.

T1.justification: v4 adds the depth-score definition governing adaptive interval boundaries and a detailed computational-cost derivation separating attention and other operations for compressed processing (Supplement D, Equations 7–10). The earlier VST attention formalization is also shortened and revised in Supplement C. The new cost analysis substantially extends the mathematical treatment.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses v1's limited validation of compression and efficiency through matched alternative-compressor comparisons, quantitative resource measurements, and systematic mechanism and training ablations. Expanded implementation details and explicit limitations further strengthen the paper. These gains are substantial, although conflicting learning-rate schedules and Supplement D's disagreement between training-ablation prose and Table 3 limit reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Video-XL and retain the same underlying VST compression approach. Text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. v1 has no appendix; v4 includes readable supplementary Sections A–G.

arxiv_record.abstract: Character video synthesis aims to produce realistic videos of animatable characters within lifelike scenes. As a fundamental problem in the computer vision and graphics community, 3D works typically require multi-view captures for per-case training, which severely limits their applicability of modeling arbitrary characters in a short time. Recent 2D methods break this limitation via pre-trained diffusion models, but they struggle for pose generality and scene interaction. To this end, we propose MIMO, a novel framework which can not only synthesize character videos with controllable attributes (i.e., character, motion and scene) provided by simple user inputs, but also simultaneously achieve advanced scalability to arbitrary characters, generality to novel 3D motions, and applicability to interactive real-world scenes in a unified framework. The core idea is to encode the 2D video to compact spatial codes, considering the inherent 3D nature of video occurrence. Concretely, we lift the 2D frame pixels into 3D using monocular depth estimators, and decompose the video clip to three spatial components (i.e., main human, underlying scene, and floating occlusion) in hierarchical layers based on the 3D depth. These components are further encoded to canonical identity code, structured motion code and full scene code, which are utilized as control signals of synthesis process. The design of spatial decomposed modeling enables flexible user control, complex motion expression, as well as 3D-aware synthesis for scene interactions. Experimental results demonstrate effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method.
arxiv_record.authors: Yifang Men, Yuan Yao, Miaomiao Cui, Liefeng Bo
arxiv_record.title: MIMO: Controllable Character Video Synthesis with Spatial Decomposed Modeling

C1.justification: The central claims about character, motion and scene control remain. V2 adds an explicit abstract claim of outperforming prior methods by a large margin and recasts the existing controllable-synthesis task as a new task contribution; v1 already described video character replacement as an application.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands component-specific explanations: background distortions are attributed to absent scene guidance, limitations of 3D maps to undefined dense body-part labels, and reduced hand/foot confusion to canonical appearance transfer improving motion learning. These interpretations accompany new comparator and ablation evidence beyond v1's general architectural rationale.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies PyTorch, 80 GB GPU memory and 6,890 SMPL-anchored codes, and describes obtaining and fine-tuning comparator implementations. Initialization, frozen components and eight A100 GPUs were already documented. The project URL remains unchanged.

E1.justification: HUD-7K training data, AMASS/Mixamo motions, arbitrary-character animation and interactive real-world video scenarios remain. The new 100-clip evaluation formalizes testing within this existing coverage rather than introducing a distinct task or domain.

E2.justification: V1 cites animation methods but reports no direct baseline evaluation. V2 Figure 6 and Table 1 add qualitative and quantitative comparisons against Animate Anyone, Mimic-Motion and Champ, with reported fine-tuning on the authors' training data.

E3.justification: V2 introduces evaluation on 100 collected videos randomly truncated to 150-frame clips, using PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS and FVD, plus baseline fine-tuning. The reported training batch size also changes from 4 to 8, while approximately 50,000 iterations and 24-frame training clips remain; this does not establish whether earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 Section 4.3 adds tests removing spatial decomposition, independent occlusion encoding and canonical appearance transfer, and replacing structured motion codes with 2D skeletons or 3D maps. Table 2 and Figures 7–8 provide quantitative and visual evidence; the occlusion-removal variant is shown qualitatively. V1 contains no corresponding component ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's quantitative tables contain point estimates only.

E6.justification: V2 adds numerical results absent from v1. Table 1 reports MIMO at 25.210 PSNR, 0.883 SSIM, 0.125 LPIPS and 221.4 FVD, leading all three comparators on these metrics. Table 2 adds component results, including PSNR 22.148 without spatial decomposition. These are newly reported evaluations, not measured gains over v1 under matched settings.

M1.justification: The spatial decomposition, SMPL-anchored motion codes, canonical appearance transfer, scene/occlusion encoding, diffusion decoder and training objective are retained. Specifying 6,890 SMPL vertices adds implementation detail without establishing a changed method.

P1.justification: Most existing introduction and method prose is retained. V2 revises the abstract and contribution bullets, inserts Related Work before the method, groups implementation details, and converts the three numbered control subsections into paragraph headings. Much of the additional text documents new scientific comparisons rather than rewriting existing material.

P2.justification: The standalone diverse-character gallery in v1 Figure 5 is omitted, while selected motion and scene panels from v1 Figures 6–7 are condensed into v2 Figure 5. New baseline and ablation Figures 6–8 and Tables 1–2 substantially reorganize the experimental presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds a dedicated Related Work section substantially expanding discussion of 3D human modeling and diffusion-based animation. Newly discussed works include NeuMan, HOSNeRF, AG3D and EVA3D, with fuller positioning around reconstruction costs, motion representation and human–scene interaction.

T1.justification: The spatial masking equation and diffusion noise-prediction loss remain equivalent. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs, and specifying the existing SMPL representation's vertex count introduces no new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V1 relies on selected visual demonstrations without comparative or component validation. V2 substantially addresses this deficiency through a defined evaluation protocol, three-baseline comparisons and targeted ablations in Tables 1–2 and Figures 6–8. after.justification: V2 reports original synthesis examples, quantitative baseline comparisons and component ablations in Figures 5–8 and Tables 1–2.

before.justification: V1 reports original generated-video examples demonstrating character, motion and scene control, particularly in Figures 5–7.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Today's most advanced vision-language models (VLMs) remain proprietary. The
strongest open-weight models rely heavily on synthetic data from proprietary
VLMs to achieve good performance, effectively distilling these closed VLMs into
open ones. As a result, the community has been missing foundational knowledge
about how to build performant VLMs from scratch. We present Molmo, a new family
of VLMs that are state-of-the-art in their class of openness. Our key
contribution is a collection of new datasets called PixMo, including a dataset
of highly detailed image captions for pre-training, a free-form image Q&A
dataset for fine-tuning, and an innovative 2D pointing dataset, all collected
without the use of external VLMs. The success of our approach relies on careful
modeling choices, a well-tuned training pipeline, and, most critically, the
quality of our newly collected datasets. Our best-in-class 72B model not only
outperforms others in the class of open weight and data models, but also
outperforms larger proprietary models including Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini
1.5 Pro and Flash, second only to GPT-4o based on both academic benchmarks and
on a large human evaluation. Our model weights, new datasets, and source code
are available at https://molmo.allenai.org/blog.

C1.justification: The central claims about open Molmo/PixMo models, avoiding proprietary-VLM distillation for the main models, and competitive benchmark/human performance persist. v2's introduction additionally presents overlapping cropping, efficient multi-annotation training, and systematic model/data design insights as contributions. The more explicit abstract comparisons largely repeat claims already present in v1's introduction.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations and qualifications concerning crop-mismatch failures, weaker reasoning performance, text-only knowledge loss, caption-metric errors, and differences between its human evaluation and Chatbot Arena. It explicitly cautions that caption/downstream correlation does not establish causality. Appendix H also acknowledges that using closed text-only LLMs leaves the data-generation pipeline incompletely open.

D1.justification: v1 gives a high-level recipe and promises full data and training-code releases; v2 states that datasets and source code are available. Appendices A–C and Tables 6–8 add architecture dimensions, optimizer settings, sampling rates, prompts, preprocessing, precision and gradient handling, sequence limits, evaluation details, H100 hardware, and training times. Much of this is newly disclosed information about retained experiments.

E1.justification: v2 adds text-only knowledge, reasoning, mathematics, and programming evaluations, plus experiments incorporating Tulu 3 training data. It also evaluates real-world clocks from COCO, OpenImages, and Clock Movies, and introduces dedicated captioning and pointing evaluation sets. The original Flickr Count benchmark is retained as PixMo-Count, rather than being a new benchmark.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Llama-3.2V-11B-Instruct and Llama-3.2V-90B-Instruct. The Chameleon-7B/30B human-evaluation entries in v1 Figure 4 are omitted from v2's reported comparison. Additional comparisons introduce a specialized clock-reading model, the underlying Qwen2-7B language model, and a broader externally reported Chatbot Arena comparator set in Tables 9, 10, and 13.

E3.justification: New studies introduce caption scoring, point-assignment evaluation, controlled crop configurations, high-resolution post-training, and a balanced 500-question human ablation study distinct from the retained main study. Reported PixMo-Points image counts also change from 428k to 223k, and point-explanation images from 29k to 14k. These count revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun; newly disclosed original settings belong under D1.

E4.justification: v1 lacks corresponding systematic ablations. v2 Tables 2–5 and 15 test encoders, crops, dropout, pooling, caption conditioning, data scale/composition, and counting representations. Appendix D additionally investigates crop-mismatch failures and recovery, text-only knowledge loss and mitigation, opaque AI2D boxes, human-evaluation ties, and the relationship between caption quality and downstream accuracy.

E5.justification: v2 adds explicit 95% confidence intervals for externally reported Arena scores in Table 9 and a Pearson correlation/least-squares analysis across 22 ablations in Figure 9. Conversely, the boxes and whiskers accompanying v1's own-study Elo scores in Figure 4 disappear when those results are tabulated. Neither version documents repeated training seeds.

E6.justification: All 25 retained Table 1 rows have unchanged academic scores, including Molmo-72B's 81.2 average. However, v2 adds extensive ablation and supplementary results, including Molmo-7B-D's 68.2% clock-reading accuracy, Molmo-72B's 75.2 pointing F1, and text-only performance losses and recovery experiments. The new Arena scores concern a different evaluation, not a same-setting performance change.

M1.justification: The specified connector order changes from MLP projection followed by pooling in v1 Section 2 to pooling followed by MLP projection in v2 Section 2. v2 also introduces an optional high-resolution post-training adaptation in Appendix D. The core model family and two-stage pipeline remain; expanded architectural descriptions do not establish wholesale changes to the released models.

P1.justification: The introduction and technical exposition are extensively rewritten and subdivided. Data and Training become separate sections, the Release Plan section disappears, and appendices organize model, training, evaluation, results, ablations, data, examples, and related work. Existing material, including annotator questions, is relocated. The title also changes 'Multimodal Models' to 'Vision-Language Models.'

P2.justification: v2 redraws the architecture figure and adds dataset-overview, cropping, tokenization, mixture, diagnostic, and example figures, alongside numerous experimental and implementation tables. Table 1 gains Elo score/rank columns while v1's benchmark-summary and Elo plots disappear. The openness comparison is retained and relocated from v1 Figure 3 to v2 Figure 11.

R1.justification: v2 adds an extensive related-work discussion in Appendix H, covering contrastive encoders, multimodal architectures, instruction data, synthetic documents, grounding, and dependence on closed LLMs. It substantively compares PixMo with approaches such as GRES/RefCOCO and ExpertQA and discusses alternative architectures. This substantially expands v1's brief introductory positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix C newly defines caption precision and recall through atomic-statement matching and consistency judgments, then defines cap F1 from their image-averaged values. Appendix D specifies assignment-based pointing precision/recall and no-target cases. These are new task-specific mathematical definitions, beyond merely restating the standard F1 formula; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's lack of controlled ablation evidence and reproducibility detail through Section 6 and Appendices A–E. It also exposes important failures and applicability limits, including crop sensitivity, text-only degradation, and less favorable independent human rankings. These gains outweigh the lost own-study Elo uncertainty display and occasional overclaims, such as the RealWorldQA summary not matching Table 1. The improvement comes from stronger evidence and transparency, while retained benchmark scores remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Molmo/PixMo research. The complete text, tables, and figures support reliable matching. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v2 includes substantial appendices A–H, all inspected.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds model/data ablations, clock-reading, pointing, and text-only experiments in Section 6 and the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original Molmo results on 11 benchmarks, a human preference study, and AndroidControl in Section 4, Table 1, and Figures 2 and 4.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Extracting physical dynamical system parameters from recorded observations is
key in natural science. Current methods for automatic parameter estimation from
video train supervised deep networks on large datasets. Such datasets require
labels, which are difficult to acquire. While some unsupervised
techniques--which depend on frame prediction--exist, they suffer from long
training times, initialization instabilities, only consider motion-based
dynamical systems, and are evaluated mainly on synthetic data. In this work, we
propose an unsupervised method to estimate the physical parameters of known,
continuous governing equations from single videos suitable for different
dynamical systems beyond motion and robust to initialization. Moreover, we
remove the need for frame prediction by implementing a KL-divergence-based loss
function in the latent space, which avoids convergence to trivial solutions and
reduces model size and compute. We first evaluate our model on synthetic data,
as commonly done. After which, we take the field closer to reality by recording
Delfys75: our own real-world dataset of 75 videos for five different types of
dynamical systems to evaluate our method and others. Our method compares
favorably to others. %, yet, and real-world video datasets and demonstrate
improved parameter estimation accuracy compared to existing methods. Code and
data are available
online:https://github.com/Alejandro-neuro/Learning_physics_from_video.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion add Delfys75 as a central contribution and claim favorable performance in a structured real-world benchmark. V1 centers its contributions on decoder-free estimation, dynamics beyond motion, extrapolation, and initialization robustness; those claims are retained.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations relating real-world baseline weaknesses to single-video training and spatial-transformer reconstruction, discusses prior rescaling, and identifies Euler-step tradeoffs and sliding-block parameter ambiguity. The principal limitations concerning absolute scale, discretization, interacting-object masks, and autonomous dynamics remain.

D1.justification: V2 provides recording specifications, camera controls, SAM2 mask annotation information, ground-truth measurement procedures, and detailed per-experiment training settings. It also specifies the previously described default initialization more precisely. A concrete code-and-data link and availability statement replace v1's promise of a future GitHub release; external availability was not checked.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluation on Delfys75: real pendulum, draining-water, sliding-block, exponentially decaying LED, and apparent-scale free-fall videos. This substantially expands physical and environmental coverage. V1's linear LED and pendulum examples remain in v2 Appendix A.9, alongside the retained synthetic datasets.

E2.justification: V2 adds an evaluated MSE-only comparator against the full MSE-plus-KL model in Appendix A.4 and Table 3; v1 only discusses its potential collapse. PAIG, NIRPI, and the PAIG-without-U-Net cost comparison remain. Extending the retained baselines to Delfys75 does not itself change their membership.

E3.justification: Delfys75 introduces three settings per system, five videos per setting, individual-video training, a 500-epoch budget for the proposed model, and experiment-specific temporal sampling and batch settings. Separately, the reported synthetic pendulum angle range changes from [-90,90] degrees to [-180,180] degrees; the PDFs do not establish whether that experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a KL-loss ablation testing latent collapse and parameter accuracy (Appendix A.4, Table 3, Figure 9), plus an Euler-step sensitivity study across intensity, Torricelli, and pendulum experiments (Appendix A.8, Table 6). The original initialization-robustness analyses remain.

E5.justification: The original mean-and-standard-deviation reporting over seven initializations is retained. V2 additionally documents ground-truth measurement uncertainty, including instrument resolution and standard deviations calculated across five or fifteen recordings (Appendix A.6, Table 4). Table 2 reports variability across five videos per setting, rather than additional initialization runs.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive Delfys75 results and both ablation result sets. For example, Table 3 reports oscillator parameters of 3.99 and 0.08 with KL, versus 5.7 and 6.6 with MSE alone. These are newly reported comparisons. The original oscillator estimates survive with equivalent rounding, and the earlier pendulum estimate remains 1.22 m against 1.20 m.

M1.justification: The encoder, Euler physics block, and MSE-plus-KL loss remain. V2 Section 5.4 introduces a Torricelli-specific adaptation, changing the KL target prior from N(0,1) to N(1,0.2) to accommodate square-root dynamics.

P1.justification: V2 substantially edits the abstract, introduction, methodological explanations, and discussion. It introduces a dedicated dataset section, consolidates the synthetic experiments, and moves the original real-world examples into the appendix. The author header also changes.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the method diagrams, adds dataset and ablation displays, and extensively reorganizes tables and figures. V1 Table 1 becomes v2 Figure 4b, replacing the separate encoder-versus-ground-truth panel; the cost table is transposed. The original real-world displays move to the appendix, with the LED visualization reformatted.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a dataset discussion positioning Delfys75 against Physics101 and distinguishes the approach from latent-control and equation-learning methods, including NewtonianVAE and LaSDI. Additional citations support annotation and oscillation discussions. The central positioning against PAIG and NIRPI remains.

T1.justification: V2 Equation 1 adds an affine constant term to the general ODE formulation. Section 4.1 and Appendix A.6 add physical equations and parameter-calibration derivations. The central Euler and loss derivations remain, with no new theorem or proof. Some added formulas are inconsistent, notably the Torricelli sign across Equations 15 and 23.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens two weak points in v1: limited real-world validation and the absence of direct loss-ablation evidence. arxiv_record.abstract:
Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models have revolutionized visual content
creation, but extending these capabilities to text-to-video (T2V) generation
remains a challenge, particularly in preserving temporal consistency. Existing
methods that aim to improve consistency often cause trade-offs such as reduced
imaging quality and impractical computational time. To address these issues we
introduce VideoGuide, a novel framework that enhances the temporal consistency
of pretrained T2V models without the need for additional training or
fine-tuning. Instead, VideoGuide leverages any pretrained video diffusion model
(VDM) or itself as a guide during the early stages of inference, improving
temporal quality by interpolating the guiding model's denoised samples into the
sampling model's denoising process. The proposed method brings about
significant improvement in temporal consistency and image fidelity, providing a
cost-effective and practical solution that synergizes the strengths of various
video diffusion models. Furthermore, we demonstrate prior distillation,
revealing that base models can achieve enhanced text coherence by utilizing the
superior data prior of the guiding model through the proposed method. Project
Page: https://dohunlee1.github.io/videoguide.github.io/

C1.justification: The abstract, three introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the central claims of training-free temporal improvement, flexible teacher guidance, and prior distillation. Sections 2–3 additionally present optimization-based video-consistency guidance as an explicit contribution and claim priority for that formulation, adding a specific novelty claim.

C2.justification: v3 adds an explicit consistency-versus-dynamic-degree trade-off, interprets filtering as accelerating convergence and preserving the student's domain, and connects excessive interpolation to SDS-related blurring. Supplement H newly states the shared-VAE-space requirement and discusses the computational and detail-loss risks of decoding and re-encoding across incompatible spaces.

D1.justification: v3 clarifies that the pseudocode uses CFG++ throughout for presentation, while the experimental implementation switches back to CFG. It documents settings for the new filter, Open-Sora, and UniCtrl experiments and changes the printed project-page address. Most original prompt-selection and hyperparameter information is retained.

E1.justification: Both versions specify text-to-video evaluation using 800 prompts from VBench categories. Open-Sora adds model and scheduler configurations, without documenting a new dataset, task, population, or input scenario. The personalized-model domains and original qualitative galleries are retained.

E2.justification: The original AnimateDiff/LaVie comparisons with FreeInit remain. v3 adds UniCtrl and the UniCtrl-plus-VideoGuide combination to the AnimateDiff comparison in Table 7. Table 2 also adds unguided baseline timings to the existing timing comparison.

E3.justification: v3 adds RAFT-based dynamic degree as a fifth evaluation metric. New experiments introduce Open-Sora DiT configurations with DDIM and rectified-flow schedulers, filter-versus-no-filter controls over a longer interpolation sweep, and UniCtrl with motion injection degree 0.2. The original 800-prompt, 50-step DDIM evaluation settings remain documented.

E4.justification: Supplement A and Figure 5 newly isolate the low-pass filter's effects on consistency, imaging quality, and efficiency, extending the no-filter sweep to 50 interpolation steps. Supplements F and G add architecture/scheduler robustness and UniCtrl composability analyses. The original parameter ablations and CFG-versus-CFG++ analysis are retained, although reorganized.

E5.justification: Shared-seed qualitative comparisons remain, and neither version reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. The new filter plots show averages across prompts without introducing uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes all four AnimateDiff self-guided scores, including subject consistency from 0.9596 to 0.9520, and adds dynamic-degree results. Table 2 revises existing timings and adds baseline times. Figure 5 and Tables 6–7 introduce filter, Open-Sora, and UniCtrl findings. The original parameter-ablation, CFG++, and user-study values remain unchanged; the PDFs do not explain the revised existing scores.

M1.justification: The original interpolation, renoising, filtering, and self/external guidance procedures remain; Algorithms 1 and 2 are unchanged. Supplement F adds a velocity-based rectified-flow adaptation, with a corresponding inference update in Equation 18. The rewritten main derivation does not establish a replacement of the original DDIM procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction, mathematical exposition, and results discussion undergo substantial rewriting, including increased teacher/student terminology. CFG discussion moves into the supplement, Section 3.3 is refocused on prior distillation, and existing appendix material is extensively reordered within a new supplementary structure. These changes exceed ordinary copyediting.

P2.justification: The document changes from predominantly single-column to two-column layout. The original six-panel qualitative comparison is redistributed between main Figure 3 and supplementary Figure 11, and the guidance-scale illustration moves to the supplement. v3 also transposes the CFG comparison table, expands the main results table, and adds filter plots and Open-Sora/UniCtrl displays.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands the optimization-guidance positioning through diffusion posterior sampling, decomposed diffusion sampling, score distillation, and consistency models, while removing the earlier DreamSampler citation. It also adds discussion of UniCtrl and I4VGen and references supporting DiT, rectified flow, and Open-Sora. The explicit optimization-priority claim changes its stated relationship to prior research.

T1.justification: v1 derives interpolation from a quadratic proximal objective using a temporally consistent reference latent. v3 replaces this reasoning with a teacher-denoising loss, gradient-based guidance, a different derivation of the interpolation coefficient, and a consistency-model/PF-ODE approximation in Sections 2–3. improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens assessment of the central consistency, quality, and efficiency claims. arxiv_record.abstract:
The text-to-video (T2V) generation models, offering convenient visual
creation, have recently garnered increasing attention. Despite their
substantial potential, the generated videos may present artifacts, including
structural implausibility, temporal inconsistency, and a lack of motion, often
resulting in near-static video. In this work, we have identified a correlation
between the disparity of temporal attention maps across different blocks and
the occurrence of temporal inconsistencies. Additionally, we have observed that
the energy contained within the temporal attention maps is directly related to
the magnitude of motion amplitude in the generated videos. Based on these
observations, we present ByTheWay, a training-free method to improve the
quality of text-to-video generation without introducing additional parameters,
augmenting memory or sampling time. Specifically, ByTheWay is composed of two
principal components: 1) Temporal Self-Guidance improves the structural
plausibility and temporal consistency of generated videos by reducing the
disparity between the temporal attention maps across various decoder blocks. 2)
Fourier-based Motion Enhancement enhances the magnitude and richness of motion
by amplifying the energy of the map. Extensive experiments demonstrate that
ByTheWay significantly improves the quality of text-to-video generation with
negligible additional cost.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Efficiently retrieving and synthesizing information from large-scale
multimodal collections has become a critical challenge. However, existing video
retrieval datasets suffer from scope limitations, primarily focusing on
matching descriptive but vague queries with small collections of professionally
edited, English-centric videos. To address this gap, we introduce
$\textbf{MultiVENT 2.0}$, a large-scale, multilingual event-centric video
retrieval benchmark featuring a collection of more than 218,000 news videos and
3,906 queries targeting specific world events. These queries specifically
target information found in the visual content, audio, embedded text, and text
metadata of the videos, requiring systems leverage all these sources to succeed
at the task. Preliminary results show that state-of-the-art vision-language
models struggle significantly with this task, and while alternative approaches
show promise, they are still insufficient to adequately address this problem.
These findings underscore the need for more robust multimodal retrieval
systems, as effective video retrieval is a crucial step towards multimodal
content understanding and generation.

C2.justification: The expanded Table 4 caption explicitly interprets Chinese/Korean difficulty and modality-specific performance. The appendix adds concrete qualifications about transcription and translation errors, incomplete OCR coverage, and posting dates differing from event dates.

D1.justification: New Sections 8–9 provide extensive annotation instructions, including Label Studio interfaces, sampling rounds, resolution-based selection, minimum language/type coverage, query constraints, relevance decision rules, and escalation procedures. The introduction also adds a data-access link. v1 supplied substantially less operational documentation.

E1.justification: The collection, six languages, event and video categories, and query tasks remain the same. MSR-VTT comparisons are retained. Removing the results paragraph's reference to VALOR-32k does not establish lost coverage: v1's corresponding table already contained no VALOR-32k results.

E2.justification: Table 3 removes the fine-tuned VAST comparison on MSR-VTT, which reported R@10 of 0.896. Pretrained VAST and all comparators reporting MultiVENT 2.0 results remain.

E3.justification: No protocol revision is reported for the retained experiments: collection splits, ten-keyframe extraction, retrieval metrics, and 0/1/3 relevance scoring remain unchanged. The appendix's sampling rounds and selection rules are newly disclosed construction details, not evidence of changed experiments.

E4.justification: The language, video-type, query-type, and event-type analyses are retained unchanged, moving from Figure 4 to Table 4. Appendix examples illustrate annotation instructions rather than adding evaluated case studies or robustness analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2 introduces no uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the unknown MultiVENT 2.0 average clip length with 145 seconds. Table 3 deletes the fine-tuned VAST MSR-VTT score of 0.896. All 39 retained retrieval scores, 96 subgroup scores, and Table 2 relevance percentages are unchanged.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction framework and baseline retrieval pipelines remain unchanged. The supplement documents the existing annotation workflow rather than introducing a revised algorithm or model.

P1.justification: v2 substantially expands the exposition through two structured annotation manuals with detailed subsections, decision rules, and worked examples. The main section sequence remains intact, with smaller wording, terminology, and author/affiliation edits.

P2.justification: v2 adds three annotation-interface figures, including two multipanel displays. It also rearranges Figure 3 panels and legends, relocates Table 1, simplifies Table 3, and relabels the former Figure 4 as Table 4 with an expanded caption.

R1.justification: Section 2 changes its characterization of DiDeMo filtering from excluding edited videos generally to excluding non-professional edited videos. The 43 cited works and the paper's broader research positioning remain unchanged.

T1.justification: No mathematical definitions, derivations, assumptions, or proofs are added or revised. The appendix's event and relevance definitions are operational annotation guidance.

improvement.justification: For this benchmark paper, v2 substantially improves reproducibility and usability by supplying data-access instructions and detailed guidance for creating queries and judging relevance. These additions address important documentation gaps in v1's central human-annotation process. Core empirical evidence is preserved; removing one peripheral fine-tuned MSR-VTT comparison is a limited loss.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MultiVENT 2.0 and are readable throughout. Their main text, tables, figures, and references can be matched reliably. v2 adds supplementary annotation guidelines; v1 contains no appendix.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Closed-loop simulation is essential for advancing end-to-end autonomous
driving systems. Contemporary sensor simulation methods, such as NeRF and 3DGS,
rely predominantly on conditions closely aligned with training data
distributions, which are largely confined to forward-driving scenarios.
Consequently, these methods face limitations when rendering complex maneuvers
(e.g., lane change, acceleration, deceleration). Recent advancements in
autonomous-driving world models have demonstrated the potential to generate
diverse driving videos. However, these approaches remain constrained to 2D
video generation, inherently lacking the spatiotemporal coherence required to
capture intricacies of dynamic driving environments. In this paper, we
introduce DriveDreamer4D, which enhances 4D driving scene representation
leveraging world model priors. Specifically, we utilize the world model as a
data machine to synthesize novel trajectory videos, where structured conditions
are explicitly leveraged to control the spatial-temporal consistency of traffic
elements. Besides, the cousin data training strategy is proposed to facilitate
merging real and synthetic data for optimizing 4DGS. To our knowledge,
DriveDreamer4D is the first to utilize video generation models for improving 4D
reconstruction in driving scenarios. Experimental results reveal that
DriveDreamer4D significantly enhances generation quality under novel trajectory
views, achieving a relative improvement in FID by 32.1%, 46.4%, and 16.3%
compared to PVG, S3Gaussian, and Deformable-GS. Moreover, DriveDreamer4D
markedly enhances the spatiotemporal coherence of driving agents, which is
verified by a comprehensive user study and the relative increases of 22.6%,
43.5%, and 15.6% in the NTA-IoU metric.
