C1.justification: v3 adds CDTS and its perceptual regularization as explicit contributions in the abstract and introduction. The central claim of using video world-model priors to improve 4D driving reconstruction, its novelty positioning, and the supported maneuver scope remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 explains temporal pairing as mitigating the real/synthetic data gap and regularization as promoting perceptual coherence; Section 8 interprets CDTS as improving vehicle-edge reconstruction. The former mixing-ratio tradeoff discussion disappears. Explanations concerning incomplete LiDAR supervision and FID's limited usefulness for speed changes are retained.

D1.justification: The new supplement supplies SVD initialization, 798 training videos and approximately 64K clips, optimizer settings, batch size, generator training iterations, H20 hardware, exact evaluation scene IDs and frame ranges, and user-study presentation details. These substantially improve reproducibility. Conversely, v1's explicit 50,000-iteration 4DGS budget disappears; v3's supplementary 50K count describes generator training.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate eight Waymo scenes using forward-facing views and lane-change, acceleration, and deceleration trajectories. v3 documents the generator's training data more precisely without establishing expanded coverage. Its nuScenes discussion concerns the cited source model, not an additional dataset used by this work.

E2.justification: PVG, S3Gaussian, and Deformable-GS remain the comparators in Tables 1–3. Supplementary Section 6 explains these existing baselines. The new CDTS variants are component ablations rather than additional comparison methods.

E3.justification: The ablation design adds a regularization-weight sweep and controls separating temporal pairing from regularization. The beta sweep and the lambda_novel=0.7 setting disappear. The established evaluation metrics, image resolution, clip length, and camera selection remain. Newly documented generator and user-study settings do not establish changes to those existing experiments.

E4.justification: The analyses substantially refocus on the new CDTS mechanism: v3 Table 5 tests regularization strength, Table 6 separately enables temporal pairing and regularization, and supplementary Figure 4 provides a visual ablation. The earlier mixing-ratio analysis is removed, while depth-loss testing and most of the novel-view loss-weight analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and user-preference percentages without repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The newly described random left/right assignment in the user study is an experimental control, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Primary results are extensively revised for the CDTS method. Table 2 FID scores change from 79.54/76.24/82.67 to 71.52/66.93/77.32 for PVG/S3Gaussian/Deformable-GS, while baseline scores remain fixed. Tables 1 and 3 also change; PVG's reported average preference rises from 88.6% to 93.2%. New CDTS ablation results replace mixing-ratio results. These are results for a revised training procedure.

M1.justification: Section 3.2.2 replaces beta-weighted mixing of original and generated data with the Cousin Data Training Strategy (CDTS): temporally aligned pairs enter each optimization step, and a new perceptual feature regularizer augments the loss. These change the training procedure substantively; the trajectory-generation algorithm and underlying 4DGS framework remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution discussion, Sections 3.2.2 and 4.3 receive targeted revisions. New supplementary sections explain baselines and implementation, and speed-change discussion moves there. Author and affiliation information also changes. Most introductory, related-work, preliminary, and evaluation prose retains its earlier structure.

P2.justification: Figure 2 gains paired-data markings and a regularization connection. v3 adds the CDTS visual comparison and scene-identification table, revises the ablation-table structures, and adds frame-direction arrows to qualitative panels. The lane-change comparison becomes Figure 3, while the earlier speed-change comparison moves to supplementary Figure 5. The overall layout remains similar.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to nuScenes, UC-NeRF, XLD, HO-Gaussian, and EgoVid-5M. These extend contextual coverage without substantially changing the positioning against earlier driving reconstruction and diffusion-prior methods. Existing references are retained, including bibliographic updates that do not constitute new works.

T1.justification: Section 3.2.2 removes the beta-weighted hybrid-dataset definition and introduces the aligned-batch formulation, perceptual regularizer, and expanded total objective in v3 Equations 8–11. The Gaussian, diffusion, trajectory-safety, and IoU formulations remain substantively unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses reproducibility gaps in v1 by documenting the central video generator's training recipe and identifying the exact evaluation segments. It also supports the new CDTS mechanism with component ablations and visual evidence, making its contribution easier to assess. These gains outweigh the loss of the explicit 4DGS iteration count, although uncertainty reporting and user-study participant counts remain absent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DriveDreamer4D and contain readable text, equations, figures, and tables supporting reliable comparison. The supplied v1 ends with references; v3 additionally includes supplementary Sections 6–8.

after.justification: v3 reports original reconstruction experiments, updated user-study results, and additional quantitative and visual CDTS ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original Waymo reconstruction experiments, quantitative comparisons, a user study, and ablations in Tables 1–6.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Neural network performance scales with both model size and data volume, as
shown in both language and image processing. This requires scaling-friendly
architectures and large datasets. While transformers have been adapted for 3D
vision, a `GPT-moment' remains elusive due to limited training data. We
introduce ARKit LabelMaker, a large-scale real-world 3D dataset with dense
semantic annotation that is more than three times larger than prior largest
dataset. Specifically, we extend ARKitScenes with automatically generated dense
3D labels using an extended LabelMaker pipeline, tailored for large-scale
pre-training. Training on our dataset improves accuracy across architectures,
achieving state-of-the-art 3D semantic segmentation scores on ScanNet and
ScanNet200, with notable gains on tail classes. Our code is available at
https://labelmaker.org and our dataset at
https://huggingface.co/datasets/labelmaker/arkit_labelmaker.

Guangda Ji, Silvan Weder, Francis Engelmann, Marc Pollefeys, Hermann
  Blum

This requires scaling-friendly architectures and large datasets. While transformers have been adapted for 3D vision, a 'GPT-moment' remains elusive due to limited training data. We introduce ARKit LabelMaker, the first large-scale, real-world 3D dataset with dense semantic annotations. Specifically, we enhance ARKitScenes with automatically generated dense labels using an extended LabelMaker pipeline, tailored for large-scale pre-training. Training on this dataset improves accuracy across architectures, achieving state-of-the-art results on ScanNet and ScanNet200, with notable gains on tail classes. We compare our results with self-supervised methods and synthetic data, evaluating the effects on downstream tasks and zero-shot generalization. The dataset will be publicly available.

C1.justification: The largest-dataset and state-of-the-art segmentation claims remain. v2 recasts the contribution list by explicitly claiming a trade-off analysis of unsupervised, synthetic, and automatically labeled training, replacing the pipeline-improvement bullet. Its highlighted 2.1-point overall and 5.5-point tail-class gains quantify comparisons already present in v1's tables.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations about transferable features, log-linear mIoU scaling despite absent loss scaling, and differing tail-class benefits for PTv3 and MinkowskiNet. It explains NeuS geometry difficulties on inside-out scans. ScanNet++ discussion changes from test deterioration and limited benefits to validation gains qualified by baseline non-reproducibility and unequal training data.

D1.justification: Most preprocessing, hardware, and scheduling details survive in the reorganized appendices. However, v2 removes explicit training-repository links and the DOI from v1 Appendix A, the mobile coordinate/depth-rendering recipe, and the stated PTv3 pretraining learning rate of 0.0016. Project and dataset links remain, and v2 adds an estimated 12 GPU hours per scene for the omitted neural-rendering step.

E1.justification: v2 adds zero-shot semantic evaluation on Matterport3D and instance segmentation on ScanNet and ScanNet200 (Section 4.6, Tables 7–8). These extend both target-domain and task coverage. ScanNet++ remains evaluated in Appendix B, and the self-captured scenes are retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds reported comparisons with LabelMakerV1 and ScanNet's manual annotations in Table 5, and OpenScene and Matterport3D-supervised MinkowskiNet in Table 7. Table 2 also adds a PTv3-PPT ablation comparator. The original MinkowskiNet, PTv3, Mix3D, and PonderV2 comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include label-quality evaluation on five ScanNet and three ARKitScenes scenes, 10/20/50/100% pretraining subsets, size-matched Structured3D, Top-40/80/160 NYU label mappings, accuracy metrics, and instance-segmentation AP metrics. Table 1 also changes the reported ARKit validation/test split from 548/no test set to 274/274, although the caption and prose still state 548 validation scenes.

E4.justification: v2 adds Grounded-SAM/gravity-alignment ablations, direct annotation-quality checks, dataset-size sensitivity and a size-matched synthetic-data comparison (Tables 4–6). New figures analyze gravity-related errors, class frequencies, and individual tail-class detections. The earlier aggregate head/common/tail analysis is retained in the expanded main table.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for benchmark scores. The two Mask3D seeds used for test-time augmentation and the stored vote-count information are documented in both versions; v2 adds no uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Numerous validation scores change: joint PTv3-PPT ScanNet200 mIoU changes from 40.3 to 37.5, while its test score remains 41.4; fine-tuned MinkowskiNet ScanNet20 validation mIoU changes from 77.0 to 74.1. Reasons for these revisions are not stated. v2 adds scaling, annotation-quality, transfer, and instance results, but removes all ScanNet++ test top-1/top-3 scores while retaining its validation scores in Appendix B.

M1.justification: Grounded-SAM integration, gravity alignment, ensemble voting, point lifting, and mobile-scanner integration already appear in v1. v2's explicit NeuS-omission discussion elaborates the neural-rendering omission already documented in v1 Section 4.6 and Appendix C.1; it does not establish a changed annotation procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, methodological explanations, and conclusion receive extensive rewriting. Experiments are reorganized into thematic comparisons, ablations, and transferability sections; ScanNet++ moves to the supplement and references move before it. ALC/ALS200 terminology is replaced with descriptive ARKit LabelMaker names.

P2.justification: v2 adds dataset-size, gravity-alignment, annotation-comparison, class-distribution, tail-detection, and scaling figures, plus several experimental tables. It merges v1 Table 3 and Appendix Table B1 into a wide ScanNet200 table and relocates the ScanNet++ table. Existing pipeline and self-captured-scene figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 broadens introductory coverage to distillation, denoising, and additional open-vocabulary approaches, citing works such as OpenScene, OpenNeRF, Search3D, and P2P-Bridge. It also adds references supporting Matterport3D, PointGroup, and NeuS discussions. The central positioning as a LabelMaker extension addressing scarce annotated 3D data remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The gravity-alignment mathematical rule is unchanged, and neither version develops formal theorems or proofs. v2's log-linear scaling discussion describes empirical observations rather than a new mathematical derivation or formal result.

improvement.justification: Tables 4–6 address important gaps in v1 by directly evaluating annotation quality, isolating pipeline components, and testing dataset-size effects against size-matched synthetic data. Transfer experiments further strengthen the evidence for usefulness beyond the original evaluations. These gains substantially improve the paper's empirical foundation, despite removed ScanNet++ test results and reproducibility details, unexplained score revisions, and inconsistent split reporting.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Perspective projection has been extensively utilized in monocular 3D object
detection methods. It introduces geometric priors from 2D bounding boxes and 3D
object dimensions to reduce the uncertainty of depth estimation. However, due
to depth errors originating from the object's visual surface, the height of the
bounding box often fails to represent the actual projected central height,
which undermines the effectiveness of geometric depth. Direct prediction for
the projected height unavoidably results in a loss of 2D priors, while
multi-depth prediction with complex branches does not fully leverage geometric
depth. This paper presents a Transformer-based monocular 3D object detection
method called MonoDGP, which adopts perspective-invariant geometry errors to
modify the projection formula. We also try to systematically discuss and
explain the mechanisms and efficacy behind geometry errors, which serve as a
simple but effective alternative to multi-depth prediction. Additionally,
MonoDGP decouples the depth-guided decoder and constructs a 2D decoder only
dependent on visual features, providing 2D priors and initializing object
queries without the disturbance of 3D detection. To further optimize and
fine-tune input tokens of the transformer decoder, we also introduce a Region
Segment Head (RSH) that generates enhanced features and segment embeddings. Our
monocular method demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on the KITTI
benchmark without extra data. Code is available at
https://github.com/PuFanqi23/MonoDGP.

C1.justification: The core contributions and KITTI state-of-the-art claim without extra data remain. The introduction adds a specific claim that height-ratio mapping avoids cascaded uncertainty and offers efficiency and noise-robustness advantages over Deep3DBox/Shift R-CNN-style projection-alignment constraints.

C2.justification: Appendix A qualifies perspective invariance when camera and object heights differ. Other new discussions explain cyclist difficulties, coupled errors in height predictions, dependence on pretrained depth domains and failure under height occlusion. These substantially expand the mechanism explanations and applicability limitations beyond v1.

D1.justification: Appendix C explicitly documents focal, L1 and GIoU losses and the 2D/3D loss decomposition; the stated loss-weight vector expands from eight to nine coefficients. v2 also identifies pretrained-depth variants and timing conditions. These expand the documented specification without establishing that retained experiments were rerun; the main training schedule, hardware and code access remain.

E1.justification: Reported evaluation expands from KITTI cars to KITTI pedestrians and cyclists in Appendix D and Waymo vehicles in Appendix G. These additions substantially broaden the evaluated populations and dataset coverage.

E2.justification: KITTI car Table 1 adds MonoDDE and MonoUNI. The new Waymo comparison in Table 10 additionally introduces M3D-RPN, PatchNet and PCT alongside retained comparators. MonoDDE was discussed in v1 but did not participate in its Table 1 comparison.

E3.justification: New protocols include Waymo training/validation sets of 52,386/39,848 images sampled every third frame, AP3D/APH3D evaluation across difficulty levels and distance ranges, and IoU thresholds of 0.5 and 0.7. Other additions include KITTI pedestrian/cyclist evaluation at IoU 0.5 and ground-truth height substitution controls. The original KITTI split and training budget remain.

E4.justification: Beyond retained ablations, v2 adds computational-cost analysis, independent removal of RSH and decoupled queries, and a projected-central-height prediction control. Appendices add other-category ablations, ground-truth height sensitivity tests, pretrained-depth variants and qualitative occlusion/failure cases (Tables 2, 4-6, 8-9 and Figure 10).

E5.justification: Both versions describe five training runs with median moderate AP3D reporting for validation/ablation results. v2 introduces no new confidence intervals, significance tests or repeated-run reporting practice.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 MonoDGP scores remain unchanged, while v2 adds substantial category, Waymo, cost, sensitivity and depth-variant results. For example, Table 10 reports Waymo Level 1 overall AP3D of 4.28 at IoU 0.7. Adding MonoDDE reduces the reported KITTI hard-test AP3D lead from 1.18 to 0.87; MonoDGP's score remains 15.97.

M1.justification: The core RSH, decoupled decoders and geometric-depth correction remain. Appendix F adds an exploratory variant using pretrained Depth Anything V2 predictions as initial depth before learned error correction, extending the procedure beyond projection-based initialization.

P1.justification: The main section order and much of the prose remain. v2 makes localized revisions to the abstract, introduction, decoder explanations and results discussion, standardizes terminology and organizes supplementary material into Appendices A-H. New camera-height diagrams and qualitative detection panels substantially expand the visual evidence. v1 Tables 2-4 correspond to v2 Tables 3-5.

R1.justification: The introduction and new Appendix B expand positioning through a dedicated comparison of height-ratio and projection-alignment constraints, including stability, efficiency and occlusion arguments. Citations expand to new baselines, pretrained depth, datasets and loss components. v1's original Pseudo-LiDAR citation is removed; the main multi-depth comparison remains.

T1.justification: New Appendix A defines the camera/object height ratio and derives wheel-depth bias, corrected depth errors and bounds for cameras below or above object height (Equations 11-24). improvement.justification: v1 left generalization beyond KITTI cars and important geometric assumptions insufficiently tested. v2 substantially strengthens validation through Waymo and other-category results, independent controls and sensitivity tests, while camera-height derivations and failure analysis clarify applicability. This local reporting weakness does not outweigh the broader gains in evidence and qualification.

arxiv_record.abstract:
We present StdGEN, an innovative pipeline for generating semantically
decomposed high-quality 3D characters from single images, enabling broad
applications in virtual reality, gaming, and filmmaking, etc. Unlike previous
methods which struggle with limited decomposability, unsatisfactory quality,
and long optimization times, StdGEN features decomposability, effectiveness and
efficiency; i.e., it generates intricately detailed 3D characters with
separated semantic components such as the body, clothes, and hair, in three
minutes. At the core of StdGEN is our proposed Semantic-aware Large
Reconstruction Model (S-LRM), a transformer-based generalizable model that
jointly reconstructs geometry, color and semantics from multi-view images in a
feed-forward manner. A differentiable multi-layer semantic surface extraction
scheme is introduced to acquire meshes from hybrid implicit fields
reconstructed by our S-LRM. Additionally, a specialized efficient multi-view
diffusion model and an iterative multi-layer surface refinement module are
integrated into the pipeline to facilitate high-quality, decomposable 3D
character generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate our state-of-the-art
performance in 3D anime character generation, surpassing existing baselines by
a significant margin in geometry, texture and decomposability. StdGEN offers
ready-to-use semantic-decomposed 3D characters and enables flexible
customization for a wide range of applications. Project page:
https://stdgen.github.io

Yuze He, Yanning Zhou, Wang Zhao, Zhongkai Wu, Kaiwen Xiao, Wei Yang,
  Yong-Jin Liu, Xiao Han

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: high-quality, semantically decomposed characters from arbitrary-pose single images in approximately three minutes, using S-LRM and layered refinement. Additional evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Appendix H adds substantive explanations for using shared semantic-equivalent SDFs instead of separate class decoders, including transfer and scalability arguments. It also discusses real-human stylistic bias, limited semantic categories, resolution constraints, speed-quality tradeoffs, and restricted applicability beyond human-centric inputs.

D1.justification: Appendices E–G substantially expand reproducibility information: data filtering and connectivity checks, camera and rendering settings, semantic-loss weights, diffusion conditioning, frozen/trainable components, the 100×100×150 extraction grid, and texture-projection weights. The original implementation settings are largely retained; these are primarily newly disclosed details.

E1.justification: Anime3D++ training and evaluation coverage is retained. Appendix H adds realistic-human reconstruction on THuman 2.0, real-human editing, and furry and 2.5D inputs, substantially broadening the demonstrated input domains. These additions are qualitative and do not involve newly reported real-human training.

E2.justification: The comparator sets in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged. The supplement adds bounded qualitative comparisons against D-IF and HiLo on THuman 2.0 and against AvatarPopUp for real-human editing in Figures 11 and 13.

E3.justification: Appendix D adds substantial evaluation protocols: semantic-mask IoU across eight views, geometric Chamfer distance and F-score with a 0.01 threshold, and a quantitative control using S-LRM plus color back-projection without refinement. The original split and main evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: The original qualitative decomposition and refinement ablations move to Appendix A. New analyses quantify refinement's contribution in Table 5, profile processing stages in Table 3, and probe generalization beyond anime training data in Appendix H.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests for its experimental results. The additional measurements retain point-estimate reporting; the user-study participant and mesh counts are unchanged.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 1–2 are unchanged. New results include hair/clothing/body mask IoUs of 0.73/0.86/0.88, StdGEN Chamfer distance/F-score of 0.023/0.664 in Table 4, and SSIM of 0.912 without refinement versus the retained full-method value of 0.916 in Table 5. Runtime measurements and additional qualitative outputs also expand the evidence.

M1.justification: The canonicalization, multi-view diffusion, semantic-aware reconstruction, three-stage training, and layered refinement pipeline remain unchanged. Appendices F–G disclose additional conditioning, semantic weighting, trainable-layer, and projection details without establishing a revision to the underlying procedure.

P1.justification: The document is substantially reorganized: implementation details, mesh dilation, qualitative ablations, and animation demonstrations move into the supplement. Main-text method and dataset descriptions are condensed, while supplementary Sections A–I organize extensive technical explanations, analyses, and discussion.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 3–5 and Figures 11–19, reformats Table 1, resizes the main qualitative comparison, and relocates the original ablation and animation figures. The visual presentation expands substantially, although most original illustrations are retained rather than replaced.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 and Appendix H substantially expand positioning against decomposition methods, adding GALA and Frankenstein and developing comparisons with the already-cited TELA. The discussion distinguishes inputs, representations, texture preservation, cost, and scalability, replacing v1's broad characterization of prior character methods as holistic. Reference deduplication alone is not counted.

T1.justification: Appendices F–G add explicit mathematical definitions for previously described operations, including the deviation loss in Equation 17 and color back-projection in Equation 19. The central semantic-equivalent NeRF/SDF mathematics remains unchanged, with no new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's validation by adding quantitative semantic checks, direct 3D geometry metrics, and a controlled refinement comparison. Detailed implementation disclosures and substantive limitations also improve reproducibility and interpretation. Non-anime evidence remains qualitative, and Equation 19's printed projection normalization appears incorrect, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in support for the paper's central contributions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe StdGEN and retain matching core methods and experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary material support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 includes supplementary Sections A–I.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds semantic and geometric measurements, runtime profiling, a quantitative refinement ablation, and non-anime examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original Anime3D++ experiments, qualitative ablations, application demonstrations, and a user study involving 28 volunteers and 16 meshes.

arxiv_record.abstract: Masked Image Modeling (MIM) has emerged as a powerful self-supervised learning paradigm for visual representation learning, enabling models to acquire rich visual representations by predicting masked portions of images from their visible regions. While this approach has shown promising results, we hypothesize that its effectiveness may be limited by optimization challenges during early training stages, where models are expected to learn complex image distributions from partial observations before developing basic visual processing capabilities. To address this limitation, we propose a prototype-driven curriculum leagrning framework that structures the learning process to progress from prototypical examples to more complex variations in the dataset. Our approach introduces a temperature-based annealing scheme that gradually expands the training distribution, enabling more stable and efficient learning trajectories. Through extensive experiments on ImageNet-1K, we demonstrate that our curriculum learning strategy significantly improves both training efficiency and representation quality while requiring substantially fewer training epochs compared to standard Masked Auto-Encoding. Our findings suggest that carefully controlling the order of training examples plays a crucial role in self-supervised visual learning, providing a practical solution to the early-stage optimization challenges in MIM.
arxiv_record.authors: Jinhong Lin, Cheng-En Wu, Huanran Li, Jifan Zhang, Yu Hen Hu, Pedro Morgado
arxiv_record.title: From Prototypes to General Distributions: An Efficient Curriculum for Masked Image Modeling

These are newly disclosed recipes, not demonstrated changes to the original experiments.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands from ImageNet to five-shot classification on CUB-200, SUN397, OxfordPets, Caltech101, UCF101, DTD, Flowers102, and Food101. This substantially broadens transfer domains and introduces evaluation with scarce labels; pretraining coverage remains ImageNet.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains standard MAE and the hard-sample curriculum adapted from Sorscher et al. The prototype-identification comparators also remain unchanged. The added transfer evaluation introduces no distinct competing algorithm.

E3.justification: The new transfer protocol trains linear classifiers with five labeled examples per class, comparing 200/400-epoch curriculum models with a 1600-epoch baseline. Separately, the temperature-table caption changes the annealing range from 0.05–0.2 to 0.07–0.6, matching Section 4.1 in both versions. This is a reported-setting correction, without evidence that the retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Supplementary Figures 6–8 add qualitative comparisons of centroid-distance ordering across SIFT, untrained, MAE, and DINO feature spaces for nine ImageNet categories. These extend the existing prototype-identification analysis; the quantitative temperature, architecture, feature-space, and cluster-count ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: New Table 3 reports means and standard deviations over three runs. This introduces uncertainty reporting for the added transfer evaluation, while the original ImageNet results retain point estimates. The PDFs do not establish increased repetition of existing experiments.

E6.justification: New Table 3 reports eight-dataset average five-shot accuracies of 41.77% for the 1600-epoch baseline, 42.18% for the 200-epoch curriculum, and 47.23% for the 400-epoch curriculum. These are newly reported comparisons at different training budgets, not revisions to earlier scores. Existing ImageNet numerical results are retained, and supplementary figures add qualitative findings.

M1.justification: The MAE objective, clustering procedure, normalized centroid distances, temperature-controlled sampling, and effective-dataset-size scheduling remain unchanged. The supplementary material documents and analyzes the existing method.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are largely retained. Changes include a few-shot results paragraph, supplementary explanatory text, and limited caption editing. Section 4.4 retains stale references to Table 4a–c after the corresponding table becomes Table 5.

P2.justification: v2 adds the transfer-results table, two configuration tables, and three substantial multi-panel supplementary figures. R1.justification: v2 adds references for the eight transfer datasets and removes the DATA reference by Chang et al. The related-work discussion and positioning relative to MIM, dataset selection, and importance sampling remain essentially unchanged.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Language-image pre-training faces significant challenges due to limited data
in specific formats and the constrained capacities of text encoders. While
prevailing methods attempt to address these issues through data augmentation
and architecture modifications, they continue to struggle with processing
long-form text inputs, and the inherent limitations of traditional CLIP text
encoders lead to suboptimal downstream generalization. In this paper, we
propose FLAME (Frozen Large lAnguage Models Enable data-efficient
language-image pre-training) that leverages frozen large language models as
text encoders, naturally processing long text inputs and demonstrating
impressive multilingual generalization. FLAME comprises two key components: 1)
a multifaceted prompt distillation technique for extracting diverse semantic
representations from long captions, which better aligns with the multifaceted
nature of images, and 2) a facet-decoupled attention mechanism, complemented by
an offline embedding strategy, to ensure efficient computation. Extensive
empirical evaluations demonstrate FLAME's superior performance. When trained on
CC3M, FLAME surpasses the previous state-of-the-art by 4.9% in ImageNet top-1
accuracy. On YFCC15M, FLAME surpasses the WIT-400M-trained CLIP by 44.4\% in
average image-to-text recall@1 across 36 languages, and by 34.6% in
text-to-image recall@1 for long-context retrieval on Urban-1k. Code is
available at https://github.com/MIV-XJTU/FLAME.

E4.justification: v3 adds semantic-level ablations (Table C7), patch-to-word interpretability examples (Figure 5), and Urban-1k retrieval case studies (Figure D2). E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, independent-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Table C4 introduces repetition settings within the few-shot evaluation, without identifying them as statistical replications or providing uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results for the new benchmarks, semantic-level ablations, and larger models; Table C4 reports FLAME averages of 86.8% and 68.4% for 2-way and 5-way comprehension. arxiv_record.abstract: Human's perception of the visual world is shaped by the stereo processing of 3D information. Understanding how the brain perceives and processes 3D visual stimuli in the real world has been a longstanding endeavor in neuroscience. Towards this goal, we introduce a new neuroscience task: decoding 3D visual perception from EEG signals, a neuroimaging technique that enables real-time monitoring of neural dynamics enriched with complex visual cues. To provide the essential benchmark, we first present EEG-3D, a pioneering dataset featuring multimodal analysis data and extensive EEG recordings from 12 subjects viewing 72 categories of 3D objects rendered in both videos and images. Furthermore, we propose Neuro-3D, a 3D visual decoding framework based on EEG signals. This framework adaptively integrates EEG features derived from static and dynamic stimuli to learn complementary and robust neural representations, which are subsequently utilized to recover both the shape and color of 3D objects through the proposed diffusion-based colored point cloud decoder. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to explore EEG-based 3D visual decoding. Experiments indicate that Neuro-3D not only reconstructs colored 3D objects with high fidelity, but also learns effective neural representations that enable insightful brain region analysis. The dataset and associated code will be made publicly available.
arxiv_record.authors: Zhanqiang Guo, Jiamin Wu, Yonghao Song, Jiahui Bu, Weijian Mai, Qihao Zheng, Wanli Ouyang, Chunfeng Song

arxiv_record.abstract:
Real-world image super-resolution (Real-ISR) aims to reconstruct
high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs degraded by complex, unknown
processes. While many Stable Diffusion (SD)-based Real-ISR methods have
achieved remarkable success, their slow, multi-step inference hinders practical
deployment. Recent SD-based one-step networks like OSEDiff and S3Diff alleviate
this issue but still incur high computational costs due to their reliance on
large pretrained SD models. This paper proposes a novel Real-ISR method, AdcSR,
by distilling the one-step diffusion network OSEDiff into a streamlined
diffusion-GAN model under our Adversarial Diffusion Compression (ADC)
framework. We meticulously examine the modules of OSEDiff, categorizing them
into two types: (1) Removable (VAE encoder, prompt extractor, text encoder,
etc.) and (2) Prunable (denoising UNet and VAE decoder). Since direct removal
and pruning can degrade the model's generation capability, we pretrain our
pruned VAE decoder to restore its ability to decode images and employ
adversarial distillation to compensate for performance loss. This ADC-based
diffusion-GAN hybrid design effectively reduces complexity by 73% in inference

arxiv_record.abstract:
Camera-based Semantic Scene Completion (SSC) is gaining attentions in the 3D
perception field. However, properties such as perspective and occlusion lead to
the underestimation of the geometry in distant regions, posing a critical issue
for safety-focused autonomous driving systems. To tackle this, we propose
ScanSSC, a novel camera-based SSC model composed of a Scan Module and Scan
Loss, both designed to enhance distant scenes by leveraging context from
near-viewpoint scenes. The Scan Module uses axis-wise masked attention, where
each axis employing a near-to-far cascade masking that enables distant voxels
to capture relationships with preceding voxels. In addition, the Scan Loss
computes the cross-entropy along each axis between cumulative logits and
corresponding class distributions in a near-to-far direction, thereby
propagating rich context-aware signals to distant voxels. Leveraging the
synergy between these components, ScanSSC achieves state-of-the-art
performance, with IoUs of 44.54 and 48.29, and mIoUs of 17.40 and 20.14 on the
SemanticKITTI and SSCBench-KITTI-360 benchmarks.
arxiv_record.authors: Jongseong Bae, Junwoo Ha, Ha Young Kim

  Tri-Axis Voxel Scanning for Camera-based Semantic Scene Completion

arxiv_record.abstract: Since 2023, Vector Quantization (VQ)-based discrete generation methods have rapidly dominated human motion generation, primarily surpassing diffusion-based continuous generation methods in standard performance metrics. However, VQ-based methods have inherent limitations. Representing continuous motion data as limited discrete tokens leads to inevitable information loss, reduces the diversity of generated motions, and restricts their ability to function effectively as motion priors or generation guidance. In contrast, the continuous space generation nature of diffusion-based methods makes them well-suited to address these limitations and with even potential for model scalability. In this work, we systematically investigate why current VQ-based methods perform well and explore the limitations of existing diffusion-based methods from the perspective of motion data representation and distribution. Drawing on these insights, we preserve the inherent strengths of a diffusion-based human motion generation model and gradually optimize it with inspiration from VQ-based approaches. Our approach introduces a human motion diffusion model enabled to perform masked autoregression, optimized with a reformed data representation and distribution. Additionally, we propose a more robust evaluation method to assess different approaches. Extensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate our method outperforms previous methods and achieves state-of-the-art performances.
arxiv_record.authors: Zichong Meng, Yiming Xie, Xiaogang Peng, Zeyu Han, Huaizu Jiang
arxiv_record.title: Rethinking Diffusion for Text-Driven Human Motion Generation: Redundant Representations, Evaluation, and Masked Autoregression

arxiv_record.abstract:
Collaborative perception in autonomous driving significantly enhances the
perception capabilities of individual agents. Immutable heterogeneity, where
agents have different and fixed perception networks, presents a major challenge
due to the semantic gap in exchanged intermediate features without modifying
the perception networks. Most existing methods bridge the semantic gap through
interpreters. However, they either require training a new interpreter for each
new agent type, limiting extensibility, or rely on a two-stage interpretation
via an intermediate standardized semantic space, causing cumulative semantic
loss. To achieve both extensibility in immutable heterogeneous scenarios and
low-loss feature interpretation, we propose PolyInter, a polymorphic feature
interpreter. It provides an extension point where new agents integrate by
overriding only their specific prompts, which are learnable parameters that
guide interpretation, while reusing PolyInter's remaining parameters. By
leveraging polymorphism, our design enables a single interpreter to accommodate
diverse agents and interpret their features into the ego agent's semantic
space. Experiments on the OPV2V dataset demonstrate that PolyInter improves
collaborative perception precision by up to 11.1% compared to SOTA
interpreters, while comparable results can be achieved by training only 1.4% of
PolyInter's parameters when adapting to new agents. Code is available at
https://github.com/yuchen-xia/PolyInter.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation (OVSS) has advanced with recent
vision-language models (VLMs), enabling segmentation beyond predefined
categories through various learning schemes. Notably, training-free methods
offer scalable, easily deployable solutions for handling unseen data, a key
goal of OVSS. Yet, a critical issue persists: lack of object-level context
consideration when segmenting complex objects in the challenging environment of
OVSS based on arbitrary query prompts. This oversight limits models' ability to
group semantically consistent elements within object and map them precisely to
user-defined arbitrary classes. In this work, we introduce a novel approach
that overcomes this limitation by incorporating object-level contextual
knowledge within images. Specifically, our model enhances intra-object
consistency by distilling spectral-driven features from vision foundation
models into the attention mechanism of the visual encoder, enabling
semantically coherent components to form a single object mask. Additionally, we
refine the text embeddings with zero-shot object presence likelihood to ensure
accurate alignment with the specific objects represented in the images. By
leveraging object-level contextual knowledge, our proposed approach achieves
state-of-the-art performance with strong generalizability across diverse
datasets.

arxiv_record.abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated impressive performance in face restoration. Yet, their multi-step inference process remains computationally intensive, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios. Moreover, existing methods often struggle to generate face images that are harmonious, realistic, and consistent with the subject's identity. In this work, we propose OSDFace, a novel one-step diffusion model for face restoration. Specifically, we propose a visual representation embedder (VRE) to better capture prior information and understand the input face. In VRE, low-quality faces are processed by a visual tokenizer and subsequently embedded with a vector-quantized dictionary to generate visual prompts. Additionally, we incorporate a facial identity loss derived from face recognition to further ensure identity consistency. We further employ a generative adversarial network (GAN) as a guidance model to encourage distribution alignment between the restored face and the ground truth. Experimental results demonstrate that OSDFace surpasses current state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in both visual quality and quantitative metrics, generating high-fidelity, natural face images with high identity consistency. The code and model will be released at https://github.com/jkwang28/OSDFace.

native_poster_event.abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated impressive performance in face restoration. Yet, their multi-step inference process remains computationally intensive, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios. Moreover, existing methods often struggle to generate face images that are harmonious, realistic, and consistent with the subject’s identity. In this work, we propose OSDFace, a novel one-step diffusion model for face restoration. Specifically, we propose a visual representation embedder (VRE) to better capture prior information and understand the input face. In VRE, low-quality faces are processed by a visual tokenizer and subsequently embedded with a vector-quantized dictionary to generate visual prompts. Additionally, we incorporate a facial identity loss derived from face recognition to further ensure identity consistency. We further employ a generative adversarial network (GAN) as a guidance model to encourage distribution alignment between the restored face and the ground truth. Experimental results demonstrate that OSDFace surpasses current state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in both visual quality and quantitative metrics, generating high-fidelity, natural face images with high identity consistency. The code and model will be released soon.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims: one-step face restoration, VRE-based visual conditioning, identity and distribution alignment, and strong quality with efficient inference. Additional experiments support these claims without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: Supplementary Section E adds specific limitations involving color shifts, skin textures and non-facial regions such as fingers, and minimally degraded inputs, including explanations tied to training coverage. Sections C–D also interpret VRE transfer and downstream recognition benefits. v1 lacks this substantive discussion of applicability and failure conditions.

D1.justification: v2 identifies the recognition evaluator as the official ArcFace MS1MV3 R50 model, describes parallel execution, and clarifies that existing OSEDiff* retraining uses OSDFace's dataset and experimental settings. Core training details remain unchanged, and both versions still promise future code and model release.

E1.justification: v2 adds zero-shot cartoon restoration using Anime Face Dataset (main Figure 6) and downstream LFW face recognition under previously unseen atmospheric turbulence (Supplementary Section D). These substantially extend the evaluated domain, task requirements, and degradation conditions beyond the retained restoration benchmarks.

E2.justification: The original restoration comparator set is retained. Supplementary Tables 2–3 add OSEDiff*+VRE to comparisons against OSDFace. The new recognition experiment also includes a no-restoration control alongside DAEFR, DiffBIR, and OSEDiff*.

E3.justification: The new recognition protocol evaluates 3,000 positive and 3,000 negative LFW pairs at turbulence propagation lengths of 20,000, 30,000, and 40,000, reporting PR, ROC, F1, and similarity-separation measurements. Supplementary Section B also compares serialized and parallel execution. Existing main-text training and restoration-evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds experiments testing whether VRE improves OSEDiff, recognition robustness across unseen turbulence severities, and the computational benefit of parallel execution. Supplementary Section F adds case analyses involving occlusions, profiles, multiple faces, accessories, and backgrounds. The original prompt and loss ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new recognition curves and mean-distance bars introduce evaluation measurements without adding uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The unstarred OSEDiff scores change throughout main Tables 1–2. For example, CelebA-Test LPIPS changes from 0.4708 to 0.3306, overtaking OSDFace's unchanged 0.3365; the reason for this revision is unspecified. v2 also adds VRE-transfer results, serialized/parallel timings, recognition curves, and qualitative outputs. The original OSDFace benchmark scores and main ablation results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core OSDFace architecture, two-stage training, and losses remain unchanged. Supplementary Sections B–C add an evaluated procedure that executes the prompt embedder and VAE encoder in parallel, and an OSEDiff*+VRE adaptation integrating VRE into another restoration model.

P1.justification: v2 lightly edits main-text wording, updates terminology, adds acknowledgments, and organizes additional material into Supplementary Sections A–F. The original section order, narrative, and method exposition are largely retained; there is no extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds a cartoon-restoration figure, supplementary comparison and timing tables, a multi-panel recognition figure, and extensive synthetic and real-world comparison grids. Main Figure 3 gains explicit component labels, and Table 1 is resized beside the cartoon examples. These substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for Anime Face Dataset, DialogueNeRF, atmospheric-turbulence simulation, and AdaIN. The DFOSD-to-D3SR rename matches the same arXiv:2410.04224 reference. The main related-work discussion and positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Supplementary Figure 3 newly defines mean sample distance as the difference between average cosine similarities for predicted positive and negative pairs. This is a limited mathematical-definition addition associated with evaluation. The original diffusion and loss equations remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: The supplement substantially strengthens validation by testing VRE in another model and evaluating downstream identity recognition under unseen degradation. Concrete failure conditions also make the paper's applicability clearer than in v1. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: the OSEDiff score revisions are unexplained, and Section 4.2 retains an LPIPS-superiority statement inconsistent with revised Table 1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OSDFace, with matching core methods and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 adds a separately numbered supplement, which was included in this assessment.

after.justification: v2 retains original restoration experiments and adds VRE-transfer experiments, parallel-inference measurements, recognition tests under atmospheric turbulence, and cartoon-restoration examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original face-restoration results on synthetic and real-world datasets, computational measurements, and component ablations in Tables 1–5.

arxiv_record.abstract:
We propose SelfSplat, a novel 3D Gaussian Splatting model designed to perform
pose-free and 3D prior-free generalizable 3D reconstruction from unposed
multi-view images. These settings are inherently ill-posed due to the lack of
ground-truth data, learned geometric information, and the need to achieve
accurate 3D reconstruction without finetuning, making it difficult for
conventional methods to achieve high-quality results. Our model addresses these
challenges by effectively integrating explicit 3D representations with
self-supervised depth and pose estimation techniques, resulting in reciprocal
improvements in both pose accuracy and 3D reconstruction quality. Furthermore,
we incorporate a matching-aware pose estimation network and a depth refinement
module to enhance geometry consistency across views, ensuring more accurate and
stable 3D reconstructions. To present the performance of our method, we
evaluated it on large-scale real-world datasets, including RealEstate10K, ACID,
and DL3DV. SelfSplat achieves superior results over previous state-of-the-art
methods in both appearance and geometry quality, also demonstrates strong
cross-dataset generalization capabilities. Extensive ablation studies and
analysis also validate the effectiveness of our proposed methods. Code and
pretrained models are available at https://gynjn.github.io/selfsplat/

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about pose-free and 3D-prior-free reconstruction, reciprocal benefits of self-supervision and Gaussian splatting, and cross-dataset generalization. The supplement adds supporting evidence without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: The supplement adds interpretations of efficiency and multi-view scalability, and attributes Splatt3R's DTU scale inconsistencies to pretrained metric geometry and intrinsic-parameter differences. It also explains the choice of self-supervised initialization. The earlier limitations concerning wide-baseline reconstruction and dynamic scenes are retained in Appendix C.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly documents encoder initialization, frozen-backbone adapters and dimensions, spherical-harmonic order, optimizer settings, batch sizes, training budgets, hardware, frame sampling, and evaluation splits. It also explains baseline adaptations and DL3DV initialization. These substantially improve documentation without establishing changes to the underlying retained experiments.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained RE10k, ACID, and DL3DV evaluations, v4 adds out-of-distribution evaluation on DTU object scenes. Appendix B.2 also evaluates three and four context views over longer sequences and measures camera-trajectory reconstruction, substantially extending domain and test-scenario coverage.

E2.justification: Table 12 introduces evaluated comparisons with Splatt3R, pixelSplat, and MVSplat on DTU. Table 13 adds VAE and DBARF to cross-dataset comparisons that previously included only FlowCAM and CoPoNeRF. The original comparator sets remain present.

E3.justification: New protocols measure peak memory and inference time for 256-by-256 images on an RTX 4090, and evaluate three/four context views over 80/120 frames using Absolute Trajectory Error. Section 5.1 also changes overlap thresholds from percentage notation to fractions. Newly disclosed settings for retained experiments do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: The original component and loss ablations remain. Table 14 adds tests removing CroCo initialization, the monocular encoder, and the multi-view encoder. Additional analyses examine inference cost, scaling to more context views and longer trajectories, and rendered depth quality, substantially expanding the questions investigated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bars. The supplementary results continue point-estimate reporting; the retained pose-error means and medians are not run-to-run uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Main Tables 2-8 are unchanged, but v4 adds substantial numerical and qualitative evidence in Tables 10-14 and Figures 8-14. For example, DTU PSNR is 13.14 for SelfSplat, 10.24 for Splatt3R, 12.89 for pixelSplat, and 13.94 for MVSplat. These are new comparisons with differing training or pose requirements, not same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: The encoders, feature fusion, matching-aware pose network, depth refinement, and training objectives remain unchanged. Appendix A supplies implementation details, while the additional context-view experiments test the existing model without establishing an algorithmic revision.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain nearly identical. Changes include author and affiliation edits, limited related-work and evaluation wording revisions, an organized supplement, and relocation of the limitations and project link. There is little rewriting of the retained scientific exposition.

P2.justification: The original figures and tables remain with small layout adjustments. v4 adds Tables 9-14 and Figures 7-14, including a detailed architecture diagram, trajectory plots, DTU and depth comparisons, and extensive qualitative galleries. This substantially expands the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Section 2.1 adds PF3plat and No Pose, No Problem alongside GGRT and revises discussion of pretrained-model dependencies. Appendix B.3 positions SelfSplat against Splatt3R and pose-required Gaussian methods. Additional supporting references broaden coverage while preserving the original research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds an explicit first-order spherical-harmonic expression and permutation matrix for color-coordinate warping. The original mathematical definitions, objectives, and pose-gradient expression in Equations 1-11 remain unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v4 fills substantial reproducibility gaps through its training, implementation, and sampling details. New encoder ablations, measured efficiency, trajectory tests, and DTU comparisons make important aspects of the unchanged method more assessable. DTU comparisons remain qualified by differing training and pose requirements, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but the gains in documentation and empirical scrutiny substantially improve the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SelfSplat and provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures. v1 ends after its references; v4 includes supplementary Sections A-D. The retained material and additions support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds efficiency measurements, multiple-context-view experiments, DTU evaluation, additional baseline comparisons, and encoder ablations.

before.justification: Tables 2-8 report original novel-view synthesis, pose estimation, cross-dataset generalization, and ablation results on RE10k, ACID, and DL3DV.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Identity-preserving text-to-video (IPT2V) generation aims to create
high-fidelity videos with consistent human identity. It is an important task in
video generation but remains an open problem for generative models. This paper
pushes the technical frontier of IPT2V in two directions that have not been
resolved in literature: (1) A tuning-free pipeline without tedious case-by-case
finetuning, and (2) A frequency-aware heuristic identity-preserving DiT-based
control scheme. We propose ConsisID, a tuning-free DiT-based controllable IPT2V
model to keep human identity consistent in the generated video. Inspired by
prior findings in frequency analysis of diffusion transformers, it employs
identity-control signals in the frequency domain, where facial features can be
decomposed into low-frequency global features and high-frequency intrinsic
features. First, from a low-frequency perspective, we introduce a global facial
extractor, which encodes reference images and facial key points into a latent
space, generating features enriched with low-frequency information. These
features are then integrated into shallow layers of the network to alleviate
training challenges associated with DiT. Second, from a high-frequency
perspective, we design a local facial extractor to capture high-frequency
details and inject them into transformer blocks, enhancing the model's ability
to preserve fine-grained features. We propose a hierarchical training strategy
to leverage frequency information for identity preservation, transforming a
vanilla pre-trained video generation model into an IPT2V model. Extensive
experiments demonstrate that our frequency-aware heuristic scheme provides an
optimal control solution for DiT-based models. Thanks to this scheme, our
ConsisID generates high-quality, identity-preserving videos, making strides
towards more effective IPT2V. Code: https://github.com/PKU-YuanGroup/ConsisID.

It is an important task in video generation but remains an open problem for generative models. This paper pushes the technical frontier of IPT2V in two directions that have not been resolved in the literature: (1) A tuning-free pipeline without tedious case-by-case finetuning, and (2) A frequency-aware heuristic identity-preserving Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based control scheme. To achieve these goals, we propose **ConsisID**, a tuning-free DiT-based controllable IPT2V model to keep human-**id**entity **consis**tent in the generated video. Inspired by prior findings in frequency analysis of vision/diffusion transformers, it employs identity-control signals in the frequency domain, where facial features can be decomposed into low-frequency global features (e.g., profile, proportions) and high-frequency intrinsic features (e.g., identity markers that remain unaffected by pose changes). First, from a low-frequency perspective, we introduce a global facial extractor, which encodes the reference image and facial key points into a latent space, generating features enriched with low-frequency information. These features are then integrated into the shallow layers of the network to alleviate training challenges associated with DiT. Second, from a high-frequency perspective, we design a local facial extractor to capture high-frequency details and inject them into the transformer blocks, enhancing the model's ability to preserve fine-grained features. To leverage the frequency information for identity preservation, we propose a hierarchical training strategy, transforming a vanilla pre-trained video generation model into an IPT2V model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our frequency-aware heuristic scheme provides an optimal control solution for DiT-based models. Thanks to this scheme, our **ConsisID** achieves excellent results in generating high-quality, identity-preserving videos, making strides towards more effective IPT2V.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Diffusion models achieved unprecedented fidelity and diversity for
synthesizing image, video, 3D assets, etc. However, subject mixing is an
unresolved issue for diffusion-based image synthesis, particularly for
synthesizing multiple similar-looking subjects. We propose Self-Cross Diffusion
Guidance to penalize the overlap between cross-attention maps and the
aggregated self-attention map. Compared to previous methods based on
self-attention or cross-attention alone, our guidance is more effective in
eliminating subject mixing. What's more, our guidance addresses subject mixing
for all relevant patches beyond the most discriminant one, e.g., the beak of a
bird. For each subject, we aggregate self-attention maps of patches with higher
cross-attention values. Thus, the aggregated self-attention map forms a region
that the whole subject attends to. Our training-free method boosts the
performance of both Unet-based and Transformer-based diffusion models such as
the Stable Diffusion series. We also release a similar subjects dataset (SSD),
a challenging benchmark, and utilize GPT-4o for automatic and reliable
evaluation. Extensive qualitative and quantitative results demonstrate the
effectiveness of our self-cross diffusion guidance.

arxiv_record.abstract:
3D scene understanding has become an essential area of research with
applications in autonomous driving, robotics, and augmented reality. Recently,
3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a powerful approach, combining
explicit modeling with neural adaptability to provide efficient and detailed
scene representations. However, three major challenges remain in leveraging
3DGS for scene understanding: 1) an imbalance between appearance and semantics,
where dense Gaussian usage for fine-grained texture modeling does not align
with the minimal requirements for semantic attributes; 2) inconsistencies
between appearance and semantics, as purely appearance-based Gaussians often
misrepresent object boundaries; and 3) reliance on top-down instance
segmentation methods, which struggle with uneven category distributions,
leading to over- or under-segmentation. In this work, we propose
InstanceGaussian, a method that jointly learns appearance and semantic features
while adaptively aggregating instances. Our contributions include: i) a novel
Semantic-Scaffold-GS representation balancing appearance and semantics to
improve feature representations and boundary delineation; ii) a progressive
appearance-semantic joint training strategy to enhance stability and
segmentation accuracy; and iii) a bottom-up, category-agnostic instance
aggregation approach that addresses segmentation challenges through farthest
point sampling and connected component analysis. Our approach achieves
state-of-the-art performance in category-agnostic, open-vocabulary 3D
point-level segmentation, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed
representation and training strategies. Project page:
https://lhj-git.github.io/InstanceGaussian/

arxiv_record.abstract:
We introduce LumiNet, a novel architecture that leverages generative models and latent intrinsic representations for effective lighting transfer. Given a source image and a target lighting image, LumiNet synthesizes a relit version of the source scene that captures the target's lighting. Our approach makes two key contributions: a data curation strategy from the StyleGAN-based relighting model for our training, and a modified diffusion-based ControlNet that processes both latent intrinsic properties from the source image and latent extrinsic properties from the target image. We further improve lighting transfer through a learned adaptor (MLP) that injects the target's latent extrinsic properties via cross-attention and fine-tuning.
  Unlike traditional ControlNet, which generates images with conditional maps from a single scene, LumiNet processes latent representations from two different images - preserving geometry and albedo from the source while transferring lighting characteristics from the target. Experiments demonstrate that our method successfully transfers complex lighting phenomena including specular highlights and indirect illumination across scenes with varying spatial layouts and materials, outperforming existing approaches on challenging indoor scenes using only images as input.

snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract:
We introduce LumiNet, a novel architecture that leverages generative models and latent intrinsic representations for effective lighting transfer. Given a source image and a target lighting image, LumiNet synthesizes a relit version of the source scene that captures the target's lighting. Our approach makes two key contributions: a data curation strategy from the StyleGAN-based relighting model for our training, and a modified diffusion-based ControlNet that processes both latent intrinsic properties from the source image and latent extrinsic properties from the target image. We further improve lighting transfer through a learned adaptor (MLP) that injects the target's latent extrinsic properties via cross-attention and fine-tuning.
  Unlike traditional ControlNet, which generates images with conditional maps from a single scene, LumiNet processes latent representations from two different images - preserving geometry and albedo from the source while transferring lighting characteristics from the target. Experiments demonstrate that our method successfully transfers complex lighting phenomena including specular highlights and indirect illumination across scenes with varying spatial layouts and materials, outperforming existing approaches on challenging indoor scenes using only images as input.

arxiv_record.abstract: Mesh quality assessment (MQA) models play a critical role in the design, optimization, and evaluation of mesh operation systems in a wide variety of applications. Current MQA models, whether model-based methods using topology-aware features or projection-based approaches working on rendered 2D projections, often fail to capture the intricate interactions between texture and 3D geometry. We introduce HybridMQA, a first-of-its-kind hybrid full-reference colored MQA framework that integrates model-based and projection-based approaches, capturing complex interactions between textural information and 3D structures for enriched quality representations. Our method employs graph learning to extract detailed 3D representations, which are then projected to 2D using a novel feature rendering process that precisely aligns them with colored projections. This enables the exploration of geometry-texture interactions via cross-attention, producing comprehensive mesh quality representations. Extensive experiments demonstrate HybridMQA's superior performance across diverse datasets, highlighting its ability to effectively leverage geometry-texture interactions for a thorough understanding of mesh quality. Our implementation will be made publicly available.
arxiv_record.authors: Armin Shafiee Sarvestani, Sheyang Tang, Zhou Wang
arxiv_record.title: HybridMQA: Exploring Geometry-Texture Interactions for Colored Mesh Quality Assessment

arxiv_record.abstract:
Autonomous agents often require accurate methods for detecting and localizing
changes in their environment, particularly when observations are captured from
unconstrained and inconsistent viewpoints. We propose a novel label-free,
pose-agnostic change detection method that integrates information from multiple
viewpoints to construct a change-aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)
representation of the scene. With as few as 5 images of the post-change scene,
our approach can learn an additional change channel in a 3DGS and produce
change masks that outperform single-view techniques. Our change-aware 3D scene
representation additionally enables the generation of accurate change masks for
unseen viewpoints. Experimental results demonstrate state-of-the-art
performance in complex multi-object scenes, achieving a 1.7x and 1.5x
improvement in Mean Intersection Over Union and F1 score respectively over
other baselines. We also contribute a new real-world dataset to benchmark
change detection in diverse challenging scenes in the presence of lighting
variations.
arxiv_record.authors:
Chamuditha Jayanga Galappaththige, Jason Lai, Lloyd Windrim, Donald
  Dansereau, Niko Suenderhauf, Dimity Miller

arxiv_record.abstract:
Contrastively-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP have become the de facto approach for discriminative vision-language representation learning. However, these models have limited language understanding, often exhibiting a "bag of words" behavior. At the same time, Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), which combine vision encoders with LLMs, have been shown to be capable of detailed vision-language reasoning, yet their autoregressive nature renders them less suitable for discriminative tasks.
  In this work, we propose to combine "the best of both worlds": a new training approach for discriminative fine-tuning of LVLMs that results in strong discriminative and compositional capabilities. Essentially, our approach converts a generative LVLM into a discriminative one, unlocking its capability for powerful image-text discrimination combined with enhanced language understanding.
  Our contributions include (1) a carefully designed training/optimization framework that utilizes image-text pairs of variable length and granularity for training the model with both contrastive and next-token prediction losses. This is accompanied by ablation studies that justify the necessity of our framework's components; (2) a parameter-efficient adaptation method using a combination of soft prompting and LoRA adapters; (3) significant improvements over state-of-the-art CLIP-like models of similar size, including standard image-text retrieval benchmarks and notable gains in compositionality.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Recent advances in large-scale text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models have
enabled a variety of downstream applications, including style customization,
subject-driven personalization, and conditional generation. As T2I models
require extensive data and computational resources for training, they
constitute highly valued intellectual property (IP) for their legitimate
owners, yet making them incentive targets for unauthorized fine-tuning by
adversaries seeking to leverage these models for customized, usually profitable
applications. Existing IP protection methods for diffusion models generally
involve embedding watermark patterns and then verifying ownership through
generated outputs examination, or inspecting the model's feature space.
However, these techniques are inherently ineffective in practical scenarios
when the watermarked model undergoes fine-tuning, and the feature space is
inaccessible during verification ((i.e., black-box setting). The model is prone
to forgetting the previously learned watermark knowledge when it adapts to a
new task. To address this challenge, we propose SleeperMark, a novel framework
designed to embed resilient watermarks into T2I diffusion models. SleeperMark
explicitly guides the model to disentangle the watermark information from the
semantic concepts it learns, allowing the model to retain the embedded
watermark while continuing to be adapted to new downstream tasks. Our extensive
experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of SleeperMark across various types
of diffusion models, including latent diffusion models (e.g., Stable Diffusion)
and pixel diffusion models (e.g., DeepFloyd-IF), showing robustness against
downstream fine-tuning and various attacks at both the image and model levels,
with minimal impact on the model's generative capability. The code is available
at https://github.com/taco-group/SleeperMark.

  Chen, Zhengzhong Tu

arxiv_record.abstract:
Accurate 3D objects relighting in diverse unseen environments is crucial for
realistic virtual object placement. Due to the albedo-lighting ambiguity,
existing methods often fall short in producing faithful relights. Without
proper constraints, observed training views can be explained by numerous
combinations of lighting and material attributes, lacking physical
correspondence with the actual environment maps used for relighting. In this
work, we present ReCap, treating cross-environment captures as multi-task
target to provide the missing supervision that cuts through the entanglement.
Specifically, ReCap jointly optimizes multiple lighting representations that
share a common set of material attributes. This naturally harmonizes a coherent
set of lighting representations around the mutual material attributes,
exploiting commonalities and differences across varied object appearances. Such
coherence enables physically sound lighting reconstruction and robust material
estimation - both essential for accurate relighting. Together with a
streamlined shading function and effective post-processing, ReCap outperforms
all leading competitors on an expanded relighting benchmark.

arxiv_record.title: ReCap: Better Gaussian Relighting with Cross-Environment Captures

native_poster_event.abstract: Accurate 3D objects relighting in diverse unseen environments is crucial for realistic virtual object placement. Due to the albedo-lighting ambiguity, existing methods often fall short in producing faithful relights. Without proper constraints, observed training views can be explained by numerous combinations of lighting and material attributes, lacking physical correspondence with the actual environment maps used for relighting. In this work, we present ReCap, treating cross-environment captures as multi-task target to provide the missing supervision that cuts through the entanglement. Specifically, ReCap jointly optimizes multiple lighting representations that share a common set of material attributes. This naturally harmonizes a coherent set of lighting representations around the mutual material attributes, exploiting commonalities and differences across varied object appearances. Such coherence enables physically sound lighting reconstruction and robust material estimation — both essential for accurate relighting. Together with a streamlined shading function and effective post-processing, ReCap outperforms the leading competitor by $3.4$ dB in PSNR on an expanded relighting benchmark.
