C2.justification: Section 4.3 changes from favoring identical views for decoupling to arguing that additional unique views provide greater practical benefit, with a new explanation involving sufficient decoupling and synthetic pose calibration. V2 also explains dual-environment baseline failures and TensoIR's scaling/material limitations, explicitly notes residual chair-color contamination, and discusses pose-alignment requirements and semi-controlled capture.

D1.justification: V2 clarifies the 100-view A/B split construction and documents real-capture alignment using COLMAP poses, SuperGlue correspondence pairs, and transform/scale estimation. It changes code/data availability from a future promise to stated availability. The core hardware and optimization details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same 13 synthetic objects under eight HDR environments. V2 adds two real-capture examples, gnome and teapot from StanfordORB (Figure 8), providing limited coverage beyond synthetic data. Removing the per-object results table does not establish removal of those objects from evaluation.

E2.justification: V1's quantitative comparison contains four Gaussian baselines. V2 retains them and adds multi-light TensoIR with and without ground-truth albedo scaling, plus GShader+ours (Table 2). This substantially broadens the comparison to a relevant NeRF-based competitor and an adapted Gaussian comparator.

E3.justification: V2 expands Table 2 to evaluate ReCap and the existing Gaussian baselines under both single- and dual-environment inputs. It also introduces scaled/unscaled TensoIR evaluation, testing all provided hyperparameter settings and reporting the best results. The 200-view training total, evaluation metrics, and ReCap's 30,000-iteration budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New controls test whether unmodified Gaussian models benefit from dual-environment inputs, whether multi-light querying transfers to GShader, and how TensoIR depends on ground-truth scaling. Figure 8 adds a real-capture feasibility case study. The existing post-processing, shading, regularization, and environment-count ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. Results remain point estimates and averages across objects or environments.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds numerous results and updates existing entries, including ReCap's average relighting PSNR from 25.52 to 25.82. TensoIR newly reports 24.49 with scaling and 23.11 without it. The extra-view ablation changes from 25.52 to 26.25 PSNR, reversing its ordering against the unchanged 26.14 identical-view result. V1's detailed per-object Table 3 is absent from v2.

M1.justification: The core ReCap formulation, shading function, regularizers, lighting representation, and normal estimation remain unchanged. V2 additionally introduces GShader+ours by augmenting GShader with ReCap's multi-light querying (Section 4.2, Table 2), constituting a limited method adaptation.

P1.justification: Section 3.4 is renamed and rewritten, and the comparison narrative is reorganized around single-environment, dual-environment, and qualitative comparisons. Other edits include revised discussion, a corresponding-author designation, and acknowledgments. Most methodological prose and the conclusion remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn with explicit data and gradient flows. Table 2 is substantially expanded and reorganized with training-split and scaling columns. Figures 6 and 7 are rearranged and expanded for TensoIR, the per-object table is removed, retained ablation tables are relocated/renumbered, and Figure 8 adds real-capture examples.

R1.justification: V2 adds StanfordORB and SuperGlue references and sharpens its positioning against TensoIR by discussing ground-truth albedo scaling. Most related-work coverage is retained; reference renumbering does not represent additional changes.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, shading derivation, and loss expressions in Equations (1)-(10) are retained. V2 adds explanatory interpretations but no new formal assumptions, propositions, proofs, or mathematical corrections.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses a central evaluation gap: v1 compared dual-environment ReCap with single-environment Gaussian baselines, whereas v2 adds a multi-light NeRF competitor, input-condition controls, and explicit scaling comparisons. Removing per-object scores reduces diagnostic transparency, but the better-controlled comparisons materially strengthen support for the central empirical claim.

A1.justification: Both readable 10-page PDFs describe the same ReCap work, with matching methods and benchmark foundations. All supplied pages were inspected. Neither PDF includes an appendix; both reference supplementary material that is absent from the supplied files.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Video Frame Interpolation aims to recover realistic missing frames between
observed frames, generating a high-frame-rate video from a low-frame-rate
video. However, without additional guidance, the large motion between frames
makes this problem ill-posed. Event-based Video Frame Interpolation (EVFI)
addresses this challenge by using sparse, high-temporal-resolution event
measurements as motion guidance. This guidance allows EVFI methods to
significantly outperform frame-only methods. However, to date, EVFI methods
have relied on a limited set of paired event-frame training data, severely
limiting their performance and generalization capabilities. In this work, we
overcome the limited data challenge by adapting pre-trained video diffusion
models trained on internet-scale datasets to EVFI. We experimentally validate
our approach on real-world EVFI datasets, including a new one that we
introduce. Our method outperforms existing methods and generalizes across
cameras far better than existing approaches.

arxiv_record.abstract:
We tackle the ill-posed inverse rendering problem in 3D reconstruction with a
Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) approach informed by Physics-Based Rendering (PBR)
theory, named PBR-NeRF. Our method addresses a key limitation in most NeRF and
3D Gaussian Splatting approaches: they estimate view-dependent appearance
without modeling scene materials and illumination. To address this limitation,
we present an inverse rendering (IR) model capable of jointly estimating scene
geometry, materials, and illumination. Our model builds upon recent NeRF-based
IR approaches, but crucially introduces two novel physics-based priors that
better constrain the IR estimation. Our priors are rigorously formulated as
intuitive loss terms and achieve state-of-the-art material estimation without
compromising novel view synthesis quality. Our method is easily adaptable to
other inverse rendering and 3D reconstruction frameworks that require material
estimation. We demonstrate the importance of extending current neural rendering
approaches to fully model scene properties beyond geometry and view-dependent
appearance. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/s3anwu/pbrnerf

arxiv_record.abstract: We introduce Omni-ID, a novel facial representation designed specifically for generative tasks. Omni-ID encodes holistic information about an individual's appearance across diverse expressions and poses within a fixed-size representation. It consolidates information from a varied number of unstructured input images into a structured representation, where each entry represents certain global or local identity features. Our approach uses a few-to-many identity reconstruction training paradigm, where a limited set of input images is used to reconstruct multiple target images of the same individual in various poses and expressions. Section 4.2 replaces the claim of better pose accuracy with an interpretation of similar pose errors as evidence of convergence. Section 4.4 also explains the restricted ablation input counts through diminishing returns.

D1.justification: Appendix A supplies extensive previously unavailable details: feature extraction and aggregation, decoder configurations, optimizers, learning rates, batch sizes, GPU hardware, training resolutions, downstream schedules, and initialization. Figure I documents MFHQ filtering and pose-based sampling. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although conflicting training-step counts and main-text versus appendix ArcFace dimensions leave some settings ambiguous.

E1.justification: v2 adds filtered WebFace21M identities as a controllable-generation test set; v1 used WebFace21M as alternative pretraining data in an ablation. The two downstream tasks, MFHQ coverage, and licensed personalized-generation training data remain. Additional generator backbones extend model settings rather than task coverage.

Table I evaluates IPA-FaceID, IPA-FaceIDPlusV2, IPA-Full, and PuLID; Figure IV also evaluates IPA-Plus and displays InstantID and PhotoMakerV2 comparisons previously only alluded to in v1. Table 1 retains the same controllable-generation comparators.

Section 4.1 changes MTD training from 250K to 200K steps and replaces the explicit ArcFace evaluation-feature description with features citing facenet-pytorch. However, Appendix A.2 reports 250K MTD and 5K flow-matching steps, conflicting with v2's main-text 200K and 10K. These are reported setting differences; actual reruns and exact budgets remain unresolved.

Appendix A adds qualitative findings about token counts, feature aggregation, and injection locations. Appendix B adds template-driven examples and demonstrates transfer of the FLUX-dev-trained representation to Schnell and SD1.5.

E5.justification: Table I newly reports means and standard deviations across identities for personalized generation. v1 provides no corresponding uncertainty reporting. These describe variation across identities, not repeated training runs; neither PDF establishes additional runs or seed-based uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds seven-input MFHQ results, WebFace results, and quantitative personalized-generation comparisons. Examples include Omni-ID's seven-input MFHQ similarity of 0.742 and Table I's 0.8026 ± 0.0421 versus PuLID's 0.7289 ± 0.0572. Previously reported MFHQ entries and Tables 2–3 retain their numbers. arxiv_record.abstract:
Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have expanded
research in video understanding, primarily focusing on high-level tasks such as
video captioning and question-answering. Meanwhile, a smaller body of work
addresses dense, pixel-precise segmentation tasks, which typically involve
category-guided or referral-based object segmentation. Although both directions
are essential for developing models with human-level video comprehension, they
have largely evolved separately, with distinct benchmarks and architectures.
This paper aims to unify these efforts by introducing ViCaS, a new dataset
containing thousands of challenging videos, each annotated with detailed,
human-written captions and temporally consistent, pixel-accurate masks for
multiple objects with phrase grounding. Our benchmark evaluates models on both
holistic/high-level understanding and language-guided, pixel-precise
segmentation. We also present carefully validated evaluation measures and
propose an effective model architecture that can tackle our benchmark. Project

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: a human-annotated grounded-caption dataset, a two-task benchmark, user-study-validated caption scoring and an end-to-end model for both tasks. Expanded data and revised experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the frame-count ablations as evidence that the benchmark requires temporal context and adds explanations of the newer comparisons. It retains the interpretation that captioning helps segmentation. However, deleting supplementary Section E removes v1's explicit qualification that automatic mask propagation introduces annotation errors.

D1.justification: Training-budget documentation changes, while preprocessing, token counts, learning rates, hardware and project access information largely remain. v3 introduces a reproducibility inconsistency: its prose describes segmentation training using only ViCaS, but supplementary Table 5 still lists MeViS and Ref-YTVOS. Their actual removal from training cannot be established.

E1.justification: Section 3.1 expands ViCaS from Oops fail videos alone to Oops, UVO and Kinetics-700, broadening coverage beyond accidental events. Both captioning and language-guided instance segmentation remain. The dataset grows from 7,331 to 20,416 videos.

E2.justification: The benchmark adds VideoLISA and replaces standalone LLaVA-NeXT captioning comparisons with LLaVA-OneVision and MiniCPM-o 2.6; LMPM and DsHmp remain. A revised LLaVA-NeXT segmentation comparison appears in Table 3. The scoring study's Table 2 removes Distiluse-B, BCE Rerank.-B, MiniLM and QNLI Electra-B.

E3.justification: Train/validation/test sizes change from 5,131/1,100/1,100 to 14,516/2,950/2,950. Supplementary training tables change the reported stage-3 batch size from 64 to 128 and iterations from 15,718 to 10,752. Captioning comparisons introduce off-the-shelf zero-shot models, and ablations introduce different frame-count settings. CA and segmentation metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 3 extends temporal-context analysis to one-, two- and four-frame inputs, replacing v1's direct slow-fast pooling toggle. Single-task versus joint-training ablations remain, and the LLaVA-NeXT comparison is incorporated into this table. The caption-scoring robustness study retains its procedure with fewer comparison methods.

E5.justification: Human-score filtering, Pearson-correlation calculations and pooling across reference captions are unchanged. Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: The reported Llama3-based model changes from 22.0 validation and 13.5 test mAP in v1 to 20.5 and 16.5 in v3; changed datasets and settings prevent interpreting these as direct performance gains or losses. Dataset statistics and ablation scores are extensively revised. v3 supplies LMPM and DsHmp test scores where v1 had blank cells. Retained Table 2 scores match.

M1.justification: The architecture and procedure remain the same: slow-fast video features, an MLLM generating per-object SEG tokens, a SAM2-initialized segmentation network, and three-stage training. Llama3-8B, emphasized in v3, was already evaluated in v1.

P1.justification: The introduction and acknowledgements are shortened, selected related-work and experimental paragraphs are rewritten, and supplementary Section E is deleted. Appendix citation placeholders are resolved. The main section sequence and most methodological explanations remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 3's word cloud and histograms are redrawn with revised axes. Table 3 gains explicit configuration columns, benchmark tables lose the LLM column, and several tables change row membership. Appendix review headers and line numbers disappear. Core illustrative figures remain; v3 also incorrectly labels the supplementary test-results table as validation results.

R1.justification: Sections 2.2 and 5.1 add focused discussion of recent LLM-based video segmentation, including VideoLISA and more detailed treatment of the already-cited VISA. New references include LLaVA-OneVision and MiniCPM, while several audio and multimodal references are removed. The overall holistic-versus-pixel-level research framing remains.

T1.justification: The feature-shape definitions, slow-fast token-count expression and caption-scoring calculations are retained. Neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs that are added, removed or revised.

improvement.justification: Broadening the Oops-only benchmark with UVO and Kinetics-700 addresses a substantial coverage limitation. Newer comparison models, temporal-context ablations and more complete test comparisons strengthen the paper's central dataset and benchmark contribution. The contradictory training-data descriptions, incorrect Table 7 caption and removed mask-error caveat weaken reporting, but the broader coverage and stronger benchmark validation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ViCaS and Video-LLaVA-Seg. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and included supplementary sections support reliable comparison, including identification of incomplete tables and internal inconsistencies.

after.justification: v3 retains the original user study and reports revised dataset statistics, ablations and benchmark results, including supplementary test results.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Indoor scene texture synthesis has garnered significant interest due to its
important potential applications in virtual reality, digital media and creative
arts. Existing diffusion-model-based researches either rely on per-view
inpainting techniques, which are plagued by severe cross-view inconsistencies
and conspicuous seams, or adopt optimization-based approaches that involve
substantial computational overhead. In this work, we present RoomPainter, a
framework that seamlessly integrates efficiency and consistency to achieve
high-fidelity texturing of indoor scenes. The core of RoomPainter features a
zero-shot technique that effectively adapts a 2D diffusion model for
3D-consistent texture synthesis, along with a two-stage generation strategy
that ensures both global and local consistency. Specifically, we introduce
Attention-Guided Multi-View Integrated Sampling (MVIS) combined with a
neighbor-integrated attention mechanism for zero-shot texture map generation.
Using the MVIS, we firstly generate texture map for the entire room to ensure
global consistency, then adopt its variant, namely Attention-Guided Multi-View
Integrated Repaint Sampling
  (MVRS) to repaint individual instances within the room, thereby further
enhancing local consistency and addressing the occlusion problem. Experiments
demonstrate that RoomPainter achieves superior performance for indoor scene
texture synthesis in visual quality, global consistency and generation
efficiency.

arxiv_record.abstract:
We introduce a single-view reconstruction technique of volumetric fields in
which multiple light scattering effects are omnipresent, such as in clouds. We
model the unknown distribution of volumetric fields using an unconditional
diffusion model trained on a novel benchmark dataset comprising 1,000
synthetically simulated volumetric density fields. The neural diffusion model
is trained on the latent codes of a novel, diffusion-friendly, monoplanar
representation. The generative model is used to incorporate a tailored
parametric diffusion posterior sampling technique into different reconstruction
tasks. A physically-based differentiable volume renderer is employed to provide
gradients with respect to light transport in the latent space. This stands in
contrast to classic NeRF approaches and makes the reconstructions better
aligned with observed data. Through various experiments, we demonstrate
single-view reconstruction of volumetric clouds at a previously unattainable
quality.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Recent open-world representation learning approaches have leveraged CLIP to
enable zero-shot 3D object recognition. However, performance on real point
clouds with occlusions still falls short due to unrealistic pretraining
settings. Additionally, these methods incur high inference costs because they
rely on Transformer's attention modules. In this paper, we make two
contributions to address these limitations. First, we propose occlusion-aware
text-image-point cloud pretraining to reduce the training-testing domain gap.
From 52K synthetic 3D objects, our framework generates nearly 630K partial
point clouds for pretraining, consistently improving real-world recognition
performances of existing popular 3D networks. Second, to reduce computational
requirements, we introduce DuoMamba, a two-stream linear state space model
tailored for point clouds. By integrating two space-filling curves with 1D
convolutions, DuoMamba effectively models spatial dependencies between point
tokens, offering a powerful alternative to Transformer. When pretrained with
our framework, DuoMamba surpasses current state-of-the-art methods while
reducing latency and FLOPs, highlighting the potential of our approach for
real-world applications. Our code and data are available at
https://ndkhanh360.github.io/project-occtip.
arxiv_record.authors: Khanh Nguyen, Ghulam Mubashar Hassan, Ajmal Mian
arxiv_record.title:
Occlusion-aware Text-Image-Point Cloud Pretraining for Open-World 3D
  Object Recognition

arxiv_record.abstract:
In this work we study Weakly Supervised Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding
(WSTVG), a challenging task of localizing subjects spatio-temporally in videos
using only textual queries and no bounding box supervision. Inspired by recent
advances in vision-language foundation models, we investigate their utility for
WSTVG, leveraging their zero-shot grounding capabilities. However, we find that
a simple adaptation lacks essential spatio-temporal grounding abilities. To
bridge this gap, we introduce Tubelet Referral Grounding (TRG), which connects
textual queries to tubelets to enable spatio-temporal predictions. Despite its
promise, TRG struggles with compositional action understanding and dense scene
scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose STPro, a novel progressive
learning framework with two key modules: (1) Sub-Action Temporal Curriculum
Learning (SA-TCL), which incrementally builds compositional action
understanding, and (2) Congestion-Guided Spatial Curriculum Learning (CG-SCL),
which adapts the model to complex scenes by spatially increasing task
difficulty. STPro achieves state-of-the-art results on three benchmark
datasets, with improvements of 1.0% on VidSTG-Declarative and 3.0% on
HCSTVG-v1.
arxiv_record.authors: Aaryan Garg, Akash Kumar, Yogesh S Rawat
arxiv_record.title:
STPro: Spatial and Temporal Progressive Learning for Weakly Supervised
  Spatio-Temporal Grounding

Inspired by recent advances in vision-language foundation models, we investigate their utility for WSTVG, leveraging their zero-shot grounding capabilities. However, we find that a simple adaptation lacks essential spatio-temporal grounding abilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce Tubelet Referral Grounding (TRG), which connects textual queries to tubelets to enable spatio-temporal predictions. Despite its promise, TRG struggles with compositional action understanding and dense scene scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose STPro, a novel progressive learning framework with two key modules: (1) Sub-Action Temporal Curriculum Learning (SA-TCL), which incrementally builds compositional action understanding, and (2) Congestion-Guided Spatial Curriculum Learning (CG-SCL), which adapts the model to complex scenes by spatially increasing task difficulty. STPro achieves state-of-the-art results on three benchmark datasets, with improvements of 1.0% on VidSTG-Declarative and 3.0% on HCSTVG-v1. Code and models will be released publicly.

P1.justification: Sections 2–5 undergo broad paragraph rewriting and compression, covering related work, baseline motivation, method explanations, implementation and experimental discussion. arxiv_record.abstract: Recently, vision-language models (e.g. CLIP) have demonstrated remarkable performance in zero-shot anomaly detection (ZSAD). By leveraging auxiliary data during training, these models can directly perform cross-category anomaly detection on target datasets, such as detecting defects on industrial product surfaces or identifying tumors in organ tissues. Existing approaches typically construct text prompts through either manual design or the optimization of learnable prompt vectors. However, these methods face several challenges: 1) handcrafted prompts require extensive expert knowledge and trial-and-error; 2) single-form learnable prompts struggle to capture complex anomaly semantics; and 3) an unconstrained prompt space limits generalization to unseen categories. To address these issues, we propose Bayesian Prompt Flow Learning (Bayes-PFL), which models the prompt space as a learnable probability distribution from a Bayesian perspective. Specifically, a prompt flow module is designed to learn both image-specific and image-agnostic distributions, which are jointly utilized to regularize the text prompt space and improve the model's generalization on unseen categories. These learned distributions are then sampled to generate diverse text prompts, effectively covering the prompt space. Additionally, a residual cross-model attention (RCA) module is introduced to better align dynamic text embeddings with fine-grained image features. Extensive experiments on 15 industrial and medical datasets demonstrate our method's superior performance. The code is available at https://github.com/xiaozhen228/Bayes-PFL.

By leveraging auxiliary data during training, these models can directly perform cross-category anomaly detection on target datasets, such as detecting defects on industrial product surfaces or identifying tumors in organ tissues. To address these issues, we propose Bayesian Prompt Flow Learning (Bayes-PFL), which models the prompt space as a learnable probability distribution from a Bayesian perspective. Specifically, a prompt flow module is designed to learn both image-specific and image-agnostic distributions, which are jointly utilized to regularize the text prompt space and enhance model's generalization on unseen categories. These learned distributions are then sampled to generate diverse text prompts, effectively covering the prompt space. Additionally, a residual cross-attention (RCA) module is introduced to better align dynamic text embeddings with fine-grained image features. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in ZSAD across 15 public industrial and medical anomaly detection datasets. Code will be released upon acceptance.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: Bayesian prompt distributions, ISD/IAD modeling, RCA alignment, and superior zero-shot performance across 15 datasets. Additional supporting evidence does not materially alter these claims.

C2.justification: The supplement adds substantive interpretations of distribution flexibility, hyperparameter complexity, overfitting trajectories, and embedding clusters. It also discusses speed–accuracy and memory tradeoffs against baselines. Appendix E explicitly identifies sampling overhead and CLIP's limited textual and fine-grained visual capabilities as limitations.

D1.justification: Appendices A and C supply previously unavailable sampling pseudocode, architecture details, random prompt selection during training, cosine scheduling, warm-up, early stopping, focal-loss settings, baseline code provenance, and dataset construction details such as RSDD cropping and DAGM reannotation. The abstract adds a code-access link. These are documented disclosures, not evidence that all underlying procedures changed.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same seven industrial and eight medical datasets for the same classification and segmentation tasks. Appendix C adds dataset descriptions and preparation details, without establishing changed dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The five external comparators remain WinCLIP, APRIL-GAN, CLIP-AD, AnomalyCLIP, and AdaCLIP. Appendix B.2 adds an explicitly evaluated Gaussian-distribution alternative to the proposed prompt-flow model in Figure 7, extending the methodological comparison.

E3.justification: The main training-transfer protocol and default settings are retained. The supplement substantially expands evaluated configurations through separate training/inference prompt controls, B/K/P/Q sweeps, three CLIP backbone variants, and input resolutions of 336, 518, and 700 pixels. Table 7 also introduces comparative GPU-memory measurement.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds single-prompt versus ensemble controls, Gaussian versus flow modeling, hyperparameter and backbone/resolution ablations, and embedding visualizations. Figure 9 expands the existing test-AP comparison with training AP and training/test-loss trajectories, providing additional evidence about overfitting.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five random seeds and retain Table 3's mean±standard-deviation reporting. Appendix A.1 additionally states that five experimental rounds are averaged, clarifying aggregation across runs beyond v1's statement about category averaging. An increase in run count is not reported.

E6.justification: The supplement adds substantial numerical and qualitative results, including category-level scores, configuration comparisons, and baseline runtime/memory measurements. For example, new Table 5 reports APRIL-GAN pixel AP of 37.4 with single prompts at both stages versus 40.8 with ensembles. Main Tables 1–4 retain their results apart from equivalent rounding.

M1.justification: Section 3.5 corrects the stated text-branch anomaly score to use the original text embeddings Z^t instead of RCA-refined F^t, bringing the formula into agreement with Figure 2. This is a localized revision of the written inference rule; the prompt banks, ISD/IAD flows, RCA architecture, and overall loss are retained.

P1.justification: The main section order and narrative are retained, with grammatical corrections, clearer notation, revised cross-references, and acknowledgments. The added material is organized into Appendices A–E; the existing main text is not extensively reorganized.

P2.justification: v3 adds Algorithm 1, Tables 5–13, and Figures 7–40, including sensitivity plots, diagnostic trajectories, embedding visualizations, category-level tables, and extensive segmentation galleries. Existing main figures and tables largely retain their designs, with limited annotation and layout adjustments.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to Kanade and Gumaste's BrainMRI work, Qu et al.'s shift-equivalence study, and YOLOv10. It expands baseline descriptions and explains dataset-processing differences from VCP-CLIP. The principal positioning relative to existing prompt-based anomaly detectors remains.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 corrects the marginal likelihood from 'tractable' to 'intractable' in the variational-inference justification. Appendix B.2 adds the Gaussian alternative's KL-divergence objective in Equation 19. The principal Bayesian and normalizing-flow derivations remain.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves an important deficiency of the supplied v1: implementation, dataset preparation, and supplementary analyses were referenced but unavailable. The added details substantially improve reproducibility, while controlled Gaussian/flow comparisons, sensitivity studies, category-level results, and explicit limitations make the central claims more assessable. Headline performance remains unchanged. Some protocol ambiguity persists, particularly the unspecified validation split for early stopping, but the overall gains in documentation and evidential support are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Bayes-PFL work and support reliable text, equation, table, and figure comparison. The supplied v1 ends after its references despite referring to appendices; v3 includes Appendices A–E. Their contents can therefore be assessed as newly documented material.

after.justification: The original experiments are retained, and the appendices report additional controlled comparisons, sensitivity studies, efficiency measurements, and category-level results.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original anomaly-detection experiments across 15 industrial and medical datasets, including benchmark comparisons and ablations.

arxiv_record.abstract: Despite their success, Segment Anything Models (SAMs) experience significant performance drops on severely degraded, low-quality images, limiting their effectiveness in real-world scenarios. To address this, we propose GleSAM, which utilizes Generative Latent space Enhancement to boost robustness on low-quality images, thus enabling generalization across various image qualities. Specifically, we adapt the concept of latent diffusion to SAM-based segmentation frameworks and perform the generative diffusion process in the latent space of SAM to reconstruct high-quality representation, thereby improving segmentation. Additionally, we introduce two techniques to improve compatibility between the pre-trained diffusion model and the segmentation framework. Our method can be applied to pre-trained SAM and SAM2 with only minimal additional learnable parameters, allowing for efficient optimization. We also construct the LQSeg dataset with a greater diversity of degradation types and levels for training and evaluating the model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GleSAM significantly improves segmentation robustness on complex degradations while maintaining generalization to clear images. Furthermore, GleSAM also performs well on unseen degradations, underscoring the versatility of our approach and dataset.
arxiv_record.authors: Guangqian Guo, Yong Guo, Xuehui Yu, Wenbo Li, Yaoxing Wang, Shan Gao
arxiv_record.title: Segment Any-Quality Images with Generative Latent Space Enhancement

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: generative latent enhancement for SAM/SAM2, FDA and CRE, LQSeg, and robustness across degraded, clear, and unseen-degradation images. The additional experiments support these existing claims without redefining their central scope.

C2.justification: Section 7.3 newly attributes noisy-box robustness to enhanced latent representations reducing noise-induced ambiguity. Section 7.4 connects increasing point counts with reduced prompt ambiguity and performance gains. These extend the interpretation to prompt conditions, although Figure 8 does not support the accompanying claim of superiority at every point count. No substantive limitations discussion is added.

D1.justification: Sections 8–9 add degradation-generation settings, including kernel choices, parameter ranges, noise probabilities, and JPEG quality factors. They also disclose T=1000, prompt-generation procedures, and training/inference pseudocode. The abstract adds a code/dataset release link. These substantially fill documentation gaps; they do not establish changes to the previously used method or data-generation procedure.

E1.justification: V3 adds evaluation on real driving imagery from BDD-100K, extending coverage beyond the synthetic degradation benchmarks in v1. It also evaluates ground-truth and perturbed bounding-box prompts, broadening input conditions beyond the earlier point-prompt experiments. The original training and evaluation datasets remain.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the original comparisons remains unchanged: SAM, SAM2, RobustSAM, and the PromptIR/DiffBIR restoration pipelines. Added experiments use existing comparator families. The ViT and Hiera variants are model configurations, while newly cited DN-DETR supplies a box-noise convention rather than an evaluated segmentation baseline.

E3.justification: Sections 7.2–7.4 add systematic evaluations across ViT-B/L/H and Hiera-T/S/B/L, point counts from 1 to 10, and ground-truth versus noisy boxes with noise scale 0.2. The original three-click default, metrics, optimizer, batch size, and training budgets remain unchanged. These are substantial additional protocols.

E4.justification: V3 retains the original component, decoder, channel-expansion, gamma, LoRA-rank, and degradation-level analyses. It adds backbone and prompt sensitivity studies in Tables 11–13 and Figure 8, further feature-reconstruction comparisons, and extensive qualitative cases under unseen degradations and on COCO. These broaden the evidence about robustness and generalization.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, performance error bars, or significance tests. The added tables and curves continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice. Noise standard deviations in v3 describe degradation generation, not uncertainty in experimental results.

E6.justification: Tables 1–9 retain their numerical results. New Table 10 reports BDD-100K IoU of 0.8775 for GleSAM versus 0.8650 for SAM, and 0.9087 for GleSAM2 versus 0.8891 for SAM2. Tables 11–13 and Figure 8 add backbone and prompt results; Figure 8 includes a one-point case where GleSAM2 trails SAM2. These are additional evaluations, not improved scores for the original experiments.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.4 retain the same single-step latent denoising, FDA scaling, CRE weight replication, LoRA adaptation, and two-stage training with unchanged losses. Algorithms 1–2 document the existing procedure; the additional backbone evaluations do not establish a method change.

P1.justification: The retained abstract, introduction, method, experimental discussion, and conclusion are largely unchanged in wording and organization. arxiv_record.abstract: High-resolution perception of visual details is crucial for daily tasks. Current vision pre-training, however, is still limited to low resolutions (e.g., 378 x 378 pixels) due to the quadratic cost of processing larger images. We introduce PS3 that scales CLIP-style vision pre-training to 4K resolution with a near-constant cost. Instead of contrastive learning on global image representation, PS3 is pre-trained by selectively processing local regions and contrasting them with local detailed captions, enabling high-resolution representation learning with greatly reduced computational overhead. The pre-trained PS3 is able to both encode the global image at low resolution and selectively process local high-resolution regions based on their saliency or relevance to a text prompt. When applying PS3 to multi-modal LLM (MLLM), the resulting model, named VILA-HD, significantly improves high-resolution visual perception compared to baselines without high-resolution vision pre-training such as AnyRes and S^2 while using up to 4.3x fewer tokens. PS3 also unlocks appealing scaling properties of VILA-HD, including scaling up resolution for free and scaling up test-time compute for better performance. Compared to state of the arts, PS3 and VILA-HD outperform previous vision encoders (e.g., SigLIP2 and Perception Encoder) and MLLMs (e.g., NVILA and Qwen2.5-VL) respectively across multiple benchmarks and achieve better efficiency than latest token pruning approaches. Finally, we find current benchmarks do not require 4K-resolution perception, which motivates us to propose 4KPro, a new benchmark of image QA at 4K resolution, on which VILA-HD outperforms all previous MLLMs, including a 16.1% improvement over GPT-4o and a 7.5% improvement and 1.67x speedup over Qwen2.5-VL.

arxiv_record.abstract: Modeling label correlations has always played a pivotal role in multi-label image classification (MLC), attracting significant attention from researchers. However, recent studies have overemphasized co-occurrence relationships among labels, which can lead to overfitting risk on this overemphasis, resulting in suboptimal models. To tackle this problem, we advocate for balancing correlative and discriminative relationships among labels to mitigate the risk of overfitting and enhance model performance. To this end, we propose the Multi-Label Visual Prompt Tuning framework, a novel and parameter-efficient method that groups classes into multiple class subsets according to label co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity relationships, and then models them respectively to balance the two relationships. In this work, since each group contains multiple classes, multiple prompt tokens are adopted within Vision Transformer (ViT) to capture the correlation or discriminative label relationship within each group, and effectively learn correlation or discriminative representations for class subsets. On the other hand, each group contains multiple group-aware visual representations that may correspond to multiple classes, and the mixture of experts (MoE) model can cleverly assign them from the group-aware to the label-aware, adaptively obtaining label-aware representation, which is more conducive to classification. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show that our proposed approach achieves competitive results and outperforms SOTA methods on multiple pre-trained models.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about balancing label relationships, parameter-efficient adaptation and group-aware MoE representations.

C2.justification: v2 hypothesizes that random grouping partially balances correlation and discrimination, and interprets conditional-error results as stronger correlation capture with reduced over-inference. These refine the existing explanation without changing its central rationale.

D1.justification: The supplement supplies clustering steps, explicit group assignments, pseudocode, ASL parameters λ0=2 and λ1=0, dataset splits and VG256 processing details. These substantially expand reproducibility information previously absent from the supplied v1, without demonstrating changes to retained experiments.

E1.justification: v2 adds Objects365, covering 365 everyday-object categories, while retaining VOC07, COCO, NUS-WIDE and VG256. This extends benchmark coverage within the existing natural-image multi-label classification task.

E2.justification: The original comparison methods remain, and Objects365 uses the same VPT, GateVPT and E2VPT baselines. New COCO comparisons evaluate random grouping in Table 8 and group-level gating against label-level gating in Table 7.

E3.justification: New protocols include conditional TPR/FPR evaluation on COCO label pairs with co-occurrence probability above 0.2, and Objects365 evaluation at 224×224 using validation images as the test set. Existing training settings remain unchanged; newly specified splits for retained datasets are disclosures.

E4.justification: v2 adds conditional-error analysis, per-class grouping and MoE effects, random-grouping and gating ablations, group heatmaps and expert-weight examples. Figures 10–11 also extend existing group/expert sensitivity analyses with CF1 and OF1 results.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or error bars. The averages in supplementary Tables 7–8 aggregate pretrained models rather than report replication or uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Original results remain unchanged, but substantial additional results appear. Table 6 reports Objects365 mAP of 52.2 for ML-VPT versus 49.3 for VPT with DINOv2/B at 224×224. Figure 12 reports higher conditional TPR for 88.4% and lower conditional FPR for 85.3% of selected label pairs; further ablation and per-class results are added.

M1.justification: CO/DC grouping, masked group prompts, label-specific MoE gating, dual ASL classifiers and averaged predictions are retained. The supplementary descriptions elaborate this procedure without establishing an implemented method change.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are nearly unchanged. v2 appends organized supplementary method and experiment explanations, with limited citation-related reflow rather than extensive rewriting of the existing paper.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–9, Figures 8–14 and Algorithm 1, substantially expanding the visual presentation. Figures 10–11 repeat existing mAP panels alongside new CF1/OF1 panels; the original tables and figures retain their displays.

R1.justification: v2 adds Han et al. on VPT versus full fine-tuning, Shao et al. on Objects365, and von Luxburg on spectral clustering. All 58 earlier references remain; the central research positioning is retained.

T1.justification: Section 7.1 adds the normalized-Laplacian definition and constrained trace-minimization formulation of spectral clustering; Section 7.2 supplies explicit loss expressions. The main mathematical development is retained, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: The supplement substantially strengthens the central grouping rationale through random-grouping controls, conditional-error analysis and per-class ablations, while supplying previously absent reproducibility details. Objects365 broadens supporting evidence. Local errors temper these gains: Algorithm 1 partitions G+ for both branches, and Section 8.3 claims an 8.7-point maximum Objects365 mAP gap although Table 6 gives 7.7. These documentation problems do not outweigh the stronger empirical scrutiny and methodological transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ML-VPT work and are fully readable. v1 ends after the references; v2 adds supplementary Sections 7–8. The main text, equations, tables and figures can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds Objects365 results, further ablations, conditional-error analyses and visualizations.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments on four datasets, component ablations, computational comparisons and prediction case studies.
